).

In formal geometry we care about infinitesimal neighborhoods, which we will call formal thickenings. Many example of formal thickenings are obtained via the formal completion of a map (Definition
1.3.8
).

To manipulate these objects, we need the construction of the “de Rham” and “reduced” stacks. Essentially, the de Rham stack of
X
is the formal completion of the map
X\to\star
(thanks to Proposition
1.3.11
) and the reduced functor is the left adjoint to the de Rham functor.

The idea is that we want to make sense of “infinitesimally close” points, which translates into saying that the “difference” of infinitesimally close points is nilpotent.

Definition 1.3.6
.

An algebra
A\in\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{\leq 0}}
is called
reduced
if it is discrete
37
37

37

A cdga is called discrete if it is concentrated in degree
0
and has no non-zero nilpotent element. In other words,
\mathrm{Nil}(A)=0
where
\mathrm{Nil}(A)
denotes the ideal of nilpotent elements in
A
. We denote by
(\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{\leq 0}})^{\mathrm{red}}
the full sub-category of
\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{\leq 0}}
of reduced algebras.

Lemma 1.3.7
.

The inclusion
i:(\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{\leq 0}})^{\mathrm{red}}\to\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{\leq 0}}
admits a left adjoint:

(-)^{\mathrm{red}}:\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{\leq 0}}\to(\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{\leq 0}})^{\mathrm{red}}

defined by:

A^{\mathrm{red}}:={\mathchoice{\raisebox{4.32pt}{$\displaystyle{H^{0}(A)}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-4.32pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathrm{Nil}(H^{0}(A))}$}}{\raisebox{4.07pt}{$\textstyle{H^{0}(A)}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-4.07pt}{$\textstyle{\mathrm{Nil}(H^{0}(A))}$}}{\raisebox{3.12001pt}{$\scriptstyle{H^{0}(A)}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.12001pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathrm{Nil}(H^{0}(A))}$}}{\raisebox{2.33333pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{H^{0}(A)}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.33333pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{Nil}(H^{0}(A))}$}}}

We drop the
i
from the notations so that the unit of the adjunction induces a map:

A\to A^{\mathrm{red}}

One of the important notion in formal geometry is the formal neighborhood of a map
f:X\to Y
which essentially is the stack whose points are points of
Y
which are infinitesimally close to points of
X
.

Definition 1.3.8
.

The formal completion of a map
f:X\to Y
, denoted by
\widehat{Y_{X}}\in\mathbf{dSt}^{\mathrm{afp}}
, is defined by sending an almost finitely presented algebra
A\in\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{\leq 0}}
to
\widehat{Y_{X}}(A)
, defined as the space of all commutative diagrams:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Spec}(A^{\mathrm{red}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Spec}(A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}

In other words, it is defined as the space:

\widehat{Y_{X}}(A):=\Map\left(\mathbf{Spec}(A),Y\right)\times_{\Map\left(\mathbf{Spec}(A^{\mathrm{red}}),Y\right)}\Map\left(\mathbf{Spec}(A^{\mathrm{red}}),X\right)

These are the points of
Y
that are “infinitesimally closed” to a point of
X
where two points
x,y\in Y(A)
are infinitesimally close
38
38

38

For example if
A:=k[\epsilon]
, with
\epsilon^{2}=0
, then a
k[\epsilon]
-point is a tangent vector of
Y
. Two such points are then infinitesimally close if they have the same underlying
k
-point in
Y
.
if they have the same image under
Y(A)\to Y(A^{\mathrm{red}})
.

Following the idea of the definition of the formal completion, we want
Y(A^{\mathrm{red}})
to represent the equivalence classes of points for the equivalence relation “being infinitesimally close”. Precomposing by the reduction functor, we get a new functor (see
[
CPT+17
, Section 2.1]
):

i^{*}:\mathbf{dSt}^{\mathrm{afp}}\to(\mathbf{dSt}^{\mathrm{afp}})^{\mathrm{red}}

where
(\mathbf{dSt}^{\mathrm{afp}})^{\mathrm{red}}
denotes the
\infty
-category of derived stacks over the category of connective reduced almost finitely presented algebras.

((\mathrm{cdga}^{\leq 0,\mathrm{afp}})^{\mathrm{red}})^{\mathrm{op}}

We have that
i^{*}
possesses both a right adjoint
i_{*}
and a left adjoint
i_{!}
satisfying:

–

i_{*}\simeq((-)^{\mathrm{red}})^{*}
, so that
i_{*}(\mathbf{Spec}(A))\simeq\mathbf{Spec}(A^{\mathrm{red}})
.

–

i_{*}
and
i_{!}
are fully-faithful.

–

i^{*}\simeq((-)^{\mathrm{red}})_{!}
.

Definition 1.3.9

(
[
CPT+17
, Definition 2.1.3]
)
.

Let
X\in\mathbf{dSt}^{\mathrm{afp}}
be a derived stack.

–

The
de Rham stack
of
X
denoted
X_{\mathrm{DR}}
is defined as:

(-)_{\mathrm{DR}}:=i_{*}i^{*}:\mathbf{dSt}^{\mathrm{afp}}\to\mathbf{dSt}^{\mathrm{afp}}

The unit of the adjunction induces natural maps
X\to X_{\mathrm{DR}}
. Moreover we have
X_{\mathrm{DR}}(A)=X(A^{\mathrm{red}})
.

–

The
reduced stack
of
X
denoted
X_{\mathrm{red}}
is defined as:

(-)_{\mathrm{red}}:=i_{!}i^{*}:\mathbf{dSt}^{\mathrm{afp}}\to\mathbf{dSt}^{\mathrm{afp}}

The counit of the adjunction induces natural maps
X_{\mathrm{red}}\to X
. Moreover we have
\mathbf{Spec}(A)_{\mathrm{red}}=\mathbf{Spec}(A^{\mathrm{red}})
.

Proposition 1.3.10
.

We have that
i_{*}
and
i_{!}
are fully-faithful and therefore the unit
\mathrm{id}\to i^{*}i_{!}
and the counit
i^{*}i_{*}\to\mathrm{id}
are object wise equivalences. This implies that
i_{!}i^{*}
is left adjoint to
i_{*}i^{*}
and in particular, this shows that
(-)_{\mathrm{DR}}
is right adjoint to
(-)_{\mathrm{red}}
.

Proposition 1.3.11
.

The formal completion of
f:X\to Y
is part of the pullback square:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{Y_{X}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{\mathrm{DR}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{\mathrm{DR}}}

Proof.

By definition the space of
A
-points in
\widehat{Y_{X}}
is:

\begin{split}\widehat{Y_{X}}(A)\simeq&\Map\left(\mathbf{Spec}(A),Y\right)\times_{\Map\left(\mathbf{Spec}(A^{\mathrm{red}}),Y\right)}\Map\left(\mathbf{Spec}(A^{\mathrm{red}}),X\right)\\
\simeq&\Map\left(\mathbf{Spec}(A),Y\right)\times_{\Map\left(\mathbf{Spec}(A)_{\mathrm{red}},Y\right)}\Map\left(\mathbf{Spec}(A)_{\mathrm{red}},X\right)\\
\simeq&\Map\left(\mathbf{Spec}(A),Y\right)\times_{\Map\left(\mathbf{Spec}(A),Y_{\mathrm{DR}}\right)}\Map\left(\mathbf{Spec}(A),X_{\mathrm{DR}}\right)\\
\simeq&\Map\left(\mathbf{Spec}(A),Y\times_{Y_{\mathrm{DR}}}X_{\mathrm{DR}}\right)\\
\simeq&\left(Y\times_{Y_{\mathrm{DR}}}X_{\mathrm{DR}}\right)(A)\end{split}

∎

Corollary 1.3.12
.

X_{\mathrm{DR}}
is the formal completion of the terminal morphism
X\to\star
:

X_{\mathrm{DR}}\simeq\widehat{\star_{X}}

Corollary 1.3.13
.

Consider a cone
X_{1}\times_{X}X_{2}
over a pullback
Y_{1}\times_{Y}\times Y_{2}
induced by compatible maps
X_{1}\to Y_{1}
,
X\to Y
and
X_{2}\to Y_{2}
. Then we have an equivalence:

\widehat{\left(Y_{1}\times_{Y}Y_{2}\right)_{X_{1}\times_{X}X_{2}}}\simeq\widehat{(Y_{1})_{X_{1}}}\times_{\widehat{Y_{X}}}\widehat{(Y_{2})_{X_{2}}}

Proof.

\begin{split}\widehat{\left(Y_{1}\times_{Y}Y_{2}\right)_{X_{1}\times_{X}X_{2}}}\simeq&\left(Y_{1}\times_{Y}Y_{2}\right)\times_{\left(Y_{1}\times_{Y}Y_{2}\right)_{\mathrm{DR}}}\left(X_{1}\times_{X}X_{2}\right)_{\mathrm{DR}}\\
\simeq&\left(Y_{1}\times_{Y}Y_{2}\right)\times_{(Y_{1})_{\mathrm{DR}}\times_{Y_{\mathrm{DR}}}(Y_{2})_{\mathrm{DR}}}\left((X_{1})_{\mathrm{DR}}\times_{X_{\mathrm{DR}}}(X_{2})_{\mathrm{DR}}\right)\\
\simeq&\left(Y_{1}\times_{(Y_{1})_{\mathrm{DR}}}(X_{1})_{\mathrm{DR}}\right)\times_{Y\times_{Y_{\mathrm{DR}}}X_{\mathrm{DR}}}\left(Y_{2}\times_{(Y_{2})_{\mathrm{DR}}}(X_{2})_{\mathrm{DR}}\right)\\
\simeq&\widehat{(Y_{1})_{X_{1}}}\times_{\widehat{Y_{X}}}\widehat{(Y_{2})_{X_{2}}}\end{split}

∎

Proposition 1.3.14

(
[
CPT+17
, Proposition 2.1.4]
)
.

We have the following:

(1)

X_{\mathrm{DR}}
is a formal derived stack.

(2)

If
Y
is a formal derived stack, then for any map
f:X\to Y
the formal completion
\widehat{Y_{f}}
is a formal derived stack.

Taking the de Rham stack forget about infinitesimally closed points and therefore, forgets about the “tangent directions” of the stack.

Lemma 1.3.15

(
[
CPT+17
, Lemma 2.1.10]
)
.

The cotangent complex of a de Rham stack exists and we have:

p^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X_{\mathrm{DR}}}\simeq 0

where
p:X\to X_{\mathrm{DR}}
is the natural projection.

Therefore the tangent complex, and the de Rham stack are complementary informations. We will see in the rest of this section that among formal stacks,
X_{\mathrm{DR}}
and
\mathbb{T}_{X}

characterize

X
in the sens that if
X
and
Y
are formal stacks such that
X
and
Y
have the “same” de Rham stacks and tangent complexes, then they are equivalent as stacks. In the rest of this section, we are going to assume that
X
and
Y
have a tangent complex.

Definition 1.3.16
.

A map
f:X\to Y
of derived stacks is called a
nil-equivalence
if it induces an equivalence
f_{\mathrm{red}}:X_{\mathrm{red}}\to Y_{\mathrm{red}}
(or equivalently an equivalence
f_{\mathrm{DR}}:X_{\mathrm{DR}}\to Y_{\mathrm{DR}}
).

Definition 1.3.17
.

A morphism
f:X\to Y
is called
formally étale
if it induces an equivalence:

\mathbb{T}_{X}\overset{\sim}{\to}f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{Y}

Definition 1.3.18
.

We define a
formal thickening
of a formal stack
X
as either:

–

A
formal pre-stack
,
Y\in\mathbf{dpSt}^{\mathrm{afp}}
, together with a nil-equivalence
f:X\to Y
. The category of such thickenings will be denoted
\mathbf{Thick}^{\mathrm{pre}}(X)
.

–

A
formal stack
,
Y\in\mathbf{dSt}^{\mathrm{afp}}
, together with a nil-equivalence
f:X\to Y
. The category of such thickenings will be denoted
\mathbf{Thick}(X)
.

The stackification
\mathbf{dpSt}^{\mathrm{afp}}\to\mathbf{dSt}^{\mathrm{afp}}
might not preserve the property of being formal. As such, we will often consider stacks given by the stackification of a formal thickening in pre-stack.

Remark 1.3.19
.

If
f:X\to Y
is a nil-equivalence, then there is an equivalence:

\widehat{Y_{X}}\simeq Y

This a direct consequence of Proposition
1.3.11
and the fact that the map
X_{\mathrm{DR}}\to Y_{\mathrm{DR}}
is an equivalence.

Lemma 1.3.20
.

Given
f:X\to Y
, the formal completion induces a factorization:

X\to\widehat{Y_{X}}\to Y

such that:

–

X\to\widehat{Y_{X}}
is a nil-equivalence.

–

\widehat{Y_{X}}\to Y
is formally étale.

Proof.

The factorization is clear from the pullback in Proposition
1.3.11
(
X
is clearly a cone over this pullback). Then we have that:

–

Since
X
is a cone over the pullback defining
\widehat{Y_{X}}
, applying
(-)_{\mathrm{DR}}
, we get a retract
39
39

39

using the fact that
(X_{\mathrm{DR}})_{\mathrm{DR}}\simeq X_{\mathrm{DR}}
.
:

X_{\mathrm{DR}}\to\left(\widehat{Y_{X}}\right)_{\mathrm{DR}}\to X_{\mathrm{DR}}

such that the second morphism is an equivalence (as pullback of the identity of
Y_{\mathrm{DR}}
). Therefore the map
X_{\mathrm{DR}}\to\left(\widehat{Y_{X}}\right)_{\mathrm{DR}}
is also an equivalence.

–

The fact that
\widehat{Y_{X}}\to Y
is formally étale follows from Lemma
1.3.15
and the fact that, thanks the pullback of Proposition
1.3.11
, we have an equivalence:

\mathbb{T}_{\widehat{Y_{X}}/Y}\overset{\sim}{\to}p^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X_{\mathrm{DR}}/Y_{\mathrm{DR}}}\simeq 0

∎

Lemma 1.3.21
.

Let
f:X\to Y
a map of formal pre-stacks such that:

–

f
is a nil-equivalence.

–

f
is formally étale.

then
f
is a weak equivalence.

Proof.

The idea of the proof is to show that for each
\mathbf{Spec}(A)\to Y
there is a unique lift:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Spec}(A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

First observe that from nil-completeness of our formal stacks, such a lift is in fact equivalent to the data of lifts:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Spec}(A_{\leq k})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{k}}

such that the following diagrams commute:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Spec}(A_{\leq k})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Spec}(A_{\leq k+1})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{k}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l_{k+1}}

Assume for now that
H^{0}(A):=A_{\leq 0}
admits a lift. Then we need to produce the lift
l_{k}
for
k\geq 1
compatible with the previous lift.

To do that, we observe that the Postnikov truncations are successive square zero extensions of each other (see
[
PV13
, Proposition 4.1]
). The condition of being formally étale implies that there is a lift to the following diagram for any
A
-module
M
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Spec}(A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Spec}(A\boxplus M)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

Indeed, we can think of this diagram as a lift of
\mathbf{Spec}(A\boxplus M)\to Y
is the category of stacks under
\mathbf{Spec}(A)
. Using the cotangent complex adjunction this can be rephrase by asking for a unique lift:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathbb{L}_{Y})_{|\mathbf{Spec}(A)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathbb{L}_{X})_{|\mathbf{Spec}(A)}}

which exactly the condition that the cotangent complexes (restricted to
\mathbf{Spec}(A)
) are equivalent. In other words, the requirement that
f
is formally étale.

We have reduced the problem to finding a lift:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Spec}(H^{0}(A))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

What we know, from the fact that
f
is a nil-equivalence, is that there is a lift:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Spec}(A^{\mathrm{red}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

Using again the lifting property against square zero extensions, we only have to prove that
\mathbf{Spec}(A^{\mathrm{red}})\to\mathbf{Spec}(A)
can be obtained as a finite composition of square zero extensions.

First recall that
A^{\mathrm{red}}:=H^{0}(A)/\mathfrak{M}
with
\mathfrak{M}:=\mathrm{Nil}(H^{0}(A))
. Since
A
is of almost finite presentation,
H^{0}(A)
is of finite presentation and there exists
N\in\mathbb{N}
such that
\mathfrak{M}^{N}=0
. Then we observe that
A
is the square zero extension of
A/\mathfrak{M}^{N-1}
by
\mathfrak{M}^{N-1}
and
A/\mathfrak{M}^{N-1}
is an algebra with nilpotent ideal
\mathfrak{M}
such that
\mathfrak{M}^{N-1}=0
. By induction, we can write
H^{0}(A)
as finitely many sucessive square zero extensions of
A^{\mathrm{red}}=A/\mathfrak{M}
. *

This proves that there is a lift:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Spec}(A^{\mathrm{red}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Spec}(H^{0}(A))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

and concludes the proof.
∎

1.3.2.
Formal stacks from formal moduli problems

As we have seen in Remark
1.3.4
, the infinitesimal cohesiveness of formal derived stacks is very similar to the pullback condition for formal moduli problems. The goal of this section is to study the relationship between formal moduli problems and formal derived stacks.
In particular, we will study in details the formal moduli problems given by formal spectra and their associated formal stack.

We start by explaining the procedure that extends formal moduli problems
F
over
A
, a connective cdga of almost finite presentation, to formal thickenings
\underline{F}
under
X=\mathbf{Spec}(A)
.

Theorem 1.3.22
.

For
A
an almost finitely presented connective cdga, there is an equivalence (see
[
CG18
, Proposition 4.1]
or
[
GR20
, Chapter 5 Proposition 1.4.2]
):

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{FMP}_{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Thick}^{\mathrm{pre}}(\mathbf{Spec}(A))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{(-)}_{\mathrm{pre}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R}

where
\FMP_{A}
denotes formal moduli problem over
A
(see Definition
D.1.6
).

Moreover, composing with the stackification functor (which is also a left adjoint), we get an adjunction:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{FMP}_{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{dSt}_{\mathbf{Spec}(A)/}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{(-)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R}

such that the completion functor
\underline{(-)}
preserves colimits and finite limits.

Sketch of proof.

The first equivalence is due to
[
GR20
, Chapter 5 Proposition 1.4.2]
(see also
[
CG18
, Proposition 4.1]
). Essentially the completion functor is the left Kan extension along the inclusion
\mathbf{Art}_{/A}\to\mathbf{dAff}
which can be shown to be valued in
\mathbf{Thick}^{\mathrm{pre}}(\mathbf{Spec}(A))
.

For the second statement, we compose this adjunction with the adjunction:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Stf}:\mathbf{dpSt}^{\mathrm{afp}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{dSt}^{\mathrm{afp}}:j}

This adjunction is a
topological localization
according to
[
Lur09b
, Lemma 6.2.2.7]
and such localizations are
left exact
thanks to
[
Lur09b
, Corollary 6.2.1.6]
and therefore preserve finite limits.
∎

Remark 1.3.23
.

The stackification functor,
\mathrm{Stf}
, does not behave quite as nicely as we would like. In particular is does not preserve the cotangent complex. We will find ourselves dealing with the following two types of situations:

–

Either we start with formal moduli problems. Then we need to do everything on the underlying pre-stacks and only then use the stackification.

–

We start with a formal thickening in stack, in which case working in stacks or pre-stacks is equivalent (because
j
is fully-faithful and preserves the tangent complexes).

We give a few results on the behavior of the stackification with respect to formal geometry.

Proposition 1.3.24
.

We have the following properties of the stackification functor:

(1)

The functor
j
is fully-faithful and for any map of stack
h:X\to Y
, with
X=\mathbf{Spec}(A)
, we have an equivalence of
A
-modules:

h^{*}\mathbb{T}_{Y}\simeq h^{*}\mathbb{T}_{j(Y)}

(2)

j
commutes with the de Rham functor
40
40

40

All our discussion in Section
1.3.1
adapts well to pre-stacks.
:

j\circ(-)_{\mathrm{DR}}=(-)_{\mathrm{DR}}\circ j

(3)

\mathrm{Stf}
commutes with the reduced functor
{(-)}_{\mathrm{red}}
:

\mathrm{Stf}\circ{(-)}_{\mathrm{red}}={(-)}_{\mathrm{red}}\circ\mathrm{Stf}

(4)

\mathrm{Stf}
preserves nil-equivalences.

Proof.

(1)

Since
j
is fully-faithful, we have the equivalences:

\begin{split}h^{*}\mathbb{T}_{Y}\simeq&\Map_{\mathbf{dSt}}\left(\mathbf{Spec}(A\boxplus A[n]),Y\right)\\
\simeq&\Map_{\mathbf{dpSt}}\left(j\left(\mathbf{Spec}(A\boxplus A[n])\right),j(Y)\right)\\
\simeq&\Map_{\mathbf{dpSt}}\left(\mathbf{Spec}(A\boxplus A[n]),j(Y)\right)\\
\simeq&h^{*}\mathbb{T}_{j(Y)}\end{split}

(2)

For all
X\in\mathbf{dSt}
and
A\in\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{\leq 0}}
, we have:

j\left(X_{\mathrm{DR}}\right)(A)=j(X)(A^{\mathrm{red}})=X(A^{\mathrm{red}})=j(X_{\mathrm{DR}})(A)

(3)

The previous result shows the commutativity of the right adjoint functors. This implies that their left adjoints also commute.

(4)

Since
\mathrm{Stf}
commutes with the reduced functor and preserves weak equivalences, then is preserves nil-equivalences.

∎

Now that we have a way to see a formal moduli problem as a formal derived stack, we will be interested in the particular example of the formal moduli problems given by formal spectra (Definition
D.1.7
).

Let us recall that the formal spectrum (relative to
A
) of

is defined as the formal moduli problem:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B):\mathbf{Art}_{/A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Gpd}_{\infty}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\qquad\qquad C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underset{\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}}{\Map}\left(B,C\right)}

Remark 1.3.25
.

It turns out that the restriction functor

does not only send formal thickenings to formal moduli problems, but it also sends any formal stack under
X

\underset{\FMP_{A}}{\Map}(\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(A),F)\simeq\star

Therefore

Remark 1.3.26
.

We have, by definition of the formal spectrum, that for all

R(\mathbf{Spec}(B))\simeq\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)

In Section

Lemma 1.3.27
.

Take
f:B\to A
with

f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{B}\simeq f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\underline{\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)}_{\mathrm{pre}}}

More generally, if

For all

\begin{split}\left|f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\underline{F}_{\mathrm{pre}}}[n]\right|_{\Delta}\simeq&\underset{\mathbf{dSt}_{\mathbf{Spec}(A)/}}{\Map}\left(\mathbf{Spec}(A[\epsilon_{n}]),\underline{F}_{\mathrm{pre}}\right)\\
{}_{(A[\epsilon_{n}]\in\mathbf{Art}_{/A})}\simeq&F(A[\epsilon_{n}])\\
{}_{\text{(Section \ref {sec:tangent-complex-of-a-formal-moduli-problem})}}\simeq&\left|f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{F}[n]\right|_{\Delta}\end{split}

where

and squares to zero

41

41

This gives exactly the square zero extension

.
. The collection for all

of these equivalences induces the equivalence between the complexes since they become equivalent as

Corollary 1.3.28

For
X:=\mathbf{Spec}(A)
affine of almost finite presentation, we have an equivalence:

\mathbb{T}_{X/\underline{\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)}_{\mathrm{pre}}}\simeq\mathbb{T}_{A/B}

\mathbb{T}_{A/B}\to\mathbb{T}_{A}\to f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{B}

∎

Remark 1.3.29

1.4.
De Rham Algebra and (Closed)
p
-Forms

This Section is mostly a recollection of
[
CPT+17
]
. In the first part, we focus on setting up notations for the different structures we can put on the de Rham algebra and its relative version in derived algebraic geometry. In the second part, we use this formalism to defined the notion of
n
-shifted (closed)
p
-form on a derived stack.

1.4.1.
De Rham complex

Classically we think of the de Rham algebra as the algebra of differential forms together with the de Rham differential,
\left(\bigwedge_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}\Gamma(T^{*}X),d_{\mathrm{dR}}\right)
. In derived geometry, we want to replace
T^{*}X
by
\mathbb{L}_{X}
, and we would like the de Rham algebra to be something like the derived global sections of
\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]
. But this object has much more structure than its classical counterpart. Namely we have that:

–

This is a cdga for the grading induced by the grading on
\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]
, which we will call
internal grading
with a vertical differential induced by the differential on
\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]
.

–

There is a weight grading given by
\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}^{p}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]
, the symmetric powers of arity
p
.

–

There is a “mixed differential” also known as the de Rham differential, which increases the weight and total degree by
1
.

This all data gives the structure of
graded mixed algebra
. We quickly recall the definitions and main properties related to graded mixed objects in Appendix
C
. We will first focus on the affine case,
X:=\mathbf{Spec}(B)
.

It turns out that there is a universal construction of a “de Rham object” that will, thanks to Proposition
1.4.4
, recover the heuristic we just discussed. We will define the de Rham graded mixed complex in the general setting of
good model category

\mathscr{M}
(see Appendix
A.1
). In particular for
\mathscr{M}=\Mod_{k}
, we recover the classical de Rham graded mixed complex of a cdga. Moreover, in this context, we can even extend the functor
\mathbf{DR}
to all derived stacks.

Lemma 1.4.1

(
[
CPT+17
, Proposition 1.3.8 and Proposition 1.3.16]
)
.

There is an adjunction:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{DR}_{\mathscr{M}}:\mathrm{cdga}_{\mathscr{M}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{cdga}_{\mathscr{M}}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}:(-)(0)}

where the right adjoint is the functor that sends a graded mixed algebra to the algebra in
\mathrm{cdga}_{\mathscr{M}}
given by the weight
0
part of the graded mixed algebra.

Moreover, this adjunction holds in the relative setting. If
A\in\mathrm{cdga}_{\mathscr{M}}
, then there is an adjunction
43
43

43

On the right hand side,
A
is viewed as a graded mixed algebra concentrated in weight
0
.
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{DR}_{\mathscr{M}}(-/A):\mathrm{cdga}_{\mathscr{M},\ A/}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{cdga}_{\mathscr{M},\ A/}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}:(-)(0)}

Definition 1.4.2
.

The
de Rham algebra of
A\in\mathrm{cdga}_{M}
is defined as the following graded mixed algebra
\mathbf{DR}_{\mathscr{M}}(A)
. We are going to write
\mathbf{DR}(A)
when
\mathscr{M}
is clear. For example we have:

–

If
\mathscr{M}=\Mod_{k}
, then
\mathbf{DR}(B):=\mathbf{DR}_{\Mod_{k}}(B)
is the de Rham graded mixed algebra associated to the algebra
B
.

–

If
\mathscr{M}=\Mod_{A}
for
A\in\mathrm{cdga}
and
A\to B
a map of algebras (and therefore
B\in\mathrm{cdga}_{\Mod_{A}}
), we define:

\mathbf{DR}(B/A):=\mathbf{DR}_{\Mod_{A}}(B)

More generally, we have:

\mathbf{DR}(-/A):=\mathbf{DR}_{\Mod_{A}}

From
[
CPT+17
, Lemma 1.3.18]
, we have that

\mathbf{DR}(B/A)\simeq\mathbf{DR}(B)\otimes_{\mathbf{DR}(A)}A

where
A
is viewed as a graded mixed complex concentrated in degree
0
. Note that
\mathbf{DR}(A)\simeq\mathbf{DR}(A/k)
and this definition coincides with the relative de Rham construction via the adjunction of Lemma
1.4.1
.

Notation 1.4.3
.

There are various structures on the de Rham algebra and we set the following notations:

–

\mathbf{DR}
is the de Rham functor valued in graded-mixed algebras.

–

\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}
is the underlying graded algebra of
\mathbf{DR}
(see Lemma
C.1.6
) where we forget the mixed structure.

–

As weak graded mixed complexes (Definition
C.2.1
) are equivalent to complete filtered objects, we denote by
\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{cpl}}
the induced complete filtered algebra. It is described, thanks to Proposition
C.2.8
, by the following filtered algebra:

F^{p}\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{cpl}}(A/B)\simeq\prod_{p^{\prime}\geq p}\Sym_{A}^{p^{\prime}}\mathbb{L}_{A/B}[-1]

Since
\mathbf{DR}(A/B)
is non-negatively weighted, each
F^{p}\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{cpl}}(A/B)
is a differential graded algebra with the differential being the
total differential
summing the vertical and the mixed differentials.

–

\left|\mathbf{DR}\right|
is the de total Rham algebra obtained by applying the realization functor
\left|-\right|
given by Proposition
C.1.9
:

\left|\mathbf{DR}(A/B)\right|\simeq\prod_{p\geq 0}\mathbf{DR}(A/B)(p)

together with the total differential. Note that we have:

\left|\mathbf{DR}\right|\simeq F^{0}\mathbf{DR}\simeq\colim F^{p}\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{cpl}}

Proposition 1.4.4
.

There is an equivalence of graded algebras:

\Sym^{\mathrm{gr}}_{B}\mathbb{L}_{B}[-1]\overset{\sim}{\to}\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(B)

Similarly, in the relative case we have an equivalence:

\Sym^{\mathrm{gr}}_{B}\mathbb{L}_{B/A}[-1]\overset{\sim}{\to}\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(B/A)

Corollary 1.4.5

(
[
CPT+17
, Corollary 1.3.14 and Remark 1.3.15]
)
.

For any object
A\in\mathrm{cdga}_{\mathscr{M}}
, the algebra
\Sym^{\mathrm{gr}}_{B}\mathbb{L}_{A/B}[-1]
possesses a canonical weak graded mixed structure
44
44

44

This structure is (weakly) transferred from
\mathbf{DR}(A/B)
. If
B\to A
is nice enough (that is cofibrant) then this can be taken as a strict (non-weak) graded mixed algebra (see
[
CPT+17
, Section 1.3.3]
).
making it into a weak graded mixed algebra in
\mathscr{M}
. The corresponding mixed differential is called the de Rham differential and is denoted
d_{\mathrm{dR}}
.

Proposition 1.4.6
.

We have the following equivalences:

\left|\mathbf{DR}\right|(B/A)\simeq\colim\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{cpl}}(B/A)

\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(B/A)\simeq\mathbf{Gr}\left(\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{cpl}}(B/A)\right)

Proof.

The first equivalence is a direct application of Lemma
C.2.10
and the second is an application of Lemma
C.2.11
.
∎

So far we only constructed to de Rham graded mixed algebra for affine objects. It turns out that
\mathbf{DR}
satisfies étale descent and is therefore a derived stack valued in graded mixed complexes. Therefore we can extend it to a functor (see
[
PTVV13
, Definition 1.13]
) on all derived stacks and it defines
45
45

45

The de Rham complex extends to all derived stacks. However if
X
does not admit a cotangent complex, there is no analogue to Proposition
1.4.4
.
a graded mixed algebra
\mathbf{DR}(X)
for all derived stack
X
.

The natural way to define this global de Rham graded mixed algebra is by taking the left Kan extension computed by following limit:

\mathbf{DR}(X):=\lim\limits_{\mathbf{Spec}(A)\to X}\mathbf{DR}(A)

Moreover the underlying graded of this limit is computed weight-wise and therefore:

\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(X)\simeq\lim\limits_{\mathbf{Spec}(A)\overset{f}{\to}X}\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)

We get that:

\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(X)(p)\simeq\lim\limits_{\mathbf{Spec}(A)\overset{f}{\to}X}\Sym_{A}^{p}\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]

Corollary 1.4.7
.

If
X
admits a cotangent complex there is a natural morphism
46
46

46

Here
\Gamma
denotes the derived global section functor that sends
\mathscr{F}\in\mathbf{QC}(X)
to:

\underset{\mathbf{dSt}_{/X}}{\Map}(X,F)\simeq\underset{\mathbf{QC}(X)}{\Map}(\mathscr{O}_{X},\mathscr{F})\simeq\lim\limits_{\mathbf{Spec}(A)\overset{f}{\to}X}\left|f^{*}\mathscr{F}\right|_{\Delta}

:

\Gamma\left(\Sym^{\mathrm{gr}}_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\right)\simeq\lim\limits_{\mathbf{Spec}(A)\overset{f}{\to}X}\left|\Sym^{\mathrm{gr}}_{A}f^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}\right|_{\Delta}\to\left|\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(X)\right|_{\Delta}

Since the de Rham functor satisfies smooth descent, this natural morphism is in fact an equivalence for
X
a Artin stack (
[
PTVV13
, Proposition 1.14]
).

Remark 1.4.8
.

In this corollary, we consider the
space
of sections by taking the mapping space of sections. If we take instead the
mapping spectra
, we get a map to
\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(X)
of graded algebras. In other words we get a map of graded algebras:

\underset{\mathbf{QC}(X)}{\iHom}^{\mathrm{gr}}\left(\mathscr{O}_{X},\Sym^{\mathrm{gr}}_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\right)\to\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(X)

Moreover, the weight
0
component always recovers the algebra of functions of
X
(even if
X
is not Artin).

Lemma 1.4.9
.

There is a natural augmentation to the algebra of global functions (viewed as a graded mixed algebra concentrated in weight
0
):

\mathbf{DR}(X)\to\mathscr{O}_{X}(X)

Proof.

For any graded mixed algebra, there is a natural map to its weight
0
part (viewed as a graded mixed algebra concentrated in weight
0
). In particular we get a map:

\mathbf{DR}(X)\to\mathbf{DR}(X)(0)

Thank to Proposition
1.4.4
, we get an equivalence:

\mathbf{DR}(A)(0)\simeq A

Therefore, we can use Definition
1.1.20
and show that:

\mathbf{DR}(X)(0)\simeq\lim\limits_{\mathbf{Spec}(A)\to X}\mathbf{DR}(A)(0)\simeq\lim\limits_{\mathbf{Spec}(A)\to X}A\simeq\mathscr{O}_{X}(X)

∎

Definition 1.4.10

(
[
CPT+17
, Definition 2.3.1]
)
.

Given a map
f:Y\to X
of derived stacks with
X=\mathbf{Spec}(A)
, we can define the relative de Rham graded mixed algebra of
f:Y\to X
as:

\mathbf{DR}(Y/X):=\lim\limits_{\mathbf{Spec}(B)\overset{f}{\to}Y}\mathbf{DR}(A/B)

Lemma 1.4.11
.

Let
X\to Y\to Z
be morphisms of derived stacks such that
X=\mathbf{Spec}(A)
and
Y=\mathbf{Spec}(B)
are affine. Then there is morphism of graded mixed complexes:

\mathbf{DR}(X/Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{DR}(X)}\mathbf{DR}(Y)\to\mathbf{DR}(X/Y)

Moreover if
Z
is also affine, then this is an equivalence.

Proof.

This is the natural morphism:

\begin{split}\mathbf{DR}(X/Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{DR}(A)}\mathbf{DR}(B)\simeq&\left(\lim\limits_{\mathbf{Spec}(C)\to Z}\mathbf{DR}(C/A)\right)\otimes_{\mathbf{DR}(A)}\mathbf{DR}(B)\\
\to&\lim\limits_{\mathbf{Spec}(C)\to Z}\left(\mathbf{DR}(C/A)\otimes_{\mathbf{DR}(A)}\mathbf{DR}(B)\right)\\
\simeq&\lim\limits_{\mathbf{Spec}(C)\to Z}\left(\mathbf{DR}(C/B)\right)\\
\simeq&\mathbf{DR}(X/Y)\end{split}

This is an equivalence whenever the limit commutes with the tensor product. This is the case if
Z
is affine.
∎

1.4.2.
Shifted (closed)
p
-forms

Recall from
[
PTVV13
]
that there are classifying stacks
\mathscr{A}^{p}(\bullet,n)
and
\mathscr{A}^{p,cl}(\bullet,n)
of respectively the space of
n
-shifted differential
p
-forms and the space of
n
-shifted closed differential
p
-forms. In this section we will recall their definition and basic properties.

Definition 1.4.12
.

Let
A\in\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{\leq 0}}
. The space of
p
-forms of degree
n
and the space of
closed
p
-forms of degree
n
on
A
are defined respectively by:

\mathscr{A}^{p}(A,n):=\underset{\Mod_{k}^{\mathrm{gr}}}{\Map}\left(k[-n-p]((-p)),\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)\right)\simeq\left|\left(\Sym^{p}\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]\right)[n+p]\right|_{\Delta}

\mathscr{A}^{p,\mathrm{cl}}(A,n):=\underset{\Mod_{k}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}}{\Map}\left(k[-n-p]((-p)),\mathbf{DR}(A)\right)

where
k[-n-p]((-p))
is the graded (mixed) complex concentrated in weight
p
and degree
n+p
.
All along, we denote the vertical differential, i.e. the differential on
\mathbb{L}_{A}
, by
\delta
and the mixed differential, i.e. the de Rham differential, by
d_{\mathrm{dR}}
.

From
[
PTVV13
, Proposition 1.11]
, we know that the functors
\mathscr{A}^{p}(-,n)
and
\mathscr{A}^{p,cl}(-,n)
are in fact stacks and therefore we can extend the definition of (closed)
p
-forms of degree
n
to any derived stacks.

Definition 1.4.13
.

The space of
p
-forms of degree
n
on a derived stack
X
is the mapping space:

\mathscr{A}^{p}(X,n):=\underset{\mathbf{dSt}}{\Map}\left(X,\mathscr{A}^{p}(\bullet,n)\right)\simeq\underset{\Mod_{k}^{\mathrm{gr}}}{\Map}\left(k[-n-p]((-p)),\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(X)\right)

The space of
closed
p
-forms of degree
n
on
X
is:

\mathscr{A}^{p,\mathrm{\mathrm{cl}}}(X,n):=\underset{\mathbf{dSt}}{\Map}\left(X,\mathscr{A}^{p,\mathrm{cl}}(\bullet,n)\right)\simeq\underset{\Mod_{k}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}}{\Map}\left(k[-n-p]((-p)),\mathbf{DR}(X)\right)

Now the following proposition says that in the case when
X
is a derived Artin stack, the spaces of shifted differential forms are spaces of sections of quasi-coherent sheaves on
X
.

Proposition 1.4.14

(Proposition 1.14 in
[
PTVV13
]
)
.

Let
X
be a derived Artin stack (see Remark
1.1.13
) and
\mathbb{L}_{X}
be its cotangent complex. Then there is an equivalence:

\mathscr{A}^{p}(X,n)\simeq\underset{\mathbf{QC}(X)}{\Map}\left(\mathscr{O}_{X},\left(\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}^{p}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\right)[p+n]\right)

Remark 1.4.15
.

For a derived Artin stack, a
n
-shifted
p
-form is therefore equivalent to the data of a section of
\left(\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}^{p}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\right)[p+n]
. Even better, thanks to Corollary
1.2.16
, the space of sections of
T^{*}X
is equivalent to the space of
n
-shifted
1
-form on
X
:

\Map_{\mathbf{dSt}_{/X}}(X,T^{*}[n]X)\simeq\mathscr{A}^{1}(X,n)

Remark 1.4.16
.

More concretely, we have from
[
Cal21
]
and
[
CPT+17
]
an explicit description of (closed)
p
-forms of degree
n
on a derived Artin stack
X
. A
p
-form of degree
n
is given by a (derived) global section

\omega\in\mathbf{DR}(X)(p)[n+p]\simeq\Gamma\left(\left(\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}^{p}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\right)[n+p]\right)

such that
\delta\omega=0
.

A closed
p
-form of degree
n
is a semi-infinite sequence
\omega=\omega_{0}+\omega_{1}+\cdots
with

\omega_{i}\in\mathbf{DR}(p+i)[n+p]=\Gamma\left(\left(\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}^{p+i}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\right)[n+p]\right)

such that
\delta\omega_{0}=0
and
d\omega_{i}=\delta\omega_{i+1}
. Equivalently, being closed means that
\omega
is a closed element in

F^{p}\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{cpl}}(X)\simeq\Gamma\left(\prod_{i\geq 0}\left(\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}^{p+i}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\right)[n+p]\right)

whose total degree is given by
n+p+i
and with the total differential.

In fact in general (without assuming
X
Artin), we have that the following description of the spaces of (closed) shifted
p
-forms (see the comment following
[
PTVV13
, Definition 1.13]
):

Proposition 1.4.17
.

For
X
a derived stack, we can also describe the spaces of (closed) differential forms as:

\mathscr{A}^{p}(X,n)\simeq\left|\mathbf{DR}(p)(X)[n+p]\right|_{\Delta}

\mathscr{A}^{p,\mathrm{cl}}(X,n)\simeq\left|F^{p}\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{cpl}}(X)[n+p]\right|_{\Delta}\simeq\left|\prod_{i\geq p}\mathbf{DR}(p+i)(X)[n+p]\right|_{\Delta}

together with the total differential.

Definition 1.4.18
.

The natural projection:

F^{p}\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{cpl}}(X)[n]\to\mathbf{DR}(p)(X)[n+p]

induces a map
\mathscr{A}^{p,\mathrm{cl}}(X,n)\to\mathscr{A}^{p}(X,n)
that forgets the closed structure. It essentially sends

\omega:=\omega_{0}+\omega_{1}+\cdots\mapsto\omega_{0}

and the image of
\omega
by this map is called the
underlying
p
-form of degree
n
of
\omega
. We will often denote it by
\omega_{0}
.

The collection of all the closures of a
p
-form of degree
n
forms a space:

Definition 1.4.19
.

Let
\alpha\in\mathscr{A}^{p}(X,n)
then the space of all closures of
\alpha
is called the
space of keys
of
\alpha
denoted
\mathbf{key}(\alpha)
. It is given by the homotopy pull-back:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{key}(\alpha)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{p,\mathrm{cl}}(X,n)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\star}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{p}(X,n)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha}

Proposition 1.4.20
.

The mixed differential of
\mathbf{DR}(X)
induces a map:

d_{\mathrm{dR}}:\mathscr{A}^{p}(X,n)\rightarrow\mathscr{A}^{p+1,\mathrm{cl}}(X,n)

that squares to zero.

Proof.

The mixed differential increases the weight by (at least)
1
therefore induces a map
d_{\mathrm{dR}}:F^{p}\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{cpl}}(X)\to F^{p+1}\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{cpl}}(X)
of degree
1
. This induces the desired map since we have, from Definition
C.1.12
, that:

F^{p}\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{cpl}}(X)\simeq\Hom_{\mathrm{cdga}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}}(k((-p))[-n-p],\mathbf{DR}(X))

∎

Remark 1.4.21
.

Given a map of derived Artin stack
f:Y\rightarrow X
, we define
\mathscr{A}^{p,\mathrm{(cl)}}(Y/X,n)
, the space of
n
-shifted (closed)
p
-forms on
Y
relative to
X
, to be the homotopy cofiber of the natural map:

f^{*}:\mathscr{A}^{p,\mathrm{(cl)}}(X,n)\rightarrow\mathscr{A}^{p,\mathrm{(cl)}}(Y,n)

Using Definition
1.4.10
, we can show
47
47

47

Because the pushout defining the relative de Rham graded mixed algebra is preserved by geometric realization.
that the relative forms can be directly obtain by using the relative de Rham
\mathbf{DR}(Y/X)
. For instance
n
-shifted relative
p
-forms are equivalent to the derived global sections of
\left(\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{Y}}^{p}\mathbb{L}_{Y/X}[-1]\right)[n+p]
.

Remark 1.4.22
.

We say that a
p
-form,
\omega_{0}
, of degree
n
on a derived Artin stack
X
can be lifted to a closed
p
-form of degree
n
if there exists a family of
(p+i)
-forms
\omega_{i}
of degree
n-i
for all
i>0
, such that
\omega=\omega_{0}+\omega_{1}+\cdots
is closed in
F^{p}\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{cpl}}(X)[n]
. In that situation, we can see that
d_{\mathrm{dR}}\omega_{0}
is in general not equal to
0
but is homotopic to
0
with
d_{\mathrm{dR}}\omega_{0}=D\left(-\sum_{i>0}\omega_{i}\right)
. The choice of such a homotopy is the same as the structure of a closure of the
p
-form of degree
n
.

Being closed is therefore no longer a property of the underlying
p
-form of degree
n
but a structure given by a homotopy between
d_{\mathrm{dR}}\omega_{0}
and zero.

Warning 1.4.23
.

When we are working with formal stacks, they will usually not be Artin and therefore
n
-shifted
p
-forms might not always come from derived global sections of
\left(\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}^{p}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\right)[p+n]
. This will be a problem in order to define symplectic structure on formal stacks or more generally any kind of “non-degeneracy condition”. To avoid this problem, recall from Corollary
1.4.7
that we have a map of graded spaces:

\Gamma\left(\mathscr{O}_{X},\Sym^{\mathrm{gr}}_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\right)\to\left|\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(X)\right|_{\Delta}

Therefore, in order to still view
p
-forms as global sections of elements of the
p
-th symmetric power of
\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]
(which is what we will need to speak of non-degeneracy conditions in Section
2
) when
X
is a derived stack with a cotangent complex, we
define
the notion of
good

p
-forms of degree
n
as the
p
-forms of degree
n
that are in the image of the map:

\Gamma\left(\mathscr{O}_{X},\left(\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}^{p}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\right)[n+p]\right)\to\left|\mathbf{DR}(p)(X)[n+p]\right|_{\Delta}\simeq\mathscr{A}^{p}(X,n)

More generally, an element in
\mathbf{DR}(p)(X)[n+p]
will be called
good
if it is in the image of the map from Remark
1.4.8
:

\underset{\mathbf{QC}(X)}{\iHom}^{\mathrm{gr}}\left(\mathscr{O}_{X},\left(\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}^{p}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\right)[n+p]\right)\to\mathbf{DR}(X)(p)[n+p]

A closed element will be considered good if its underlying
p
-form is good. In other words, the space of good closed
p
-forms of degree
n
is the pullback of the diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{p,\mathrm{cl}}(X,n)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Gamma\left(\mathscr{O}_{X},\left(\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}^{p}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\right)[n+p]\right)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{p}(X,n)}

Similarly,
good closed
elements in
\mathbf{DR}(X)(p)[n+p]
are closed elements in the pullback of the diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{p}\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{cpl}}(X)[n+p]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underset{\mathbf{QC}(X)}{\iHom}^{\mathrm{gr}}\left(\mathscr{O}_{X},\left(\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}^{p}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\right)[n+p]\right)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{DR}(X)(p)[n+p]}

Note that if
X
is Artin good and general objects coincide (because the horizontal maps of the previous pullback diagrams are equivalences).

Notation 1.4.24
.

From now on, we will make an abuse of notation and denote by
\mathscr{A}^{p}(X,n)
and
\mathscr{A}^{p,\mathrm{cl}}(X,n)
the spaces of
good
(closed)
p
-forms of degree
n
. Moreover we will simply call them (closed)
p
-forms of degree
n
(omitting the word “good”). In particular,
by definition
we get the analogue of Proposition
1.4.14
:

\mathscr{A}^{p}(X,n)\simeq\underset{\mathbf{QC}(X)}{\Map}\left(\mathscr{O}_{X},\left(\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}^{p}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\right)[p+n]\right)

2.
New Constructions in Derived Symplectic Geometry

Following the philosophy of derived geometrie, derived symplectic geometry is an extension of classical symplectic geometry where we consider shifted symplectic structures and homotopies between them. Moreover, we again would like such objects to be well behaved with respect to derived intersections and derived quotients. The study of the derived symplectic geometry of derived quotients is the object of Section
4
. In this section, we will recall and expand upon the idea that taking derived “Lagrangian intersections” is a way to produce new
shifted
symplectic structures out of old ones.

In Section
2.1
, we recall the main definitions and examples of symplectic, Lagrangian, Lagrangian correspondences and Lagrangian fibration structures.

Then Section
2.2
is devoted to constructing new structures via derived
Lagrangian intersections
. In particular, we recall the construction of shifted symplectic structures on a derived intersections of Lagrangian morphisms (Proposition
2.2.1
), and extend this result to the construction of new Lagrangian fibrations (Theorem
2.2.7
).

Then Section
2.2.3
describes the (higher) categories of Lagrangians (and Lagrangian correspondences) in order to give again a result producing new Lagrangian correspondences from derived Lagrangian intersections (Theorem
2.2.23
). This will enable us to take derived “equivariant Lagrangian intersections” of moment maps in Section
4
.

Finally Section
2.3
gives concrete examples for the construction of these new Lagrangian fibration structures.

2.1.
Derived Symplectic Geometry

In this section we will recall the basic definitions and examples of symplectic, Lagrangian and Lagrangian fibration structures for derived stacks.

All along we will assume that our derived stacks admit a cotangent complex.

Recall that Warning
1.4.23
tells us that the underlying
p
-form of a closed
p
-form comes from derived global sections of the shifted symmetric power of the cotangent complex. This will ensure that all the non-degeneracy conditions we are going to define make sense. In other words, given a derived stack

, a

\omega_{0}\in\underset{\mathbf{QC}(X)}{\Map}\left(\mathscr{O}_{X},\left(\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}^{2}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\right)[n+2]\right)

2.1.2.
Lagrangian structures

We recall from

PTVV13

Recall that classically, a Lagrangian is a sub-manifold

of a symplectic manifold

such that:

–

It is isotropic, i.e.
f^{*}\omega=0
.

–

\omega

TL\to N^{*}f

The first condition we will translate as the data of an isotropic

Definition 2.1.6
.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Symp(X,n)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\star}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{2,\mathrm{cl}}(L,n)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}

If we fix a given

-shifted symplectic structure

, we can define the space of isotropic structures on

at

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Iso(f,\omega)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\star}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Symp(X,n)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\omega}

Remark 2.1.7
.

Take

Remark 2.1.8
.

More explicitly, if

in exact in

and

.

The second condition to be Lagrangian is a non-degeneracy condition of an isotropic structure

(3)

\left[\mu\right]:\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{G}$}}}\right]\to\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.69293pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{3.44293pt}{$\textstyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{2.67209pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.8854pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{G}$}}}\right]

–

The map

\mathbf{B}{G}\to\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.69293pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{3.44293pt}{$\textstyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{2.67209pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.8854pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{G}$}}}\right]

corresponding to the zero section
\mathbf{B}G\to T^{*}[n+1]\mathbf{B}{G}
via the equivalence of Lemma
4.1.25
.

Lemma 2.1.17

(
[
Cal21
, Example 1.26]
)
.

Consider the map
X\rightarrow\star_{n}
where
\star_{n}
is the point endowed with the canonical
n
-shifted symplectic structure given by
0
. Then a Lagrangian structure on this map is equivalent to an
(n-1)
-shifted symplectic structure on
X
.

Proof.

Pick an isotropic structure
\gamma
on
p
. We know that
\gamma
is a homotopy between 0 and 0 which means that
D\gamma=0
. Therefore
\gamma
is a closed 2-form of degree
n-1
. We want to show that
\gamma
is non-degenerate as an isotropic structure if and only if it is non-degenerate as a closed 2-form on
X
. The non-degeneracy of the Lagrangian structure, as described in Remark
2.1.10
, corresponds to the requirement that the natural map
\mathbb{T}_{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{L}_{X}[n-1]
is a quasi-isomorphism. This map depends on
\gamma_{0}
and we want to show that this map is in fact
\gamma_{0}^{\flat}
. This map is the natural map that fits in the following homotopy commutative diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}_{X}[n-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}_{X}[n]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0^{\flat}}

We can show that by strictifying the homotopy commutative diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}_{X}[n]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p^{*}\omega^{\flat}=0}

Note that this diagram is already commutative but we see it as homotopy commutative using the homotopy
\gamma_{0}
. We use the homotopy
\gamma_{0}
to strictify the previous diagram and we obtain:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}_{X}[n-1]\oplus\mathbb{L}_{X}[n]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}_{X}[n]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma_{0}^{\flat}+0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p^{*}\omega^{\flat}=0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{pr}}

The homotopy fiber and also strict fiber of the projection

\mathrm{pr}:\mathbb{L}_{X}[n-1]\oplus\mathbb{L}_{X}[n]\rightarrow\mathbb{L}_{X}[n]

is
\mathbb{L}_{X}[n-1]
, and therefore the natural map we obtain is
\gamma_{0}^{\flat}:\mathbb{T}_{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{L}_{X}[n-1]
.

Since the non-degeneracy condition of the isotropic structure
\gamma
is the same as saying that the map
\gamma_{0}^{\flat}
is a quasi-isomorphism, we have shown that an isotropic structure
\gamma
is an
(n-1)
-shifted symplectic structure on
X
if and only if it is non-degenerate as an isotropic structure on
X\rightarrow\star_{n}
.
∎

A closely related notion to Lagrangian morphisms is that of Lagrangian correspondences. We will see in Section
4

symplectic reduction
and in Section

we use Lagrangian correspondences as a defining feature of the notion of “generalized symplectic reduction” and of the BV construction.

Definition 2.1.18
.

Let
X
and
Y
be derived Artin stacks with
n
-shifted symplectic structures. A

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}

and a Lagrangian structure on the map

where
X\times\overline{Y}
is endowed with the
n
-shifted symplectic structure
\pi_{X}^{*}\omega_{X}-\pi_{Y}^{*}\omega_{Y}
.

For example, a Lagrangian structure on

is equivalent to a Lagrangian correspondence from

to
\star
.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\star_{n}}

A more extensive study of Lagrangian correspondences and their properties is done in Section

Example 2.1.22
.

The natural projection

is a Lagrangian fibration. The Liouville 1-form is a section of

It turns out that the morphism expressing the non-degeneracy condition,

Proposition 2.1.23
.

If

Consider the following diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}X/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}_{T^{*}X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\omega_{0}^{\flat}}

Lemma 2.1.24
.

Let
x:\star_{n}\rightarrow X
be a point of
X
. Then, given a Lagrangian fibration structure on
x
, the non-degeneracy condition is given by a quasi-isomorphism:

x^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}\rightarrow x^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[n+1]

Proof.

The Lagrangian fibration structure on
\star_{n}\rightarrow X
is a homotopy between 0 and itself in
\mathscr{A}^{2,\mathrm{cl}}({\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.32639pt}{$\displaystyle{\star_{n}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}}{\raisebox{2.32639pt}{$\textstyle{\star_{n}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}}{\raisebox{1.62846pt}{$\scriptstyle{\star_{n}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}}{\raisebox{1.16318pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\star_{n}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}}},n)
. As in the proof of Lemma
2.1.17
, this is given by an element
\gamma\in\mathscr{A}^{2,\mathrm{cl}}({\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.32639pt}{$\displaystyle{\star_{n}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}}{\raisebox{2.32639pt}{$\textstyle{\star_{n}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}}{\raisebox{1.62846pt}{$\scriptstyle{\star_{n}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}}{\raisebox{1.16318pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\star_{n}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}}},n-1)
. Similarly to what was done in the proof of Lemma
2.1.17
, we can show that
\gamma
is non-degenerate as a Lagrangian fibration if and only if it is non-degenerate as a closed 2-form of degree
n
. Again it boils down to the fact that the natural morphism in the non-degeneracy criteria for Lagrangian fibrations is in fact
\gamma_{0}^{\flat}:\mathbb{T}_{\star_{n}/X}\rightarrow\mathbb{L}_{\star_{n}/X}[n-1]
.

Moreover, we have natural equivalences,
\mathbb{T}_{\star_{n}/X}\simeq x^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}[-1]
and
\mathbb{L}_{\star_{n}/X}[n-1]\simeq x^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[n]
because the sequence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{\star_{n}/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{\star_{n}}\simeq 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}[n]}

is fibered. This concludes the proof.
∎

Example 2.1.25
.

The natural map
\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.69293pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{3.44293pt}{$\textstyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{2.67209pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.8854pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{G}$}}}\right]\to\mathbf{B}G
is equivalent to the projection
T^{*}[n+1]\mathbf{B}G\to\mathbf{B}G
through the equivalence of Lemma
4.1.25
. Therefore this is a Lagrangian fibration.

2.2.
New Constructions from Old Ones

In this section we will recall how to construct new shifted symplectic structures by taking derived intersection of Lagrangian morphisms (Proposition
2.2.1
) and then extend this result to construct new Lagrangian fibrations (Theorem
2.2.7
).

The gymnastic of constructing new Lagrangians and Lagrangian correspondences is very well behaved, and in Section
2.2.3
we use this to described a category and a weak
2
-category structure on the space of Lagrangians. This leads to another construction that produces new Lagrangian correspondences out of derived intersections (Theorem
2.2.23
).

2.2.1.
Derived intersection of Lagrangians morphisms

Proposition 2.2.1

(
[
PTVV13
, Section 2.2]
)
.

Let
Z
be a derived Artin stack with a
n
-shifted symplectic structure
\omega
. Let
f:X\rightarrow Z
and
g:Y\rightarrow Z
be morphisms with
\gamma
and
\delta
Lagrangian structures on
f
and
g
respectively. Then the homotopy pull-back
X\times_{Z}Y
possesses a canonical
(n-1)
-shited symplectic structure called the residue of
\omega
and denoted
R(\omega,\gamma,\delta)
.

Remark 2.2.2
.

If we fix
f
and
g
as above, we can extend the previous theorem to obtain a map of spaces (see Theorem 2.4 in
[
Cal15
]
):

\mathbf{Lag}(f,n)\times_{\mathbf{Symp}(X,n)}\mathbf{Lag}(g,n)\rightarrow\mathbf{Symp}(X\times_{Z}Y,n-1)

Example 2.2.3
.

The derived critical locus is by definition the derived pullback of two closed
1
-form
s_{0},df:X\to T^{*}X
which are therefore Lagrangian thanks to Example
2.1.12
. Therefore
\mathbf{Crit}(f)
is
(-1)
-shifted symplectic.

Remark 2.2.4
.

When
X
is a derived stack and
df=0
, we have that
\mathbf{Crit}(f)\simeq T^{*}[-1]X
and
\omega_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}
is the canonical
(-1)
-shifted symplectic structure on
T^{*}[-1]X
.

Remark 2.2.5
.

Proposition
2.2.1
can also be seen as a consequence of the procedure of composition of Lagrangian correspondences (Theorem
2.2.13
). To se that, consider the following composition of Lagrangian correspondences:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\times_{Z}Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\star}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\star}

The maps
X\rightarrow Z\times\bar{\star}
and
Y\rightarrow Y\times\bar{\star}
are Lagrangian correspondences because
X\rightarrow Z
and
Y\rightarrow Z
are Lagrangian. Therefore, by composition,
X\times_{Z}Y\rightarrow\star\times\bar{\star}
is also a Lagrangian correspondence, thus
X\times_{Z}Y\rightarrow\star
is Lagrangian. From Lemma
2.1.17
, since the point is
n
-shifted symplectic, then
X\times_{Z}Y
is
(n-1)
-shifted symplectic.

2.2.2.
Derived intersections and Lagrangian fibrations

The goal of this section is to prove a similar statement to Proposition
2.2.1
but with the additional data of a Lagrangian fibration. This result is from
[
Gra22
]
and has also been generalized in
[
Saf20
]
.

Before going to the main statement, we need the following proposition:

Proposition 2.2.6
.

Suppose we have a sequence
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
of Artin stacks and
\omega
a
n
-shifted symplectic form on Y. Assume that
f
is a Lagrangian morphism and
g
is a Lagrangian fibration. Then there is a canonical equivalence
\mathbb{T}_{L/X}\rightarrow\mathbb{L}_{L/X}[n-1]
.

Proof.

Consider the following commutative diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(g\circ f)^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{L/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{Y/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}_{L/Y}[n-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}\mathbb{L}_{Y}[n]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}\mathbb{L}_{Y/X}[n]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}_{L/X}[n-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(g\circ f)^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[n]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

In the upper face, every square is bi-Cartesian because both the outer square and the right most square are bi-Cartesian. Every non-dashed vertical arrow is an equivalence by assumption (because of the various non-degeneracy conditions). Focusing on the right hand cube, it sends the upper homotopy bi-Cartesian square to the bottom square which is also homotopy bi-Cartesian. The homotopy cofiber of
(g\circ f)^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[n]\rightarrow f^{*}\mathbb{L}_{Y}[n]
is
f^{*}\mathbb{L}_{Y/X}[n]
and we obtain a quasi-isomorphism
(g\circ f)^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}\rightarrow f^{*}\mathbb{L}_{Y/X}[n]
depicted as a dashed arrow.

By the same reasoning, since the upper outer square is homotopy bi-Cartesian, it maps to the lower outer square who is also homotopy bi-Cartesian. Moreover, the homotopy fiber of the map
\mathbb{L}_{L/Y}[n-1]\rightarrow f^{*}\mathbb{L}_{Y/X}[n]
is exactly
\mathbb{L}_{L/X}[n-1]
. This proves that there is a canonical quasi-isomorphism
\mathbb{T}_{L/X}\rightarrow\mathbb{L}_{L/X}[n-1]
.
∎

Theorem 2.2.7

(
[
Gra22
, Theorem 3.5]
)
.

Let
Y
be a
n
-shifted symplectic derived Artin stack. Let
f_{i}:L_{i}\rightarrow Y
be Lagrangian morphisms (for
i=1\cdots 2
) and
\pi:Y\rightarrow X
a Lagrangian fibration. Suppose that the maps
\pi\circ f_{i}:L_{i}\rightarrow X
are weak equivalences. Then
P:Z=L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2}\rightarrow X
is a Lagrangian fibration.

Proof.

We summarize the notation in the following diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi}

We also denote
P:=\pi\circ F:Z\rightarrow X
.

To show that we can obtain an isotropic structure, we will show that we have a map of spaces (dropping at first the non-degeneracy condition of the Lagrangian fibration):

\Lag(f_{1},n)\times_{\Symp(Y,n)}\Lag(f_{2},n)\times_{\Symp(Y,n)}\IsoFib(\pi,n)\rightarrow\IsoFib(P,n-1)

If we forget the non-degeneracy of the Lagrangian structure, we obtain an element in
\Iso(f_{1},n)\times_{\Symp(Y,n)}\Iso(f_{2},n)\times_{\Symp(Y,n)}\IsoFib(\pi,n)
and we can show, with formal manipulations of the pullbacks defining the spaces of isotropic structures and isotropic fibrations, that:

\Iso(f_{1},n)\times_{\Symp(Y,n)}\Iso(f_{2},n)\times_{\Symp(Y,n)}\IsoFib(\pi,n)

=\star\times_{\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{1},n)}\Symp(Y,n)\times_{\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{2},n)}\star\times_{\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(Y/X,n)}\star

Using the pullback to
\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2},n)
we obtain a morphism:

\Iso(f_{1},n)\times_{\Symp(Y,n)}\Iso(f_{2},n)\times_{\Symp(Y,n)}\IsoFib(\pi,n)\rightarrow

\star\times_{\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2},n)}\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2},n)\times_{\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2},n)}\star\times_{\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(Y/X,n)}\star

This last space naturally maps to:

\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2},n-1)=\star\times_{\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2},n)}\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2},n)\times_{\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2},n)}\star

Moreover, if we restrict this map to non-degenerate isotropic structures, then it is valued in
\Symp(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2},n-1)
(thanks to Proposition
2.2.1
).

We also have that:

\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(Y/X,n-1)=\star\times_{\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(Y/X,n)}\star

We have the commutative diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2},n-1)\times\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(Y/X,n-1)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(Y/X,n-1)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2},n-1)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2}/X,n-1)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P^{*}}

Since the map
\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(Y/X,n-1)\rightarrow\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2}/X,n-1)
factors through
\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{i}/X,n-1)\simeq\star
, we get a morphism:

\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2},n-1)\times\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(Y/X,n-1)\rightarrow\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2},n-1)\times_{\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2}/X,n-1)}\star

Now if we restrict to
\Symp(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2},n-1)\subset\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2},n-1)
(which amounts to restricting to non-degenerate isotropic structures), we get a map:

\Symp(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2},n-1)\times\mathscr{A}^{2,cl}(Y/X,n-1)\rightarrow\IsoFib(P,n-1)

Therefore we get the desired map and we will consider the isotropic fibration on
P
given by the image along the morphism we just described of the Lagrangian structures and Lagrangian fibration structure given on
f_{1}
,
f_{2}
and
\pi
respectively. We are left to prove the non-degeneracy condition. To do that, we first consider the following diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{Z/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{L_{1}/X}\oplus p_{2}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{L_{2}/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{*}\mathbb{T}_{Y/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{Z}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{L_{1}}\oplus p_{2}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{L_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{*}\mathbb{T}_{Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}\oplus P^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}}

The vertical sequences and the last two horizontal sequences are fibered and therefore so is the first horizontal sequence. The last two horizontal sequences are fibered because the following diagrams are Cartesian:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{Z}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{L_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{2}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{L_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{*}\mathbb{T}_{Y}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{X}}

Using Proposition
2.2.6
and non-degeneracy, we get the following commutative diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{Z/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{L_{1}/X}\oplus p_{2}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{L_{2}/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{*}\mathbb{T}_{Y/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[n-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\left(p_{1}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{L_{1}/X}\oplus p_{2}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{L_{2}/X}\right)[n-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[n]}

where all vertical morphisms are quasi-isomorphisms. The fiber in the lower sequence is exactly
\mathbb{L}_{X}[n-1]
because
p_{1}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{L_{1}/X}\oplus p_{2}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{L_{2}/X}\simeq 0
since
L_{i}\to X
are equivalences. We will call
\alpha:\mathbb{T}_{Z/X}\to P^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[n-1]
the dashed equivalence obtained.

We still need to show that
\alpha
is the morphism used in the criteria for the non-degeneracy of the Lagrangian fibration. Recall that this morphism is given by means of the universal map filling Diagram (
4
):

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{Z/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[n-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{Z}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}_{Z}[n-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}_{Z/X}[n-1]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{P}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sim}

To compare
\alpha
and
\alpha_{P}
, we summarize the construction of
\alpha
and all the equivalences coming from non-degeneracy conditions in the following diagram:

(5)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{Z}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{L_{1}}\oplus p_{2}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{L_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{*}\mathbb{T}_{Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{Z/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{L_{1}/X}\oplus p_{2}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{L_{2}/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{*}\mathbb{T}_{Y/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}_{Z}[n-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\left(p_{1}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{L_{1}/Y}\oplus p_{2}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{L_{2}/Y}\right)[n-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{*}\mathbb{L}_{Y}[n]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[n-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\left(p_{1}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{L_{1}/X}\oplus p_{2}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{L_{2}/X}\right)[n-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[n]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

where all the vertical maps are quasi-isomorphism obtained from the non-degeneracy conditions. We want to prove that
\alpha_{P}
and
\alpha
are homotopic. The relevant data extracted from the Diagram (
5
) is:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{Z/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[n-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{Z}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}_{Z}[n-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{L_{1}/Y}[n-1]\oplus p_{2}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{L_{2}/Y}[n-1]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sim}

The composition:

P^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[n-1]\rightarrow\mathbb{L}_{Z}[n-1]\rightarrow p_{1}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{L_{1}/Y}[n-1]\oplus p_{2}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{L_{2}/Y}[n-1]

factorizes through
0\simeq p_{1}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{L_{1}/X}[n-1]\oplus p_{2}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{L_{2}/X}[n-1]
. This implies that the map
\mathbb{L}_{Z}[n-1]\rightarrow p_{1}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{L_{1}/Y}[n-1]\oplus p_{2}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{L_{2}/Y}[n-1]
factorizes through
\mathbb{L}_{Z/X}[n-1]
and therefore
\alpha
satisfies the same universal property as
\alpha_{P}
, proving that
\alpha
and
\alpha_{P}
are homotopic.
∎

.

This result was generalized in

Remark 2.2.9
.

Similarly to Proposition

\Lag(f_{1},n)\times_{\Symp(Y,n)}\Lag(f_{2},n)\times_{\Symp(Y,n)}\LagFib(\pi,n)\rightarrow\LagFib(P,n)

This is the simply the restriction the map described in the proof of Theorem

to the non-degenerate elements. Forgetting the extra Lagrangian fibration recovers the map in Remark
2.2.2
, that is the following diagram is commutative:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Lag(f_{1},n)\times_{\Symp(Y,n)}\Lag(f_{2},n)\times_{\Symp(Y,n)}\LagFib(\pi,n)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\LagFib(P,n)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Lag(f_{1},n)\times_{\Symp(Y,n)}\Lag(f_{2},n)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Symp(L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2},n-1)}

Example 2.2.10
.

Since the projection
T^{*}X\to X
is a Lagrangian fibration from Example
2.1.22
, and the derived intersection defining the derived critical locus (Definition

) clearly satisfies the condition of Theorem
2.2.7
, we get that
\mathbf{Crit}(f)\to X
is a Lagrangian fibration. This Lagrangian fibration will be studied in details in Section

in good situations.

Remark 2.2.11
.

When
X
is a derived stack and
df=0
, we have that
\mathbf{Crit}(f)\simeq T^{*}[-1]X
,
\omega_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}
is the canonical
(-1)
-shifted symplectic structure on
T^{*}[-1]X
and the Lagrangian fibration obtain is the canonical Lagrangian fibration

of Example
2.1.22
.

2.2.3.
The higher categories of Lagrangians

The idea behind the categorical structure on Lagrangian structures is that given
X
and
Y
,
n
-shifted symplectic derived stacks, a Lagrangian correspondence from
X
to
Y
(Definition
2.1.18
) can be though of as a kind of arrow from
X
to
Y
. But it turns out that this idea is a specific instance of a categorical structure on the set of Lagrangians structures over a fixed base given by a
n
-shifted symplectic derived stacks
X
(see Definition
2.2.17
).

In full generality, it is shown in
[
CHS21
]
that we can construct an
(\infty,n)
-category of Lagrangians as a
n
-fold Segal space. We are going to restrict ourselves to the
1
- and
2
-categorical structures.

The goal of this section is to present rather explicitly the (weak)
2
-category of Lagrangian as described in
[
ABB17
]
and give a new constructions of Lagrangian correspondences. The main goal of this section is to give the framework to prove Theorem
2.2.23
which is another “derived intersection theorem” that produces new Lagrangian correspondences (see Theorem
2.2.23
).

First recall, from Definition
2.1.18
, that a Lagrangian correspondence from
X
to
Y
is given by a Lagrangian
L\to X\times\overline{Y}
and is depicted by the diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{Y}}

where
\overline{Y}
is the same derived stack as
Y
but endowed with the “opposite” symplectic structure
-\omega_{Y}
.

Observe that there is an equivalence:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Lag(X)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Lag(\overline{X})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sim}

In particular, any Lagrangian correspondence
L
from
X
to
Y
induces an opposite
54
54

54

The “opposite” Lagrangian does not means that it is an inverse for the composition. However we will see in Corollary
2.2.22
that there is a natural
2
-morphism:

1_{X\times\overline{X}}\Rightarrow L\circ\overline{L}

Lagrangian correspondence,
\overline{L}
from
Y
to
X
and therefore we get a Lagrangian correspondence:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{X}}

.

From now on, we will make an abuse of notation and not write the overline
\overline{X}
in the diagrams describing the Lagrangian correspondence with the convention that the stack on the right is the one with the opposite structure. A Lagrangian from
X
to
Y
and its opposite will be respectively denoted by

The first step toward finding categorical structure on Lagrangian structures is the following theorem giving a way to compose Lagrangian correspondences.

Theorem 2.2.13

(
[
Cal15
, Theorem 4.4]
)
.

Given
L_{1}
and
L_{2}
Lagrangian correspondences from
X
to
Y
and
Y
to
XZ
respectively, then there is a Lagrangian structure from
X
to
Z
given by
L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2}
. The construction gives a map:

\mathbf{Lag}\left(X\times\overline{Y}\right)\times_{\Symp(Y,n)}\mathbf{Lag}\left(Y\times\overline{Z}\right)\to\mathbf{Lag}\left(X\times\overline{Z}\right)

This composition can be depicted by the following diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{1}\times_{Y}L_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}

This Theorem is itself a special case of Lemma
2.2.15
that will enable us to describe a composition is some category whose objects will be Lagrangian morphisms.

Remark 2.2.14
.

From this we can define a category
\LagCor_{n}
such that:

–

the objects are
n
-shifted symplectic derived stacks.

–

\LagCor_{n}(X,Y)
is the equivalence classes of Lagrangian correspondences from
X
to
Y
for the equivalence relation given by
Lagrangeomorphism
(see Warning
2.2.16
for an explanation of what Lagrangeomorphisms are).

Now we can rephrase and generalize this category solely in terms of Lagrangian structures thanks to the following observations:

–

A
n
-shifted symplectic structure on
X
is given by a Lagrangian morphism
X\to\star_{n+1}
where
\star_{n+1}
is seen together with the
n+1
-shifted symplectic structure
0
(see Lemma
2.1.17
).

–

A Lagrangian structure on
L\to X
is equivalent to a Lagrangian correspondence:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\star_{n}}

Therefore the objects of
\LagCor_{n}
are Lagrangian morphisms
X\to\star_{n+1}
, and a morphism from
X
to
Y
is a Lagrangian in the derived intersection
55
55

55

The shifted symplectic structure on the derived intersection is obtained from Proposition
2.2.1
where the construction of the shifted symplectic structure proves that
X\times_{\star_{n+1}}Y\simeq X\times\overline{Y}
as
n
-shifted symplectic derived stacks.

L\to X\times_{\star_{n+1}}Y\simeq X\times\overline{Y}
(up to Lagrangeomorphism).

In order to generalize this, pick a base given by a
n
-shifted symplectic derived stack
X
(here
X
plays the role of
\star_{n+1}
). Given two Lagrangians
L_{1}\to X
and
L_{2}\to X
, we can define a morphism from
L_{1}
to
L_{2}
to be a data of a Lagrangian morphism

by taking the derived intersection of Lagrangian morphisms. We then need a notion of composition which is given by the following lemma:

Lemma 2.2.15

(
[
ABB17
, Corollary 2.15]
)
.

Let

,
i=1..3
be Lagrangian morphism in

(for a fixed symplectic structure on

). Then there is a map:

\Lag(L_{1}\times_{X}L_{2})\times\Lag(L_{2}\times_{X}L_{3})\to\Lag(L_{1}\times_{X}L_{3})

that sends the Lagrangians
N_{1}\to L_{1}\times_{X}L_{2}
and
N_{2}\to L_{2}\times_{X}L_{3}
to a Lagrangian structure on:

N_{1}\times_{L_{2}}N_{2}\to L_{1}\times_{X}L_{3}

Warning 2.2.16
.

The composition obtained by Lemma
2.2.15
is not associative on the nose, but is so
up to Lagrangeomorphism
.
A Lagrangeomorphism (see
[
ABB17
, Definition 3.2]
) between two Lagrangian
L_{1}\to X
and
L_{2}\to X
is an equivalence of derived stacks
L_{1}\to L_{2}
commuting with the morphisms to
X
together with a Lagrangian structures on the natural map:

L_{1}\to L_{1}\times_{X}L_{2}

Then
[
ABB17
, Proposition 3.7]
tells us that the composition defined by Lemma
2.2.15
is associative up to canonical Lagrangeomorphism.

We can now define a category of Lagrangians over a fixed
n
-shifted shifted symplectic derived stack.

Definition 2.2.17
.

Let

–

–

up to Lagrangeomorphisms (see Warning

). The composition is given by Lemma
2.2.15
.

–

The unit morphism of a Lagrangian

is given by:

with the diagonal Lagrangian structure (see Proposition

(

, Corollary 2.19]
)

Consider a Lagrangian morphism

-shifted symplectic structure on

obtained by derived intersection.

Example 2.2.19

Corollary 2.2.22
.

Take

The purpose of presenting this

-category in such details is to obtain a

-categorical proof of the following theorem, which gives us a mean to construct
Lagrangian correspondences
via derived Lagrangian intersections.

Theorem 2.2.23
.

Consider a Lagrangian correspondence
L
from
X
to
Y
. Let
L_{1}
,
L_{2}
be two Lagrangian morphisms in
X
. Consider the diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{1}\times_{X}L}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{1}\times_{X}L}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{2}\times_{X}L}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{2}\times_{X}L}

The maps
L_{i}\times_{X}L\to Y
are Lagrangian and taking the limit long the vertical morphisms, we get a Lagrangian correspondence:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{1}\times_{X}L\times_{X}L_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{1}\times_{X}L_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{1}\times_{X}L\times_{Y}L_{2}\times_{X}L}

Proof.

We work in the
2
-category
\Lagb(\star_{n+1})
.
To show that
L_{i}\times_{X}L\to Y
is Lagrangian it is enough to view it as the composition of
1
-morphisms in
\Lagb(\star_{n+1})
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\star}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L}

Consider the following sequence of
1
-morphisms:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\star}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\star}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{L}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{L}_{2}}

The direct composition of these morphism is given by:

L_{1}\times_{X}L\times_{Y}L\times_{X}L_{2}

The key is to remember that there is a

-morphism (from Corollary

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L\times_{Y}L}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L}

where
1_{X}
the unit corresponding to the diagonal Lagrangian
X\to X\times X
and

is defined as the diagonal Lagrangian morphism
L\to\simeq L\times_{X\times Y}L
. Precomposing by

and post-composing by

we sucessively get the

-morphisms:

L_{1}\times_{X}L:L_{1}\Rightarrow L_{1}\times_{X}L\times_{Y}L

This last

\begin{split}L_{1}\times_{X}L\times_{X}L_{2}\to&(L_{1}\times_{X}L_{2})\times_{\star_{n+1}}(L_{1}\times_{X}L\times_{Y}L_{2}\times_{X}L)\\
&\simeq(L_{1}\times_{X}L_{2})\times(\overline{L_{1}\times_{X}L\times_{Y}L_{2}\times_{X}L})\end{split}

∎

2.3.
Examples of Constructions of Lagrangian Fibrations

2.3.1.
Derived critical locus

We discuss here some general result on the shifted symplectic geometry of the derived critical locus. First we want to understand in general the
(-1)
-shifted symplectic form on
\mathbf{Crit}(f)
. We use the universal property of the tautological
1
-form (Lemma
2.1.4
) to see that
(df)^{*}\omega=0
(with
\omega=d_{\mathrm{dR}}\lambda_{X}
the canonical symplectic structure on

). Using the appropriate replacement to compute the derived tensor product appearing in the proof of Proposition
1.2.21
,
\omega
induces a closed 2-form on
\mathbf{Spec}_{X}\left(\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}\left(\mathbb{T}_{X}[1]\oplus\mathbb{T}_{X}\right)\right)

(plus the differentials on

and

), the tautological

on

induces a closed 2-form on

58
58

58

Note that both

to
\omega
.
between

and

. We then have that the

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p^{*}\omega=0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\omega_{-1}}

The proof of Proposition

We have seen in Remark

(6)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)/X}\simeq 0\times_{\mathbb{L}_{T^{*}X/X}}0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0\times_{\pi_{X}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}}0\simeq\pi^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]}

Where
