2.3.2.
Non-degenerate functionals

We consider the example of the derived critical locus where
f
may have a family of critical points which are all non-degenerate in the directions normal to the strict critical locus. We want to understand the quasi-isomorphism describing the non-degeneracy condition of the Lagrangian fibration
\mathbf{Crit}(f)\to X
in that situation.

We denote by
S
the strict critical locus, which comes with a closed immersion
i:S\rightarrow X
and whose structure sheaf is
\mathscr{O}_{S}=i^{-1}{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{O}_{X}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{I}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{O}_{X}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{I}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{O}_{X}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{I}$}}{\raisebox{1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{O}_{X}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{I}$}}}
with
I=\langle df.v,\ v\in\mathbb{T}_{X}\rangle
.

We assume that both
X
and
S
are smooth algebraic varieties. We denote by
\mathbf{Crit}(f)
the derived critical locus of
f
and we get a canonical morphism:

\lambda:S\rightarrow\mathbf{Crit}(f)

In order to define the Hessian quadratic form and the non-degeneracy condition, we need to assume that the closed immersion
S\hookrightarrow X
has a first order splitting. Concretely, we assume in this Section that the following fiber sequence splits:

(7)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{S}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{S/X}[1]}

This assumption is necessary to be able to restrict
Q
to the normal part
\mathbb{T}_{S/X}[1]
.

Definition 2.3.2
.

The
Hessian quadratic form
is defined by the symmetric bilinear map:

\begin{array}[]{ccccl}Q&:&\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{S}}^{2}i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}&\to&\mathscr{O}_{S}\\
&&(w,v)&\mapsto&d(df.v).w\\
\end{array}

We define non-degeneracy to be along the "normal" direction to
S
, by considering the following diagram:

(8)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{S}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{S/X}[1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}_{S/X}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}_{S}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{Q}}

Both rows are split fiber sequences (by assumption in Diagram (
7
)). The left and right vertical maps are the zero map because
Q
restricted to
\mathbb{T}_{S}
is zero and, since
Q
is symmetric,
Q
composed with the projection to
\mathbb{L}_{S}
is also zero. We obtain a map
\widetilde{Q}
(using
Q
and following the section and retract of the fiber sequences) which corresponds to the map induced by
Q
on the normal bundle. Then the
non-degeneracy condition
is the requirement that
\widetilde{Q}
is a quasi-isomorphism.

Since the differential on
\mathscr{O}_{\textbf{Crit}(f)}
is
\delta=\iota_{df}
(see Proposition
1.2.21
), we have the commutative diagram in
\textbf{QC}(S)
:

(9)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{*}\mathscr{O}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota_{df}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d_{\mathrm{dR}}}

We will abusively write

for the map of degree
1
corresponding to the composition

of degree
0
.

In general, the natural map
\lambda:S\rightarrow\mathbf{Crit}(f)
is not an equivalence. This is due to the fact that the partial derivatives of
f
will not in general form a regular sequence and therefore
\mathbf{Crit}(f)
has higher homology. The default to be a regular sequence comes from vector fields that annihilate

. Such vector fields are in fact vector fields on
S
when

is non-degenerate. With that idea in mind, we show that an equivalent description of
\mathbf{Crit}(f)
is given by

when

is non-degenerate.

Proposition 2.3.3

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T^{*}[-1]S}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S}

Under our first order splitting assumption (Diagram (

)), the natural map

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}

We want to pull-back these zero sections along the maps induced by

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T^{*}X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{*}T^{*}X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T^{*}S}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces df}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{*}df=0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}

This induces the following morphisms between the pull-backs:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Crit}(f)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S\times_{i^{*}T^{*}X}S}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T^{*}[-1]S}

We obtain a map
\Phi:T^{*}[-1]S\rightarrow\mathbf{Crit}(f)
. The maps we obtain come from the universal properties of the pull-backs therefore if we denote
s_{0}:X\rightarrow T^{*}X
the zero section, we have
s_{0}\circ\pi\circ\Phi=s_{0}\circ i\circ\pi_{S}
. If we compose by the projection
\pi_{X}:T^{*}X\rightarrow X
, we get
\pi\circ\Phi=i\circ\pi_{S}
.
∎

\Phi
gives a relationship between the Lagrangian fibration structures on
T^{*}[-1]S\rightarrow S
and
\mathbf{Crit}(f)\rightarrow X
which we now analyse. The idea is to show that the difference between these Lagrangian fibrations is in fact controlled by
\widetilde{Q}
(see Proposition
2.3.7
and Remark
2.3.9
).

Lemma 2.3.4
.

\Phi
induces a morphism
\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}[-1]S/S}\rightarrow\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)/X}
that fits in the commutative diagram

(10)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}[-1]S/S}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{S}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\pi^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\simeq\pi_{S}^{*}i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{\pi_{S}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{\pi}}

where the bottom horizontal arrow is the pull-back along
\pi_{S}
of the section
\mathbb{L}_{S}[-1]\rightarrow i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]
in the dual of the split fiber sequence (
7
).

Proof.

The homotopy pull-back,
\mathbf{Crit}(f)=X\times_{T^{*}X}^{h}X
lives over
X
. We get the equivalences:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{X/X}\times_{{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}X}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}X}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}X}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}X}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}}}}^{h}\mathbb{T}_{X/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\star\times_{{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}X}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}X}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}X}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}X}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}}}}^{h}\star}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

Proposition
2.1.23
tells us that the canonical fibrations on the cotangent stacks are the canonical ones and therefore behave functorially (using Proposition
1.2.31
). This implies that the following commutative square is commutative:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}S/S}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}X/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{S}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta_{S}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}s}

where
s
is the section in the dual of the split fiber sequence (
7
). From Definition
2.1.20

we know that both
\alpha_{\pi_{S}}
and
\alpha_{\pi}
are the morphism induced by the morphisms
\beta_{S}
and
\beta_{X}
via Diagram (
6
). We then obtain the commutative diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}[-1]S/S}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0\times_{\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}S/S}}^{h}0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{S}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\left(0\times_{\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}X/X}}^{h}0\right)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\pi^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0\times_{\beta_{S}}^{h}0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0\times_{\beta_{X}}^{h}0}

where the composition of the horizontal maps are exactly
\alpha_{\pi_{S}}
and
\alpha_{\pi}
thanks to Proposition
2.1.23
.
∎

Lemma 2.3.5
.

We first remark that
\Phi^{*}\mathbb{L}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}
can be described, as a sheaf of graded modules (forgetting the differential), by:

\Phi^{*}\mathbb{L}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}\simeq\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{S}}\left(\mathbb{T}_{S}[1]\right)\otimes_{\mathscr{O}_{S}}\left(i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}\oplus i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}[1]\right)

where
\mathbb{L}_{X}
is generated by terms of the form
dg
with
g\in\mathscr{O}_{X}
and
\mathbb{T}_{X}[1]
is generated by terms of the form
d\xi
with
\xi\in\mathbb{T}_{X}[1]\subset\mathscr{O}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}
. Then, the internal differential on
\Phi^{*}\mathbb{L}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}
is characterised by
Q=d\circ\iota_{df}
via
\delta(d\xi)=Q(\xi)
and
\delta(dg)=0
.

Proof.

The differential on
\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{S}}\left(\mathbb{T}_{S}[1]\right)\otimes_{\mathscr{O}_{S}}\left(i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}\oplus i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}[1]\right)
is
\mathscr{O}_{T^{*}[-1]S}
-linear because
\iota_{df}
is zero on
\mathbb{T}_{S}[1]
. Moreover, for
\xi\in\mathbb{T}_{X}[1]\subset\mathscr{O}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}=\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}\mathbb{T}_{X}[1]
, we have
\delta\circ d(\xi)=d\circ\delta(\xi)=d\circ\iota_{df}(\xi)=Q(\xi)
(see Diagram (
9
)), and for
g\in\mathscr{O}_{X}
,
\delta\circ d(g)=d\circ\delta g=0
.
∎

Lemma 2.3.6
.

The composition:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\pi^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{\pi}}

is given by
\pi_{S}^{*}Q
. Similarly, the composition:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{S}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}[-1]S/S}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{S}[-1]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{\pi_{S}}}

is
0
(the restriction of
\pi_{S}^{*}Q
to
S
).

Proof.

The left morphism is the morphism fitting in the fiber sequence:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}}

Which gives us:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\pi^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\pi^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\oplus\Phi^{*}\pi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{\pi}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

The second row can be seen as the extension (by
\pi_{S}^{*}
) of the fiber sequence:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\oplus i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}}

Since
X
and
S
are smooth,
i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}[-1]
and
i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]
are both quasi-isomorphic to complexes concentrated in a single degree. This imposes that the dashed arrow is equivalent to the connecting morphism of the induced long exact sequence in cohomology. Therefore, it is equivalent to the map that sends a section
s
in
i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}[-1]
to its differential, in
i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\oplus i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}
, which can in turn be seen as an element in
i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}
. More concretely, denote
\tilde{s}
any lift of
s
to an element in
i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-2]\oplus i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}[-1]
. Using Lemma
2.3.5
, its differential is given by

Q(s)=Q(\tilde{s})\in i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\subset i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]\oplus i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}.

We then apply
\pi_{S}^{*}
to get the sequence we want. The second part of the statement is proven the same way.
∎

Proposition 2.3.7
.

The map
\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}[-1]S}\rightarrow\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}
induced by
\Phi
is an equivalence if and only if
Q
is non-degenerate.

Proof.

First, using the equivalences
\alpha_{\pi}:\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)/X}\rightarrow\pi_{S}^{*}i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]
and
\alpha_{\pi_{S}}:\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}[-1]S/S}\rightarrow\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{S}[-1]
, we can show that the cofiber of
\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}[-1]S/S}\rightarrow\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)/X}
is equivalent to
\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{S/X}[-2]
. Then Lemma
2.3.4
and
2.3.6
ensure that the upper half of the following diagram is commutative:

(11)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{S}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{S/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}[-1]S/S}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{S/X}[-2]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}[-1]S}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{F}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{Q}}

This diagram is then commutative and all rows and columns are cofiber sequences and in particular
\mathscr{F}
is both the homotopy cofiber of
\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}[-1]S}\rightarrow\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}
and the homotopy cofiber of
\widetilde{Q}
. In particular, the homotopy cofiber of
\widetilde{Q}
is zero if and only the homotopy cofiber of
\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}[-1]S}\rightarrow\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}
is also zero.
∎

We now decompose
\alpha_{\pi}
into a part along
S
and a part normal to
S
. This decomposition is by means of split fibered sequences coming from the split fiber sequence (
7
).

Proposition 2.3.8
.

When
Q
is non-degenerate, the maps expressing the non-degeneracy of the Lagrangian fibrations fit in the commutative diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}[-1]S/S}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{S/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{S}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}_{S/X}[-1]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{\pi_{S}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{\pi}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{Q}}

where the rows are fiber sequences.

Proof.

First, when
Q
is non-degenerate, the top horizontal sequence is fibered and comes from the following diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}[-1]S/S}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{S/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}[-1]S}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{S}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{S}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{S}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{S}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{S}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}}}}[1]}

where all rows and columns are fibered and the cofiber of the second row is
0
thanks to Proposition
2.3.7
since we assumed that
Q
is non-degenerate. Using Lemma
2.3.4
and Lemma
2.3.6
, we obtain the following commutative diagram:

(12)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{S}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{S/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}[-1]S/S}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{S/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{S}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{S/X}[-2]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{Q}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{\pi_{S}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{\pi}}

The only map the dashed arrow can be, in order to make the diagram commutative, is
\widetilde{Q}
.
∎

Remark 2.3.9
.

If we do not assume
Q
non-degenerate, the cofiber
\mathscr{F}
of the map
\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}[-1]S}\rightarrow\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}
will be non zero. We will denote by
\mathscr{G}
the fiber of the natural map
\mathscr{F}\rightarrow\mathbb{T}_{S/X}
. Then we can rewrite Diagram (
12
) as

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{S}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{S/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{T^{*}[-1]S/S}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{G}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{S}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi^{*}i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{X}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{S/X}[-2]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{Q}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{\pi_{S}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{\pi}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{N}}

The map
\alpha_{N}:\mathscr{G}\rightarrow\pi_{S}^{*}\mathbb{L}_{S/X}[-2]
represent the "difference" between the maps
\alpha_{\pi}
and
\alpha_{\pi_{S}}
from the Lagrangian fibrations.
\alpha_{N}
is still related to
\widetilde{Q}
in the sense that the following diagram is commutative:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{S/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{G}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}_{S/X}[-2]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{Q}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{N}}

Therefore the restriction of
\alpha_{N}
to
\mathbb{T}_{S/X}
is again
\widetilde{Q}
.

Remark 2.3.10
.

As a non-example if we take
f:\mathbb{A}^{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1}
sending
X
to
\frac{X^{3}}{3}
, the basic assumptions that made this section work are failing. The strict critical locus
S
is not smooth since it is a fat point, and the sequence (
7
) does not split.

2.3.3.
G
-equivariant twisted cotangents

For
X
a smooth scheme, a twisted cotangent stack is a twist of the ordinary cotangent stack by a closed
1
-form of degree
1
on
X
,
\alpha\in H^{1}(X,\Omega_{X}^{1,\mathrm{cl}})
. Such a closed form has an underlying 1-form of degree 1 that corresponds to a morphism
\alpha:X\rightarrow T^{*}[1]X
. The
twisted cotangent bundle
associated to
\alpha
is defined to be the following pull-back:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T_{\alpha}^{*}X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T^{*}[1]X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}

We refer to
[
Hab16
]
for more information on the relation between this definition and the usual definition of twisted cotangent bundles. This is then a derived intersection of Lagrangians (see Example
2.1.12
) and therefore it is
0
-shifted symplectic. Moreover the Lagrangian fibration
T^{*}[1]X\to X
follows the assumptions of Theorem
2.2.7
and therefore the map
T_{\alpha}^{*}X\rightarrow X
has a Lagrangian fibration structure.

Now take
G
an algebraic group acting on the algebraic variety
X
. Consider a character
\chi:G\rightarrow\mathbb{G}_{m}
. We have the logarithmic form on
\mathbb{G}_{m}
given by a map
\mathbb{G}_{m}\rightarrow\mathscr{A}^{1,cl}(-,0)
which sends
t
to
t^{-1}dt
. We get a closed
1
-form on
G
described by the composition:

G\rightarrow\mathbb{G}_{m}\rightarrow\mathscr{A}^{1,cl}(-,0)

This is also a group morphism for the additive structure on
\mathscr{A}^{1,cl}(-,0)
. We can therefore pass to classifying spaces and obtain a
1
-shifted closed
1
-form on
\mathbf{B}G
:

\alpha_{\chi}:\mathbf{B}G\rightarrow\mathbf{B}\mathscr{A}^{1,cl}(-,0)=\mathscr{A}^{1,cl}(-,1)

We can consider the pull-back of
\alpha_{\chi}
along the
G
-equivariant moment map:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.69293pt}{$\displaystyle{T^{*}X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{3.44293pt}{$\textstyle{T^{*}X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{2.67209pt}{$\scriptstyle{T^{*}X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.8854pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{T^{*}X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{G}$}}}\right]\times_{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.89883pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{2.64883pt}{$\textstyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.70331pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.31978pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{G}$}}}\right]}\mathbf{B}G}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{B}G}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.69293pt}{$\displaystyle{T^{*}X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{3.44293pt}{$\textstyle{T^{*}X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{2.67209pt}{$\scriptstyle{T^{*}X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.8854pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{T^{*}X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{G}$}}}\right]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.69293pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{3.44293pt}{$\textstyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{2.67209pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.8854pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathfrak{g}^{*}}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{G}$}}}\right]\simeq T^{*}[1]\mathbf{B}G}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{\chi}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mu}

It turns out that the equivariant moment map
\left[\mu\right]
is Lagrangian (see Proposition

3.
On the Derived Geometry of Lie Algebroids

Lie algebroids are the natural objects controlling
infinitesimal actions
. They are, in some sens, some kind of “generalized tangent bundle” and they determine (through the
anchor
) a sheaf of tangent vectors which are though as the infinitesimal directions along which a Lie algebroid acts. The reason Lie algebroids are the correct objects to encode infinitesimal actions can be explained by the heuristic saying that:

Lie algebroids are to Lie groupoids what Lie algebras are to Lie groups

In fact given a smooth groupoid (over a “nice enough” base):

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{G}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t}

with
e:X\to\mathscr{G}
the unit, we can construct a Lie algebroid (see Construction
4.2.1
) with anchor given by the natural map:

\rho:e^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathscr{G}/X}^{s}\to\mathbb{T}_{X}

The analogy is not perfect as not all Lie algebroids integrate to a
smooth groupoid
(Definition
4.1.6
). However, we will see in Section
4.2.1
that they integrate to a more general type of object, called “formal groupoids” (Definition
4.1.6
).

We will be interested, in Section
4
, by the study of “infinitesimal” equivariant geometry, as this kind of geometry naturally appears in the construction of the BV complex in Section
5
.

As we will see, equivariant geometry is simply the study of the geometry of the “quotient” stack. In the infinitesimal case, we need to make sense of the notion of
infinitesimal quotient stack
, which is the purpose of Section
3.2.1
.

We start in Section
3.1
by recalling the definition and homotopy theory of Lie algebroids mainly following
[
Nui19a
,
Nui19b
]
. In Section
3.2.1
, we define the notion of infinitesimal quotient stack of a Lie algebroid. We will see that these are indeed infinitesimal versions of the quotient by a groupoid in Section
4.2.1
by showing that they are (in good situations) the formal completions of the projections of the quotient stacks by smooth groupoids.

In Section
3.3
, we discuss the notion of infinitesimal action of a Lie algebroid (up to homotopy) on a map,
f:Y\to X
, where
X
is the base of the Lie algebroid. We also discuss the case of actions given by
representations up to homotopy
(Section
3.3.1
) with in particular the examples of the adjoint and coadjoint actions.

As we will work in formal geometry, from now on, all stacks will be locally finitely presented. Moreover, we will assume that all our stacks admit a cotangent complex.

3.1.
Lie and
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-Algebroids

In this section, we recall the definitions and homotopy theory of Lie and
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
algebroids. This section mainly follows
[
Nui19b
,
Nui19a
]
.

3.1.1.
Definitions and basic properties of Lie algebroids

We want to discuss the notion of Lie algebroid over a derived stack
X
. In differential geometry, this would be defined as some structure on the module of global sections of a vector bundle.

In algebraic geometry it is not enough to work on the algebra of global sections (because it does not recover the structure of a Lie algebroid locally), and we should therefore define Lie algebroids as an
\infty
-sheaf
of Lie algebroid structures.

We will not do that as this is beyond our goals to develop such a theory. Therefore, in order to make sense of the homotopy theory of Lie algebroids, we restrict ourselves to the context used in
[
Nui19a
,
Nui19b
]
. In practice, we are restricting ourselves to work over an affine base
X:=\mathbf{Spec}(A)
of almost finite presentation. In other words, since the base is affine, we go back to the situation where we can define the structure of a Lie algebroid on the module of global sections.

Definition 3.1.1

(
[
Nui19b
, Definition 2.1]
)
.

A
Lie algebroid over
A\in\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{\leq 0}}
is an
A
-module
\mathscr{L}
together with a
k
-linear Lie algebra structure and an
anchor map

\rho:\mathscr{L}\to\mathbb{T}_{A}
such that:

–

\rho
is a map of
A
-module and of Lie algebras
59
59

59

The fact that this is a Lie algebra morphism is in fact a consequence of the Leibniz rule and the Jacobi identity of the Lie bracket.
.

–

The failure of the Lie bracket to be
A
-linear is controlled by a Leibniz formula:

\left[w,fv\right]=(-1)^{|f||w|}f\left[w,v\right]+\rho(w)(f).v

Recall from Notation
1.2.10
that we denote by
\mathscr{L}
the linear stack associated to
\mathscr{L}
with anchor
\rho:L\to TX
. We will interchangeably refer to
L
and
\mathscr{L}
as a Lie algebroid over
X
.

Definition 3.1.2
.

A morphism of Lie algebroids over
A
is a morphism
f:\mathscr{L}\to\mathscr{L}^{\prime}
such that:

–

f
commutes with the anchors.

–

f
defines a morphism of the underlying Lie algebras.

This defines a category of Lie algebroids over
A
together with the notion of morphisms from Definition
3.1.2
. Moreover, we say that
f
is a weak equivalence if the underlying map of
A
-modules is a quasi-isomorphism
60
60

60

In particular, this definition implies that the forgetful functor
\mathrm{LieAlgd}_{A}\to\Mod_{A}
is conservative.
. Localizing at these weak-equivalences, this defines the
\infty
-category of Lie algebroids (which we also denote by
\mathrm{LieAlgd}_{A}
). We will see in Section
3.1.2
that this category can also be viewed as a semi model category.

Remark 3.1.3
.

Take
A\in\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{\leq 0}}
and
\mathscr{L}\in\Mod_{A}
. A structure of Lie algebroid on
\mathscr{L}
is the data of a Lie algebroid
\mathscr{L}^{\prime}
together with a weak equivalence of the underlying
A
-modules:

\mathscr{L}\simeq\mathscr{L}^{\prime}

In fact there is an
\infty
-category of Lie algebroid structures on
\mathscr{L}
given by the pullback of
\infty
-categories:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{LieAlgd}_{A}(\mathscr{L})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{LieAlgd}_{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\star}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Mod_{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}}

Therefore a Lie algebroid structure on an
A
-module
\mathscr{L}
is the data of a Lie algebroid whose underlying
A
-module is only weakly equivalent to
\mathscr{L}
. Unfortunately, it is not possible to transfer the structure of Lie algebroid along weak equivalences. However, it is possible to transfer a “homotopy Lie algebroid structure” and get
\infty
-quasi-isomorphisms.

Indeed, similarly to the case of Lie algebras, we can consider the notion of homotopy Lie algebroid, which we will call
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroid. Just like for Lie algebras and
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebras, it is a more complicated object but thanks to Corollary
3.1.14
, it turns out that it describes an
\infty
-category equivalent to that of Lie algebroids. The main advantage of
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroids lies in the notion of
\infty
-morphism (Definition
3.1.5
) for which we have a version of the homotopy transfer theorem (Section
3.4
).

Definition 3.1.4

(
[
Nui19a
, Definition 2.5]
)
.

A
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroid over an algebra
A\in\mathrm{cdga}
is an
A
-modules
\mathscr{L}
with the structure of a
k
-linear
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebras and an anchor map
\rho:\mathscr{L}\to\mathbb{T}_{A}
such that:

–

\rho
is both a map of
A
-module and of
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebra.

–

The failure of the
2
-bracket to be
A
-linear is controlled by the Leibniz rule:

\left[w,fv\right]=(-1)^{|f||w|}f\left[w,v\right]+\rho(w)(f).v

–

For
n\geq 3
, the
n
-ary bracket is
A
-linear:

\left[v_{1},\cdots,fv_{n}\right]_{n}=(-1)^{|f|\left(|v_{1}|+\cdots+|v_{n-1}|\right)}f\left[v_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\right]

A morphism of
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroids over
A
is a morphism
f:\mathscr{L}\to\mathscr{L}^{\prime}
such that:

–

f
commutes with the anchors.

–

f
defines a morphism of the underlying
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebras.

This defines a category of
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroids over
A
.

Moreover, we say that
f
is a weak equivalence if the underlying map of
A
-modules is a quasi-isomorphism
61
61

61

In particular, this definition implies that the forgetful functor
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}\mathrm{Algd}_{A}\to\Mod_{A}
is conservative.
. Localizing at these weak-equivalences, this defines the
\infty
-category of
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroids (which we also denote by
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}\mathrm{Algd}_{A}
). This
\infty
-category is equivalent to the localization of a semi-model category also denoted by
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}\mathrm{Algd}_{A}
.

Although this definition of morphism is simple, it is too strict. Instead, we want to define a notion of morphism that only respects the
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-structures up to homotopy. Again, up to homotopy, this changes nothing. However this is the correct notion of “weak” morphism that will appear in the homotopy transfer theorem.

Definition 3.1.5

(
[
PS20
, Definition 2.2]
)
.

A
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-morphism of
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroids over
A
,
f:\mathscr{L}\rightsquigarrow\mathscr{L}^{\prime}
, is given by
A
-linear skew-symmetric maps for
n\geq 1
:

f_{n}:\mathscr{L}^{\otimes n}\to\mathscr{L}^{\prime}[1-n]

such that:

–

f_{1}
commutes with the anchors.

–

f
defines an
\infty
-morphism of the underlying
k
-linear
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebras (see
[
LV12
, Proposition 10.2.13]
).

Definition 3.1.6
.

A Lie or
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroid
\mathscr{L}
is called

if the underlying
A
-module of
\mathscr{L}
is perfect.

3.1.2.
Homotopy theory for Lie algebroid

We will extract the essential elements of homotopy theory of Lie and
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
algebroid from
[

,
Nui19b
]
. This sets up to necessary homotopy theory and the most important idea of this section is that up to homotopy, Lie algebroids and

-algebroids give equivalent

Theorem 3.1.10

(
[
Nui19a
, Theorem 3.1]
)
.

The categories

and

both admit a right proper, tractable semi-model structure such that:

–

A map is a weak equivalence if and only if it is a quasi-isomorphism
64
64

64

These are the same weak equivalences we discussed in Definition
3.1.2
. Therefore, this makes this definition a (semi)-model for the
\infty
-categories of Lie and
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
algebroids over
A
.
.

–

A map is a fibration if and only if it is a degreewise surjection.

Remark 3.1.11
.

The classes of weak equivalences and fibrations given by Theorem

do not define a model structure as there is in general no fibrant replacement as explained in
[

, Example 3.2]
.

Theorem 3.1.12

(
[
Nui19a
, Theorem 3.3]
)
.

The forgetful functors:

U:\mathrm{LieAlgd}_{A}\to\Mod_{A}^{/\mathbb{T}_{A}}\qquad\mathscr{L}_{\infty}\mathrm{Algd}_{A}\to\Mod_{A}^{/\mathbb{T}_{A}}

are right Quillen functors with the following properties:

–

they preserve cofibrant objects.

–

they preserve sifted homotopy colimits.

The homotopy theory of Lie algebras and Lie algebroids are also related thanks to the following result:

There is a Quillen adjunction

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Lie}_{A}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{ker}}

3.2.
Infinitesimal Quotient by a Lie Algebroid and Geometric Properties

The notion of “infinitesimal quotient” by an infinitesimal action is not an obvious one. More often than not in the literature, given a Lie algebroid (i.e. an infinitesimal action on its base), its infinitesimal quotient is solely defined algebraically by the Chevalley–Eilenberg algebra of the Lie algebroid (see for example
[
PS20
]
). However there are two problems; the choice of the Chevalley–Eilenberg algebra as a representative of derived infinitesimal invariants is a priori not canonical, and the relation to a notion of geometric
infinitesimal quotient
is unclear
66
66

66

As we will see, the infinitesimal quotient is in particular
not
the spectrum of the Chevalley–Eilenberg algebra and therefore care must be taken in order to relate algebraic operations on the Chevalley–Eilenberg algebras and geometric operations on the infinitesimal quotients.
.

In this section we provide another construction of a
formal stack
that we call
infinitesimal quotient
and explain its relationship with the Chevalley–Eilenberg algebra. However, it will still not be clear from the definition that this indeed corresponds to a sensible notion of infinitesimal quotient. It is only in Section
4.2.1
that can explain (in good situations) that the infinitesimal quotient of
X
by a Lie algebroid
\mathscr{L}
, is the formal completion of the projection to the quotient by a groupoid
\mathscr{G}

integrating

\mathscr{L}
, giving a factorization:

X\to\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{L}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{L}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{L}}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{L}}$}}}\right]\simeq\widehat{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]_{X}}\to\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]

We will start by describing the relationship between Lie algebroids and

Then from formal moduli problems, we have seen in Section

Definition 3.2.5
.

The underived Chevalley–Eilenberg functor is the functor:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{CE}:\mathrm{LieAlgd}_{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\left(\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}\right)^{\mathrm{op}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\qquad\qquad\mathscr{L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\left(\iHom(\Sym_{A}\mathscr{L}[1],A),\delta_{\mathrm{CE}}\right)}

With the differential

determined by:

–

its action on
A
, given by
\delta_{A}+\rho^{*}\circ d_{\mathrm{dR}}
with

the composition:

–

its action on

, given by

where

,

(\Delta\alpha)(v,w)=\alpha([v,w])-\rho(v)(\alpha(w))+\rho(w)(\alpha(v))

–

In general the formula is given, up to signs, by:

\begin{split}\delta_{\mathbf{CE}}\alpha(v_{1},\cdots,v_{n})=&\delta_{A}\alpha(v_{1},\cdots,v_{n})-\sum\limits_{i}\alpha(v_{1},\cdots,\delta_{\mathscr{L}}v_{i},\cdots,v_{n})\\
&+\sum\limits_{i}\rho(v_{i})\left(\alpha(v_{1},\cdots,v_{i-1},v_{i+1},\cdots,v_{n})\right)-\sum\limits_{i<j}\alpha\left([v_{i},v_{j}],v_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\right)\end{split}

If

is perfect, then this is equivalently a differential on

68

68

\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-1]
.

\left(\cSym_{A}\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-1],\delta_{\mathrm{CE}}\right)

Moreover, this functor induces a functor between the associated

\mathbf{CE}:\mathrm{LieAlgd}_{A}\to\left(\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}\right)^{\mathrm{op}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{CE}:\mathrm{LieAlgd}_{A}}

Remark 3.2.7

Lemma 3.2.8
.

If

In both cases, the element in

\simeq&\mathrm{fiber}(U(\mathscr{L})\to\mathbb{T}_{A}))[n+1]\end{split}

Therefore, this spectrum object corresponds to the

-module
70
70

70

Recall that if

U(\mathscr{L})[1]\oplus^{\rho}\mathbb{T}_{A}

Therefore the functors

Corollary 3.2.9
.

Let
X=\mathbf{Spec}(A)
satisfying Assumptions
3.2.2
.
If
F\in\FMP_{A}
, then thanks to Theorem
3.2.1
, there exists a Lie algebroid
\mathscr{L}
such that
F\simeq\MC_{\mathscr{L}}
. Moreover the relative tangent
\mathbb{T}_{X/F}
has a structure of Lie algebroid making it equivalent to
\mathscr{L}
. In other words, the underlying module of
\mathscr{L}
is weakly equivalent to
\mathbb{T}_{X/F}
.

This is a rather convoluted way to obtain a Lie algebroid structure on the relative tangent,
\mathbb{T}_{X/F}
. The main problem being that the Lie algebroid structure obtained through the functor
\widetilde{\mathbb{T}}_{X/-}
is not explicit. However, in the situation where we take
F=\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)
for
B\in\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}
, we have the following:

Lemma 3.2.10
.

If
X=\mathbf{Spec}(A)
satisfies Assumptions
3.2.2
, we have an equivalence of formal moduli problems:

\MC_{\mathfrak{D}(B)}\simeq\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)

Proof.

As functors on
\mathbf{Art}_{/A}
, we have the equivalences:

\begin{split}\MC_{\mathfrak{D}(B)}\simeq&\underset{\mathrm{LieAlgd}_{A}}{\Map}\left(\mathfrak{D}(-),\mathfrak{D}(B)\right)\\
\simeq&\underset{{\left(\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}\right)}^{\mathrm{op}}}{\Map}\left(\mathbf{CE}(\mathfrak{D}(-)),B\right)\\
\simeq&\underset{\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}}{\Map}\left(B,\mathbf{CE}(\mathfrak{D}(-))\right)\\
\simeq&\underset{\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}}{\Map}\left(B,-\right)\\
\simeq&\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)\end{split}

where the fourth equivalence is due to the fact that
\mathbf{CE}
and
\mathfrak{D}
defines an equivalence between Artinian and good algebras (Proposition
D.2.9
) and therefore the unit and counit of the adjunction are equivalences when restricted to these algebras.
∎

Corollary 3.2.11
.

Let
X:=\mathbf{Spec}(A)
satisfying Assumptions
3.2.2
and
B\in\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}
. We have the following:

(1)

The underlying module of the Lie algebroid associated with the formal spectrum
\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)
is
\mathbb{T}_{A/B}\simeq\mathbb{T}_{X/\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)}
.

(2)

Therefore, from Corollary
3.2.9
,
\mathbb{T}_{A/B}
has a structure of Lie algebroid making it equivalent to
\widetilde{\mathbb{T}}_{X/\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)}
.

(3)

Using Lemma
3.2.10
, there are equivalences of Lie algebroids:

\widetilde{\mathbb{T}}_{X/\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)}\simeq\widetilde{\mathbb{T}}_{X/\MC_{\mathfrak{D}(B)}}\simeq\mathfrak{D}(B)

Therefore the Lie algebroid structure on
\widetilde{\mathbb{T}}_{A/\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)}
is the one coming from
\mathfrak{D}(B)
, described in Proposition
3.2.6
with underlying module
\mathbb{T}_{A/B}
.

Corollary 3.2.12
.

There is an equivalence of Lie algebroids:

\mathbb{T}_{A/\underline{\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)}_{\mathrm{pre}}}\simeq\mathbb{T}_{A/B}

Proof.

Using Corollary
1.3.28
, we have an equivalence of
A
-modules:

\mathbb{T}_{A/\underline{\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)}_{\mathrm{pre}}}\simeq\mathbb{T}_{A/\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)}

This gives
\mathbb{T}_{A/\underline{\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)}_{\mathrm{pre}}}
the structure of Lie algebroid coming from Corollary
3.2.11

∎

Remark 3.2.13
.

In the literature (see for example
[
PS20
]
), the infinitesimal quotient of
X
by a Lie algebroid
\mathscr{L}
is often represented by the Chevalley–Eilenberg algebra of
\mathscr{L}
. Indeed, these algebras describe some kind of “derived invariants”. However, we will see in Section
4.1.2
that
\MC_{\mathscr{L}}
(and its extension to a formal stack) is a better candidate to be some kind of quotient. We can relate
\MC_{\mathscr{L}}
to the Chevalley–Eilenberg algebra of
\mathscr{L}
by using the counit of the adjunction:

\mathscr{L}\to\mathfrak{D}(\mathbf{CE}(\mathscr{L}))

It gives us a morphism:

\MC_{\mathscr{L}}\to\MC_{\mathfrak{D}(\mathbf{CE}(\mathscr{L}))}\simeq\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(\mathbf{CE}(\mathscr{L}))

However, this will in general not be an equivalence as this would correspond to saying that the derived Chevalley–Eilenberg functor is fully-faithful. We expect that we need a variant of
\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(-)
that would remember the graded mixed structure on the Chevalley–Eilenberg algebra to solve this issue for perfect Lie algebroids.

Even if the derived Chevalley–Eilenberg functor behaves rather badly, it turns out that the
underived
Chevalley–Eilenberg functor has nice properties:

Lemma 3.2.14
.

Take
\mathscr{L}
and
\mathscr{L}^{\prime}
two Lie algebroids over

a finitely presented
71
71

71

In particular, from
[

H^{0}(A)
is finitely generated and
\mathbb{T}_{A}
is perfect.
algebra. We consider a map (over

\Phi:\mathrm{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L}^{\prime})\to\mathrm{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})

Assume that the map between the weight

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho^{\prime}}

Then

Proof.

First we want to show that

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathscr{L}^{\prime})^{\vee}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}^{\vee}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}}

For all

\begin{split}\alpha\left([f(v),f(w)]^{\prime}\right)+\rho^{\prime}(f(v))(\alpha(f(w)))-\rho^{\prime}(f(w))(\alpha(f(v)))&\\

using the fact that

and therefore

∎

This lemma has an analogue where we replace Lie algebroids by

-algebroids and graded mixed algebras by weak graded mixed algebras.

Lemma 3.2.16
.

The derived graded mixed Chevalley–Eilenberg functor,
\mathbf{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
, is conservative when restricted to perfect Lie algebroids.

Proof.

We consider the following commutative diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underset{\mathrm{LieAlgd}_{A}}{\Map}(\mathscr{L},\mathscr{L}^{\prime})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underset{\mathrm{cdga}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}_{/A}}{\Map}\left(\mathbf{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L}^{\prime}),\mathbf{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})\right)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Map_{A}(\mathscr{L},\mathscr{L}^{\prime})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Map_{A}(\mathscr{L}^{\prime\vee},\mathscr{L}^{\vee})}

Take a morphism of Lie algebroids
f:\mathscr{L}\to\mathscr{L}^{\prime}
such that it induces an equivalence
\mathbf{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L}^{\prime})\to\mathbf{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})
. In particular, it induces an equivalence
(\mathscr{L}^{\prime})^{\vee}\to\mathscr{L}^{\vee}
. The dualization functor
(-)^{\vee}
is fully-faithful on perfect modules and therefore conservative. Moreover, the forgetful functor
\mathrm{LieAlgd}_{A}\to\Mod_{A}
is also conservative which implies that the morphism of Lie algebroids
\mathscr{L}\to\mathscr{L}^{\prime}
is also an equivalence, and therefore
\mathbf{CE}
is a conservative functor.
∎

We will use the following notations:

.

\mathrm{CE}

Remark 3.2.18
.

As the
\infty
-category of
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroids is equivalent to the category of Lie algebroids (Corollary

) we can define the infinitesimal quotient of a
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroid as the infinitesimal quotient of any Lie algebroid equivalent to it.

3.2.2.
Pullback and base change of Lie algebroids

In this section we will use
X:=\mathbf{Spec}(A)
,
Y:=\mathbf{Spec}(B)
and
Z:=\mathbf{Spec}(C)
with
A
,
B
and
C
non-positively graded cofibrant cdgas of almost finite presentation.

We will described both the base change and pullbacks of Lie algebroids, defining in the process the notion of morphisms of Lie algebroids over different bases. We will show that these constructions can also be viewed from an algebraic point of view using their Chevalley–Eilenberg algebras. Many of these constructions on Lie algebroids are adapted and generalized from
[
Kla17
]
.

Definition 3.2.19
.

Take
\mathscr{L}
a Lie algebroid over
X
.
We define
f^{!}\mathscr{L}
to be the
Lie algebroid
over
Y
defined as the fiber product:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{!}\mathscr{L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}\mathscr{L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{!}\rho}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}\rho}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}}

together with:

–

An anchor
f^{!}\rho
given by the projection:

f^{!}\mathscr{L}\to\mathbb{T}_{Y}

–

Picking a model where the map
A\to B
is a cofibration, this pullback becomes strict and the Lie bracket is defined on
\mathbb{T}_{Y}\times_{f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}}f^{*}\mathscr{L}
by:

\left[X+gv,Y+hw\right]=[X,Y]+\left(gh\left[v,w\right]+\mathscr{L}_{X}(h).w-\mathscr{L}_{Y}(g).v\right)

This defines a Lie algebroid structure on
f^{!}\mathscr{L}
and given the choice of a cofibrant replacement
A\to B
, this construction defines a model for that Lie algebroid.

Remark 3.2.20
.

In
[
Kla17
]
, this base change is not always possible. The extra condition they required ensures that the strict fiber product is a
vector bundle
. Since we work in the more general context of linear stacks, such a (derived) fiber product always exists and is linear (thanks to Proposition
1.2.17
). Then the rest of the definition still makes sense of a strict model of the homotopy pullback and defines the desired Lie algebroid structure.

Warning 3.2.21
.

Although somewhat natural, we will see later in this section that Definition
3.2.19
might not be quite the definition we want. We will later on change this definition to Definition
3.2.30
. We expect both definitions to agree and everything we discuss in this section also makes sense for the second definition.

Definition 3.2.22
.

Let
\mathscr{L}^{\prime}
and

be Lie algebroids over

and

respectively. Then a morphism of Lie algebroids (over different bases) is defined by a commutative diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L^{\prime}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

of Lie algebroids over the same base (Definition

) with the natural morphism from the pullback Lie algebroid

.

We will rephrase this base change in terms of base change for their Chevalley–Eilenberg graded mixed algebras. To do so, we first need to make sense of the notion of morphism between Chevalley–Eilenberg algebras over different bases.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

Using this definition, the Chevalley–Eilenberg functor can be extended over different bases:

Construction 3.2.24
.

We can define a strict (not derived) functor:

\mathrm{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}:\mathrm{LieAlgd}\to\left(\mathrm{cdga}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}\right)^{\mathrm{op}}

that sends any morphism of Lie algebroids:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

to a morphism of graded mixed algebras
\mathrm{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L}_{2})\to\mathrm{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L}_{1})
over
f
.

The definition of this functor on objects given by the usual Chevalley–Eilenberg algebra. Any morphism of Lie algebroids as described above induces a map of modules over the morphism
f:B\to A
:

\phi:\mathscr{L}_{2}^{\vee}[-1]\to\mathscr{L}_{1}^{\vee}[-1]

We also get morphisms in higher weights:

\left(\Sym_{A}^{p}\mathscr{L}_{2}[1]\right)^{\vee}\to\left(\Sym_{A}^{p}\mathscr{L}_{1}[1]\right)^{\vee}

This defines a morphism between the graded Chevalley–Eilenberg algebras (because
f
and
\phi
preserve the internal differentials).
We only need to check that this map preserves the mixed differential. Essentially, this map preserves the mixed differential restricted to the weight
0
part
\epsilon_{|A}:=\rho^{*}\circ d_{\mathrm{dR}}
because the map
\mathscr{L}_{1}\to\mathscr{L}_{2}
is compatible with the anchors (because
\mathscr{L}_{1}\to f^{!}\mathscr{L}_{2}
must be compatible with the anchors from Definition
3.1.2
):

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}\mathscr{L}_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{T}_{Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{X}}

And the rest of the compatibilities are due to the fact that the map
\mathscr{L}_{1}\to\mathscr{L}_{2}
is a morphism of Lie algebras (because both
\mathscr{L}_{1}\to f^{!}\mathscr{L}_{2}
and
f^{!}\mathscr{L}_{2}\to\mathscr{L}_{2}
are maps of Lie algebras) and the fact that they preserve of the anchors, since the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential is build out of the Lie bracket and anchor (see Definition
3.2.5
).

It turns out that the Chevalley–Eilenberg functor over different bases behaves similarly to the one over a fixed base:

Lemma 3.2.25
.

The strict Chevalley–Eilenberg functor factors through graded mixed algebras:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{LieAlgd}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\left(\mathrm{cdga}\right)^{\mathrm{op}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\left(\mathrm{cdga}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}\right)^{\mathrm{op}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{CE}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\left|-\right|}

We assume that the bases are affine and finitely presented.
The essential image of
\mathrm{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
restricted to strictly perfect Lie algebroids is given by the graded mixed algebras
E
such that there is an equivalence
77
77

77

In other words, it is a semi-free graded mixed algebra generated by
A
, a non-positively graded and finitely presented algebra, in weight
0
and
\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-1]
in weight
1
.
:

E^{\mathrm{gr}}\simeq\iHom_{A}\left(\Sym^{\mathrm{gr}}_{A}\mathscr{L}[1],A\right)

for
A\in\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{\leq 0}}
finitely presented and
\mathscr{L}\in\mathbf{Perf}(A)
.

Moreover, restricted to strictly perfect Lie algebroids, the
strict
mixed graded Chevalley–Eilenberg functor,
\mathrm{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
, is fully-faithful.

We can now rephrase the base change construction in algebraic terms.
To do that, we observe that the anchor map
\mathscr{L}\to\mathbb{T}_{A}
is a map of Lie algebroids
78
78

78

\mathbb{T}_{A}
is viewed as a Lie algebroid over
X
with the identity as anchor map (see Example
3.1.9
).
(over the same base) and therefore induces a map of graded mixed algebras
79
79

79

The first equivalence is due to the fact that
A
is assumed to be cofibrant and finitely presented. Therefore thanks to Corollary
1.4.5
we get the desired equivalence
:

\mathbf{DR}(A)\simeq\mathrm{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathbb{T}_{A})\to\mathrm{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})

Lemma 3.2.26
.

Given a Lie algebroid
\mathscr{L}
over
X
an affine stack finitely presented and
f:Y\to X
, then we have a pushout square in the category of graded mixed algebras:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{DR}(A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{DR}(B)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(f^{!}\mathscr{L})}

where
f^{!}\mathscr{L}
is the pullback Lie algebroid of Definition
3.2.19
and the morphism:

\mathrm{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})\to\mathrm{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(f^{!}\mathscr{L})

is induced by the morphism of Lie algebroids
f^{!}\mathscr{L}\to\mathscr{L}
.

Proof.

Up to taking a cofibrant replacement of
f:A\to B
, we can chose
B
to be semi-free over
A
. This implies that
\mathbf{DR}(B)
is semi-free over
\mathbf{DR}(A)
. Indeed, if
B=\Sym_{A}\mathscr{F}^{\vee}
with
\mathscr{F}
projective. Then using a connection on
\mathscr{F}
, have an equivalence (see Section
1.2.5
):

\begin{split}\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(B)\simeq&\Sym^{\mathrm{gr}}_{\Sym_{A}\mathscr{F}^{\vee}}\left(\Sym_{A}\mathscr{F}^{\vee}\otimes_{A}\left(\mathbb{L}_{A}\oplus^{\nabla}\mathscr{F}\right)^{\vee}[-1]\right)\\
\simeq&\Sym_{A}\left(\mathscr{F}^{\vee}\oplus\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]\oplus\mathscr{F}^{\vee}[-1]\right)\\
\simeq&\Sym_{\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)}\left(\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)\otimes_{A}(\mathscr{F}^{\vee}\oplus\mathscr{F}^{\vee}[-1])\right)\end{split}

where
\mathscr{F}^{\vee}[-1]
is in weight
1
. Moreover by functoriality there is a map
\mathbf{DR}(A)\to\mathbf{DR}(B)
, which is therefore a cofibration and we can compute the homotopy pushout as a strict pushout. Its underlying graded algebra can be computes as the pushout of the underlying graded algebras:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sym^{\mathrm{gr}}_{A}\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sym^{\mathrm{gr}}_{B}\mathbb{L}_{B}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sym^{\mathrm{gr}}_{A}\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-1]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sym^{\mathrm{gr}}_{B}(f^{*}\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-1]\coprod_{f^{*}\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]}\mathbb{L}_{B}[-1])}

Since a strict model for
f^{!}\mathscr{L}
is also obtained through a cofibrant (or just semi-free) replacement of
A\to B
, we have for that model that:

\mathrm{CE}^{\mathrm{gr}}(f^{!}\mathscr{L})\cong\Sym^{\mathrm{gr}}_{B}(\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-1]\coprod_{\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]}\mathbb{L}_{B}[-1])\simeq\mathrm{CE}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})\otimes_{\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)}\mathbf{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(B)

We only have to show that the graded mixed structures coincide.

–

The weight
0
part of the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential clearly coincides with the weight
0
part of the differential of the pushout.

–

The part of the differential of weight
1
, restricted to
B
, is
\rho^{*}\circ d_{\mathrm{dR}}
with the anchor being the natural projection:

\rho:\mathbb{T}_{B}\times_{f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{A}}f^{*}\mathscr{L}\to\mathbb{T}_{B}

the natural projection. This coincides with the differential on the pushout given by the composition:

\begin{split}B\simeq B\otimes_{A}A\overset{d_{\mathrm{dR}}}{\to}&\ \mathbb{L}_{B}[-1]\simeq\mathbb{L}_{B}[-1]\coprod_{f^{*}\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]}f^{*}\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]\\
\overset{\rho^{*}}{\to}&\ \mathbb{L}_{B}[-1]\coprod_{f^{*}\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]}f^{*}\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-1]\end{split}

where the last map coincide with the natural inclusion:

\mathbb{L}_{B}[-1]\to\mathbb{L}_{B}[-1]\coprod_{f^{*}\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]}f^{*}\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-1]

–

Take
\mu\in\mathbb{L}_{B}[-1]
and
\alpha\in\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-1]
. Then
\alpha
induces an element (which we all also call
\alpha
), in
f^{*}\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-1]
, seen as a map
f^{*}\mathscr{L}\to B
with
\alpha(v):=\alpha(1\otimes v)=f(\alpha(v))
.

Then for all
X,Y\in\mathbb{T}_{B}[1]
,
g,h\in B
and
v,w\in\mathscr{L}[1]
such that
f_{*}X=g\rho(v)
and
f_{*}Y=h\rho(w)
, we have that the part of the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential on
\mathrm{CE}(f^{!}\mathscr{L})
in weight
1
can be described by:

\begin{split}\delta_{\mathbf{CE}}(\mu+\alpha)(X+gv,Y+hw)=\ &\mu([X,Y])+gh\alpha[v,w]+X(h)\alpha(w)-Y(g)\alpha(v)\\
&-X(\mu(Y))-X(h\alpha(w))\\
&+Y(\mu(X))+Y(g\alpha(v))\\
=\ &\mu([X,Y])+gh\alpha[v,w]+X(h)\alpha(w)-Y(g)\alpha(v)\\
&-X(\mu(Y))-X(h)\alpha(w)-hX(\alpha(w))\\
&+Y(\mu(X))+Y(g)\alpha(v)+gY(\alpha(v))\\
=\ &\mu([X,Y])+gh\alpha[v,w]\\
&-X(\mu(Y))-hX(f(\alpha(w)))\\
&+Y(\mu(X))+gY(f(\alpha(v)))\\
=\ &\mu([X,Y])-X(\mu(Y))+Y(\mu(X))\\
&+gh\alpha[v,w]-hg\rho(v)(\alpha(w))+gh\rho(w)(\alpha(v))\\
=\ &\mu([X,Y])-X(\mu(Y))+Y(\mu(X))\\
&gh\left(\alpha[v,w]-\rho(v)(\alpha(w))+\rho(w)(\alpha(v))\right)\end{split}

We can clearly identify both the mixed structure on
\mathbf{DR}(B)
and the mixed structure on
\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})
that defines the differential on the tensor product.

∎

Corollary 3.2.27
.

If
\mathscr{L}=0
is the trivial Lie algebroid, then
\mathbf{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})\simeq A
and we get an equivalence:

\mathrm{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(f^{!}\mathscr{L})\simeq\mathbf{DR}(B)\otimes_{\mathbf{DR}(A)}A\simeq\mathbf{DR}(B/A)

where the second equivalence comes from Definition
1.4.2
.

Moreover,
f^{!}0
is equivalent to
\mathbb{T}_{B/A}
as Lie algebroids, and we have:

\mathrm{CE}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathbb{T}_{B/A})\simeq\mathbf{DR}(B/A)

Moreover if
Y=\mathbf{Spec}(B)
satisfies Assumptions
3.2.2
, it coincides with the Lie algebroid
\mathfrak{D}(A)
described in Proposition
3.2.6
(where
B
and
A
are exchanged).

Proof.

The pushout from Lemma
3.2.26
becomes exactly the pushout describing the relative de Rham algebra in Definition
1.4.2
. The Lie algebroid structure on
\mathbb{T}_{B/A}
from Proposition
3.2.6
is clearly the one whose Chevalley–Eilenberg algebra is equivalent to
\mathbf{DR}(B/A)
.
∎

Remark 3.2.38
.

The notion of base change and pullback of
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroids along morphisms (but not
\infty
-morphisms) also makes sense. Essentially, adding higher brackets (
n\geq 3
) to the constructions add no difficulty as they are all
A
-linear. In particular, there is a Chevalley–Eilenberg
weak
graded mixed algebra functor,
\mathbf{CE}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
, characterizing the
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroid structure (in the sens of a generalization of Lemma
3.2.25
).

The easiest way to understand pullbacks and base changes in that setting is to use the tensor product in the category of weak graded mixed algebras. The underlying graded spaces are unchanged compared to the Lie algebroid part, but the tensor product in weak graded mixed algebras automatically defines the higher brackets.

3.3.
Infinitesimal Action of Lie Algebroids

The goal of this section is to make sense of the notion of the infinitesimal action (up to homotopy) of a Lie algebroid.

We start in Section
3.3.1
by discussing the special case of “linear actions” up to homotopy, which are given by
representations up to homotopy
of Lie algebroids. We then explain that these representations up to homotopy are equivalent to
\mathscr{L}
-connections that are
flat up to homotopy
. We also describe relevant examples (e.g. the adjoint and coadjoint representations) and properties of such representations.

Then we define in Section
3.3.2
the general notion of infinitesimal action of a Lie algebroid, and prove that representations up to homotopy are, under some technical assumption, actions up to homotopy.

3.3.1.
Representation up to homotopy

Our interest in representation up to homotopy of Lie algebroids lies in the fact that they are “linear” infinitesimal actions up to homotopy of Lie algebroids (Theorem
3.3.14
) and provide useful examples of actions up to homotopy such as the adjoint and coadjoint infinitesimal actions (Example
3.3.10
).

Given a vector space
V

G
on
V
is the data of a representation of
k[G]
on
V
, or in other words, the structure of a
k[G]
-module on
V
. Similarly, a representation up to homotopy will defined as a module over
\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
.

This section is mostly a rephrasing and a generalization of

For each
i>2
, we have:

\omega_{i}\in\Sym_{A}^{i}\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-1]\otimes_{A}\mathbf{End}(\mathscr{E})[i-1]

such that:

d_{E}(\omega_{i})+d_{\nabla}\omega_{i-1}+\omega_{2}\circ\omega_{i-1}+\cdots=0

We write
D=d_{E}+d_{\nabla}+\omega_{2}+\omega_{3}+\cdots
.

Proof.

Consider the weak graded mixed structure on
\mathrm{CE}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})\otimes_{A}\mathscr{E}
defining the representation up to homotopy. Then the collection of
d_{E}
together with the mixed differentials
\epsilon_{p}
for

are maps:

\mathscr{E}\to\Sym_{A}^{p}\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-1]\otimes_{A}\mathscr{E}[p-1]

For

\mathscr{E}\to\mathscr{L}^{\vee}\otimes_{A}\mathscr{E}[-1]
that defines an
\mathscr{L}
-connection on

(thanks to the Leibniz rule satisfied by
\epsilon_{1}
). Then, for

we rename the elements obtained
\omega_{i}
.

If we decompose the equations defining a weak graded mixed structure (Definition
C.2.1
) we get:

–

For
p=0
we get
d_{E}^{2}=0
.

–

For
p=1
we have
d_{E}\circ d_{\nabla}+d_{\nabla}\circ d_{E}=0
.

–

For

we have
[d_{E},\omega_{2}]+d_{\nabla}^{2}=0
and
d_{\nabla}^{2}
is the curvature of
\nabla
.

–

The other equations are straightforward. In fact all the equations can be written in the following compact form:

\sum_{p+q=i}\omega_{p}\circ\omega_{q}=0

with the convention
\omega_{0}=d_{E}
and
\omega_{1}=d_{\nabla}
.

Conversely, given the data of a connection and
\omega_{i}
as in the statement, we want to reconstruct a weak mixed structure on

. Again each

gives a map:

\mathscr{E}\to\Sym_{A}^{p}\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-1]\otimes_{A}\mathscr{E}[p-1]

and the equations:

\sum_{p+q=i}\omega_{p}\circ\omega_{q}=0

are exactly the equations of Definition
C.2.1
describing a weak graded mixed structures.
∎

Remark 3.3.7
.

A strict representation is a representation up to homotopy such that the weak graded mixed structure is in fact a graded mixed structure on the nose, in other words,
\epsilon_{\geq 2}:=\omega_{\geq 2}=0
. Therefore it is exactly given by a
A

\mathscr{E}
together with

In general the terms

).
