3.3.2.
Action of Lie algebroids

In this section, we are only going to consider
cofibrant
Lie algebroids over affine bases of almost finite presentation.

The typical example of an action is the action of
\mathscr{L}
on its base
X
, with the idea in mind that the associated infinitesimal quotient stack associated to
\mathscr{L}
is the infinitesimal quotient of
X
by the action of
\mathscr{L}
.

Taking the motivating example of a Lie algebra
\mathfrak{g}
viewed as a Lie algebroid over the point
\star
, we see that
\mathfrak{g}
act trivially on the point. However, we want to make
\mathfrak{g}
act on more geometric spaces that just the point. Classically, an action of
\mathfrak{g}
on
Y
is an
infinitesimal action
86
86

86

In this context, it is just a map of Lie algebras.

\mathfrak{g}\to\mathbb{T}_{Y}
which always gives (thanks to the second point of Example
3.1.9
) the Lie algebroid
\mathscr{O}_{Y}\otimes\mathfrak{g}
on
Y
called the
action Lie algebroid
. What we take from this example is that this action of
\mathfrak{g}
on
Y
is exactly the structure of a Lie algebroid on
f^{*}\mathfrak{g}
over
Y
where
f
is the canonical map
Y\to\star
. Keeping this idea and extending it to Lie algebroids over
X
instead of
\star
, we get the following definition:

Definition 3.3.12
.

An
infinitesimal action
of a Lie algebroid
\mathscr{L}
over
X
on
f:Y\to X
is a structure of Lie algebroid on
f^{*}\mathscr{L}
over
Y
such that the following commutative diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}L}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

defines a morphism of Lie algebroids over different bases (Definition
3.2.22
).

This infinitesimal action is
up to homotopy
if
f^{*}\mathscr{L}
has a
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-structure and the morphism is an
\infty
-morphism.

We denote the category of infinitesimal actions of
\mathscr{L}
up to homotopy by
\mathbf{Act}_{\mathscr{L}}
.

Remark 3.3.13
.

To speak about infinitesimal quotients by such an action, we would need
Y
to satisfy Assumptions
3.2.2
so that it fits into the framework of Section
3.2.1
. In concrete examples this will not always be the case. However, we will see in Section
4.2.1
how to give a generalized notion of infinitesimal quotient.

Theorem 3.3.14
.

Let
X
be affine of almost finite presentation and
\mathscr{L}
a perfect Lie algebroid over
X
. We have a strict functor:

\psi\ :\ \mathbf{Rep}_{\mathscr{L}}^{\mathrm{afp},\geq 0}\to\mathbf{Act}_{\mathscr{L}}

that sends a representation up to homotopy on
\mathscr{E}\in\mathbf{QC}^{\mathrm{afp},\geq 0}(X)
, a non-negatively graded quasi-coherent sheaf on
X
of almost finite presentation, to an infinitesimal action on the linear stack
E
along the projection
\pi_{E}:E\to X
.

Proof.

Given a representation up to homotopy given by:

M\in\Mod_{\mathrm{CE}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}

such that
M^{\mathrm{gr}}\cong\mathrm{CE}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})\otimes_{A}\mathscr{E}
with
\mathscr{E}
non-negatively graded of almost finite presentation.
We consider the associated free weak graded mixed
\mathrm{CE}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})
-algebra,
\Sym_{\mathrm{CE}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})}M^{\vee}
, whose underlying graded algebra is isomorphic to:

\Sym_{\mathrm{CE}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})}\mathrm{CE}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})\otimes_{A}\mathscr{E}^{\vee}\cong\Sym^{\mathrm{gr}}_{\Sym_{A}\mathscr{E}^{\vee}}\pi_{E}^{*}\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-1]

with
\pi_{E}:E\to X
.

This defines a
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-structure on
\pi_{E}^{*}\mathscr{L}
over
E
since a representation up to homotopy can only increase the arity in
\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-1]
and therefore the right hand side is in the essential image of the Chevalley–Eilenberg functor. This gives
\pi_{E}^{*}\mathscr{L}
a structure of Lie algebroid over
E
. Notice that because
\mathscr{E}
is almost presented and non-negatively graded,
E
is affine of finite presentation.

Moreover, there is a map (coming from the unit of the free-forget adjunction)
\mathrm{CE}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})\to\Sym_{\mathrm{CE}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})}M^{\vee}
commuting with the natural inclusion
A\to\Sym_{A}\mathscr{E}^{\vee}
. Therefore, thanks to Lemma
3.2.25
, we get a morphism of Lie algebroid
f^{*}\mathscr{L}\to\mathscr{L}
that defines the desired action.

This construction is natural in the Chevalley–Eilenberg algebras and since the strict Chevalley–Eilenberg functor is fully faithful on perfect Lie algebroids (thanks to Lemma
3.2.25
), this construction of the action is functorial.
∎

Remark 3.3.15
.

The reason we need to restrict to representations up to homotopy on
coconnective
almost finitely presented modules is that this is the necessary condition to ensure that
E
is affine of almost finite presentation which is the necessary context to speak about Lie algebroids.

3.4.
Homotopy Transfer Theorem

This section aims at proving a version of the homotopy transfer theorem for
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroids. In the context of differential geometry, a transfer theorem for Lie algebroids is proven in
[
PS20
, Section 2.3]
. We recall the proof of this result in the context of derived algebraic geometry. In this section all the Lie algebroids are strictly perfect.

Theorem 3.4.1
.

Let
f:\mathscr{L}\to\mathscr{L}^{\prime}
be a linear quasi-isomorphism of strictly perfect
A
-modules. Then for any
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
algebroid structure on
\mathscr{L}^{\prime}
over
X=\mathbf{Spec}(A)
, there is a
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroid structure on
\mathscr{L}
over
X
and an extension of
f
to an
\infty
-quasi-isomorphism
87
87

87

An
\infty
-quasi-isomorphism is an
\infty
-morphism whose linear component
f_{1}:\mathscr{L}\to\mathscr{L}^{\prime}
is a quasi-isomorphism.
:

f_{\infty}:\mathscr{L}\to\mathscr{L}^{\prime}

The rest of the section is going to be devoted to the proof of this theorem. First, we need to define the notion of deformation retract.

Definition 3.4.2
.

A
deformation retract
is a pair of map in
\Mod_{A}
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{M}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}

such that
pi=\mathrm{id}
,
p
is a quasi-isomorphism and
[d,h]=\mathrm{id}-ip
.

This is a
special deformation retract
if moreover
ph=hi=h^{2}=0
.

Lemma 3.4.3
.

For any linear quasi-isomorphism
f:\mathscr{L}\to\mathscr{L}^{\prime}
there is zig-zag of special deformation retracts:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{M}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{\prime}}

with
h,h^{\prime}:\mathscr{M}\to\mathscr{M}
the homotopies of degree
-1
of the deformation retracts and such that
p^{\prime}\circ i=f
.

Proof.

f
comes from a quasi-isomorphism of
A
-modules,
\mathscr{L}\to\mathscr{L}^{\prime}
, and therefore factor as:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{M}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{triv.cof.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{triv.fib.}}

Moreover we can chose
\mathscr{M}
to be the mapping cylinder of
f
given by:

\mathscr{L}\oplus\mathscr{L}[1]\oplus\mathscr{L}^{\prime}

with differential given by
\delta(a_{1},a_{2},a^{\prime})=(da_{1}+a_{2},-da_{2},da^{\prime}-f(a_{2}))
.

We get a special deformation retract:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}\oplus\mathscr{L}[1]\oplus\mathscr{L}^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{\prime}}

where
i^{\prime}
is the inclusion,
p^{\prime}(a_{1},a_{2},a^{\prime})=f(a_{1})+a^{\prime}
and
h^{\prime}(a_{1},a_{2},a^{\prime})=(0,a_{1},0)
.

We have another special deformation retract:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}\oplus\mathscr{L}[1]\oplus\mathscr{L}^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}

Indeed, we find a retract of
\mathscr{L}\to\mathscr{L}\oplus\mathscr{L}[1]\oplus\mathscr{L}^{\prime}
by having a lift:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}\oplus\mathscr{L}[1]\oplus\mathscr{L}^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{triv.cof.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{fib.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

This implies that
p
is a homotopy inverse for
i
, since
i
is a quasi-isomorphism and
p\circ i=\mathrm{id}
. Therefore
i\circ p
is homotopic to the identity with homotopy
h
.

These are in fact only deformation retracts but this is a classical result (see
[
Cra04
, Remark 2.3]
) that any deformation retract can be modified to a special deformation retract.
∎

We are now going to deal with transfer on the left and on the right along a special deformation retract:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{M}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}

Lemma 3.4.4
.

If
\mathscr{L}
is a
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroid, then there exists a
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroid structure on
\mathscr{M}
such that both
p
and
i
are
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-morphisms.

Proof.

Using the deformation retract we get a splitting (an isomorphism):

\mathscr{M}\cong\mathscr{L}\oplus\mathscr{N}

with
\mathscr{N}=\ker(p)
a contractible complex so that there is an isomorphism:

\mathscr{N}\cong\mathrm{cone}(\mathrm{id}:\mathscr{K}\to\mathscr{K})

Indeed, first notice that
h
restricted to
\mathscr{N}
is valued in
\mathscr{N}
and restricted to
\mathscr{N}
we have
[d,h]=\mathrm{id}
(since
i\circ p=0
on
\mathscr{N}
). Then if we take
\mathscr{K}=\ker(d)
, we can show that
\mathscr{N}=\mathscr{K}\oplus\mathscr{K}^{\prime}
where
\mathscr{K}^{\prime}
is the cokernel of
d
. It turns out that
h:\mathscr{K}^{\prime}\to\mathscr{K}[1]
is an isomorphism. With the condition
[d,h]=\mathrm{id}
, we get an isomorphism
\mathscr{N}\cong\mathscr{K}\oplus\mathscr{K}[1]
together with the differential
\mathscr{K}[1]\to\mathscr{K}
, which is exactly the cone of
\mathrm{id}:\mathscr{K}\to\mathscr{K}
.

Then picking a connection on
\mathscr{K}
(which exists since
\mathscr{K}
is projective as a direct summand of
\mathscr{M}
which is projective), we can define a representation up to homotopy on
\mathscr{N}
thanks to Example
3.3.8
. This induces an action of
\mathscr{L}
on
\mathscr{N}
(using Theorem
3.3.14
) which we will denote by
\tilde{\mathscr{N}}\in\Mod_{\mathrm{CE}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{L})}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
. Doing so, we can define a structure of Lie algebroid on
\mathscr{M}
by defining its Chevalley–Eilenberg weak graded mixed algebra as the free weak graded mixed complex:

\mathrm{CE}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathscr{M}):=\mathrm{Free}\left(\tilde{\mathscr{N}}^{\vee}[-1]\right)

This is a Chevalley–Eilenberg algebra of
\mathscr{M}
since the underlying graded object of this free weak graded mixed algebra is:

\Sym_{A}^{\mathrm{gr}}\left(\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-1]\oplus\mathscr{N}^{\vee}[-1]\right)\cong\Sym_{A}^{\mathrm{gr}}\left(\mathscr{M}^{\vee}[-1]\right)

and therefore we get a
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-structure on
\mathscr{M}
.

The natural projection and inclusion induced by
p
and
i
are compatible with the differentials and therefore induce strict morphisms of
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroids since the strict Chevalley–Eilenberg functor is fully-faithful on perfect
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroids (thanks to a
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
variation of Lemma
3.2.25
).
∎

Lemma 3.4.5
.

If
\mathscr{M}
is an
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroid, then there exists an
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroid structure on
\mathscr{L}
and an extension of
i
to an
\infty
-quasi-isomorphism
i_{\infty}
.

Proof.

We define an anchor on
\mathscr{L}
by the composite
\rho\circ i
.

To define the brackets, we use the homotopy transfer theorem for
\mathrm{Lie}_{\infty}
-algebras (see
[
LV12
, Theorem 10.3.2]
). This gives us a sequence of
k
-linear maps:

i_{n}:\mathscr{L}^{\times n}\to\mathscr{M}

These maps are in fact
A
-linear for thanks to the side condition
h^{2}=0
and
h\circ i=0
. The binary bracket is defined by:

[x,y]_{\mathscr{L}}:=p([i(x),i(y)]_{\mathscr{M}})

We can show that it satisfies the Leibniz rule using the equation
pi=\mathrm{id}
.
∎

Remark 3.4.6
.

So far we talked about Lie algebroids, the objects given by Definition
3.1.1
and Lie algebroid structures on a module, defined via Remark
3.1.3
. The first type of objects are models of Lie algebroids but this notions is not invariant by weak equivalence (unlike the second notion). The homotopy transfer theorem ensures that if a module
\mathscr{L}
has a structure of Lie algebroid, then
\mathscr{L}

is
a
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroid such that the algebroid structures are equivalent via the transfer along
\infty
-equivalences between the underlying modules of the different models.

4.
Equivariant Symplectic Geometry

In this section, we are going to develop equivariant and “infinitesimally equivariant” geometry, as well as derived symplectic geometry in that context. The study of (infinitesimal) equivariant geometry boils down to the study of the geometry of (infinitesimal) quotient stacks. The end goal is to make sense of a generalized notion of symplectic reduction for Segal groupoids actions and their infinitesimal version, Lie algebroids actions.

We start by setting up the necessary derived equivariant geometry needed for Segal groupoids actions in Section
4.1
, and for Lie algebroid actions in Section
4.2
.

In both cases, we study the geometric properties of the (infinitesimal) quotients. In particular we are interested in taking pullbacks of such quotients and in computing their tangent complexes.

Moreover, we will discuss the heuristic saying that infinitesimal quotients should be viewed as an “infinitesimal version” of quotients by Segal groupoids. This requires a precise understanding of the relationship between Segal groupoids and Lie algebroids. We discuss the “derivation” and “integration” of Segal groupoids and Lie algebroids in Section
4.2.1
.

Furthermore, we also show that much of the constructions for Lie algebroids are but the “infinitesimal versions” of the same constructions for Segal groupoids.

Then, in Section
4.3
we recall the notion of moment maps and symplectic reduction for a group action following
[
AC21
]
. We then generalize these results to Segal groupoid and Lie algebroid actions and show in each case that we can create new moment maps and symplectic reductions by a procedure of “derived intersection of Lagrangians”. This produces interesting examples of
(-1)
-shifted moment maps on the derived critical locus, which are going to be at the heart of the BV constructions in Section
5
.

4.1.
\mathscr{G}
-Equivariant Symplectic Geometry

We are interested in the equivariant geometry with respect to the action of a Segal groupoid. As we will see, it amounts to studying the associated quotient.

We will pay particular attention to the tangent and cotangent complexes of these quotient stacks, as well as their derived symplectic geometry.

4.1.1.
\mathscr{G}
-equivariant maps and quotients

We start by defining more precisely the different notions of Segal groupoids we are going to use, and make sense of the notion of
action
of a Segal groupoid.

Definition 4.1.1

(
[
TV08
, Definition 1.3.1.6]
)
.

We say that a simplicial
88
88

88

Unlike the usual conventions, we denote the simplicial stack with a
lower
bullet to have convenient notations later on.
derived stack
\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}
is a
Segal groupoid over
X
if the following conditions holds:

(1)

\mathscr{G}^{0}\simeq X

(2)

For all
n>0
, there are weak equivalences:

\prod\limits_{0\leq i<n}\sigma_{i}:\mathscr{G}^{n}\overset{\sim}{\to}\underbrace{\mathscr{G}^{1}\times_{X}\cdots\times_{X}\mathscr{G}^{1}}_{\mathrm{n-times}}

(3)

There is a weak equivalence:

d_{1}\times d_{2}:\mathscr{G}^{2}\to\mathscr{G}^{1}\times_{X}^{d_{0},d_{0}}\mathscr{G}^{1}

Given a Segal groupoid
\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}
over
X
, we define the
quotient stack
as the colimit of the simplicial diagram denoted by:

\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]

It comes with a natural projection that we will generically denote by:

p:X\to\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]

We denote by
s_{n}:\mathscr{G}^{n}\to X
the composition of all the “source maps”
d_{0}:\mathscr{G}^{n}\to\mathscr{G}^{n-1}
and
t_{n}:\mathscr{G}^{n}\to X
the composition of the “target maps”
d_{n-1}:\mathscr{G}^{n}\to\mathscr{G}^{n-1}
.

Remark 4.1.2
.

The first condition of a Segal groupoid
\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}
is essentially saying that it is a kind of
1
-category object with objects
X
and morphisms
\mathscr{G}^{1}
. In particular the composition can morally be obtained by “inverting” the the equivalence in:

\mathscr{G}^{1}\times_{X}\mathscr{G}^{1}\overset{\sim}{\leftarrow}\mathscr{G}^{2}\overset{d_{1}}{\to}\mathscr{G}^{1}

The second condition says that any horn diagram (element in
\mathscr{G}^{1}\times_{d_{0},X,d_{0}}\mathscr{G}^{1}
):

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces z}

can be filled uniquely (up to homotopy). This implies that all “morphisms” in
\mathscr{G}^{1}
are invertible.

Definition 4.1.3
.

Let
\mathscr{G}_{X}^{\bullet}
be a Segal groupoid over
X
and
\mathscr{G}_{Y}^{\bullet}
a Segal groupoid over
Y
. Then a morphism of Segal groupoids, denoted
\phi:\mathscr{G}_{X}^{\bullet}\to\mathscr{G}_{Y}^{\bullet}
over a map
f:X\to Y
is a morphism between the simplicial derived stacks
\mathscr{G}_{X}^{\bullet}\to\mathscr{G}_{Y}^{\bullet}
such that it is given by
f
on the
0
-simplices.

Example 4.1.4
.

The nerve of a groupoid:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{G}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t}

is a Segal groupoid and the quotient stack of a groupoid is by definition (see
1.1.14
) the quotient if its nerve.

Example 4.1.5
.

Given a map
f:X\to Z
, we can define a Segal groupoid over
X
,
C(f)
given by the Čech nerve:

C(f)^{n}:=\underbrace{X\times_{Z}\cdots\times_{Z}X}_{\mathrm{n-times}}

with the simplicial structure obtained from the natural projections and the diagonals. Condition (1) is the associativity of the pullback and the second condition is also clear.

Definition 4.1.6
.

Let
\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}
be a Segal groupoid over
X
.

–

The Segal groupoid is called
smooth
(
[
TV08
, Definition 1.3.4.1]
) if each
\mathscr{G}^{n}
is an Artin stack and all the structure maps
\mathscr{G}^{n}\to\mathscr{G}^{n-1}
are smooth (in the sens of
[
TV08
, Definition 1.3.3.1]
). In particular, from
[
TV08
, Proposition 1.3.4.2]
, the associated quotient stack is again Artin
89
89

89

Artin stacks can even be
defined
as successive quotients of such groupoids.
.

–

The groupoid is called formal if each
\mathscr{G}^{n}
is a formal stack and all structure morphisms are nil-equivalences.

Remark 4.1.7
.

We can also consider
Segal groupoids in pre-stacks
. The definitions are identical except for the fact that
\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}
is a simplicial pre-stack instead. The stackification-inclusion adjunction induces an adjunction between the categories of Segal groupoids in pre-stacks and Segal groupoids in stacks
90
90

90

The stackification of a Segal groupoid in pre-stacks is a groupoid in stacks because the stackification functor preserves small limits.
.

A class of examples of such groupoids come from the action of groups. By group we mean, a
group object
in derived stacks. A group can act on a stack
X
via a morphism
\rho:G\times X\to X
satisfying the usual conditions for an action.

Example 4.1.8
.

Take
G
a group acting on a derived stacks
X
with action
\rho:G\times X\to X
. Then
G\times X
has a groupoid structure given by:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G\times X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{pr}_{X}}

whose quotient is
\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{G}$}}}\right]
(see Example
1.1.14
). In fact, such a groupoid structure is equivalent to the data of an action of
G
on
X
. We will say that
G
acts smoothly on
X
if the corresponding groupoid is smooth in the sens of Definition
4.1.6
(and in particular,
G
and
X
are Artin).

Remark 4.1.9
.

Let
\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}
be a formal Segal groupoid over
X
. Then we can show that the projection:

p:X\to\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]

is a nil-equivalence. However, nothing ensures that the quotient is formal. Therefore this projection might
not
be a formal thickening according to Definition
1.3.18
.

We can obtain formal Segal groupoids out of a rather large class of groupoids.

Construction 4.1.10
.

Take
\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}
a Segal groupoid over
X
such that each
\mathscr{G}^{n}
is formal (in particular both smooth groupoids and formal groupoids verify this condition). Then we can define the
formal completion
,
\widehat{\mathscr{G}}^{\bullet}
, of this groupoid as the Segal groupoid given by formal completion at the unit:

\widehat{\mathscr{G}}^{n}:=\widehat{\mathscr{G}_{X}^{n}}

Since taking the formal completion commutes with taking the pullbacks (Corollary
1.3.13
), this is again a Segal groupoid.

Using the fact that derived stacks form a model topos, they satisfy a version Giraud’s theorem (Proposition
1.1.15
). In particular quotients are “effective”:

Lemma 4.1.11
.

Given a Segal groupoid
\mathscr{G}^{n}
over
X
, the natural projection:

p:X\to\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]

is an effective epimorphism and we have equivalences for all
n\geq 1
:

\mathscr{G}^{n}\simeq\underbrace{X\times_{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]}\cdots\times_{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]}X}_{\text{n-times}}\simeq C(p)^{n}

This defines an equivalence of groupoids over
X
:

\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}\simeq C(p)^{\bullet}

Equivariant geometry is the study of the geometry of quotient stacks and of

between derived stacks.

–

Given

,

and

groupoids over

Combining these two constructions, we can define the pullback of groupoids over different bases. This is a pullback because of Lemma
4.1.14
.

Lemma 4.1.14
.

Let
\mathscr{H}^{\bullet}
,
\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}
be groupoids over
Y
and
X
respectively and
\phi:\mathscr{H}^{\bullet}\to\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}
a morphism of groupoids over
f:Y\to X
. Then
\phi
factors through a unique morphism:

\mathscr{H}^{\bullet}\to f^{!}\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}

Proof.

First notice that there is an equivalence:

C(p\circ f)^{n}:=\underbrace{Y\times_{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]}\cdots\times_{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]}Y}_{\text{n-times}}\simeq\underbrace{\left(Y\times_{X}\mathscr{G}^{1}\times_{X}Y\right)\times_{Y}\cdots\times_{Y}\left(Y\times_{X}\mathscr{G}^{1}\times_{X}Y\right)}_{\mathrm{n-times}}

We have a unique natural (i.e. commuting with the source and target maps) morphism:

\mathscr{H}^{1}\overset{s\times\phi^{1}\times t}{\longrightarrow}Y\times_{X}\mathscr{G}^{1}\times_{X}Y

Which induces unique natural morphisms:

\mathscr{H}^{n}\overset{\sim}{\to}\underbrace{\mathscr{H}_{1}\times_{Y}\cdots\times_{Y}\mathscr{H}^{1}}_{\mathrm{n-times}}\to C(p\circ f)^{n}

which in turn define a unique morphism of groupoids:

\mathscr{H}^{\bullet}\to f^{!}\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}

∎

We can now turn to the notion of
action
of a Segal groupoid. Similarly to the motivating example in the introduction of Section
3.3.2
, we can look at the case of an action of a group
G
.
G
is naturally seen as a groupoid over the point. An action of
G
on
Y
is equivalent to the structure of a groupoid given by
Y\times G
over
Y
(Example
4.1.8
), whose source map is the natural projection (and the target map defines the action). Here the projection
Y\times G
can be viewed as the pullback of the “source map”
G\to\star
along the natural augmentation
X\to\star
. This motivates the following definition:

Definition 4.1.15
.

An
action
of a Segal groupoid
\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}
over
X
on
f:Y\to X
is the data of a groupoid:

f^{*}\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}:=\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}\times_{X}^{s_{\bullet}}Y

where
s_{n}:\mathscr{G}^{n}\to X
are the source maps
92
92

92

The choice of the source maps instead of the target maps is purely conventional as the source and target maps play an interchangeable role.
.

Given an action of
\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}
on
f
we will denote the quotient by
\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{Y}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{Y}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{Y}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{Y}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]
. We will see with Proposition
4.2.17
that a Segal groupoid action naturally induces an action of the associated Lie algebroids (Construction
4.2.1
).

Lemma 4.1.16

Consider a pullback of derived stacks:

(1)

The pullback of the effective epimorphism:

(2)

We have equivalences:

\begin{split}Y\times_{Z}Y\simeq&X\times_{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]}Z\times_{Z}Z\times_{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]}X\\
\simeq&X\times_{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]}Z\times_{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]}X\\
\simeq&X\times_{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]}X\times_{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]}Z\\
\simeq&\mathscr{G}\times_{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]}^{p\circ s}Z\\
\simeq&\mathscr{G}\times_{X}^{s}Y\end{split}

where the fourth equivalence uses Lemma
4.1.11
. This gives
\mathscr{G}\times_{X}^{s}Y
the structure of a groupoid over
Y
and the source map is clearly the projection from
Y
. More generally we get:

C(q)^{n}:=\underbrace{Y\times_{Z}\cdots\times_{Z}Y}_{\mathrm{n-times}}\simeq\mathscr{G}^{n}\times_{X}^{s_{n}}Y

Indeed we can proceed inductively and get:

\begin{split}C(q)^{n}\simeq&C(q)^{n-1}\times_{Z}Y\\
\simeq&\mathscr{G}^{n-1}\times_{X}^{s_{n-1}}Y\\
\simeq&\underbrace{\mathscr{G}^{1}\times_{X}\cdots\times_{X}\mathscr{G}^{1}}_{\mathrm{(n-1)-times}}\times_{X}^{s}Y\\
\simeq&\underbrace{\mathscr{G}^{1}\times_{X}\cdots\times_{X}\mathscr{G}^{1}}_{\mathrm{(n-1)-times}}\times_{X}^{s}\left(X\times_{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]}X\right)\times_{X}Y\\
\simeq&\underbrace{\mathscr{G}^{1}\times_{X}\cdots\times_{X}\mathscr{G}^{1}}_{\mathrm{(n-1)-times}}\times_{X}^{s,s}\mathscr{G}^{1}\times_{X}^{t}Y\\
\simeq&\underbrace{\mathscr{G}^{1}\times_{X}\cdots\times_{X}\mathscr{G}^{1}}_{\mathrm{(n-1)-times}}\times_{X}^{s,t}\mathscr{G}^{1}\times_{X}^{s}Y\\
\simeq&\underbrace{\mathscr{G}^{1}\times_{X}\cdots\times_{X}\mathscr{G}^{1}}_{\mathrm{(n)-times}}\times_{X}^{s}Y\\
\simeq&\mathscr{G}^{n}\times_{X}^{s_{n}}Y\end{split}

Moreover, having the commutative square of the statement ensures that there is a map of groupoids:

C(q)^{\bullet}\to C(p)^{\bullet}

which induces a map of groupoids:

\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}\times_{X}^{s_{\bullet}}Y\to\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}

and therefore defines an action of
\mathscr{G}
on
f
.

(3)

The equivalence follows from Proposition
1.1.15
and the previous equivalence of groupoids over
Y
:

C(q)^{n}\simeq\mathscr{G}^{n}\times_{X}^{s_{n}}Y

This shows that
\mathscr{G}^{\bullet}\times_{X}^{s_{\bullet}}Y
is the groupoid whose quotient is equivalent to
Z
.

∎
