is also part of a Lagrangian correspondence, making it an off-shell infinitesimal BV construction.
∎

5.2.
Strictification and BV Charge

The goal of this section is to compare the infinitesimal BV construction to that of
[
FK14
]
. One of the main difficulty to compare our construction to the classical one is that we define an infinitesimal quotient stack while they only construct the associated Chevalley–Eilenberg algebra.

Unfortunately, the tangent and cotangent complexes of the Chevalley–Eilenberg algebras are complicated to compute mostly because it is unclear how to take a cofibrant resolution of this algebra even for perfect Lie algebroids. We expect that working with the graded mixed Chevalley–Eilenberg algebras instead might simplify this issue.

In order to still be able to still discuss the comparison between our geometric description of the BV construction and the algebraic construction, we will need to restrict ourself to an
underived setting
. In this section only, we will consider underived construction. In particular, tensor product, direct sums, Hom functors will
not
be derived in this section.

We will adopt a framework similar to the one described in
[
PS20
, Section 3.2]
. We will consider perfect Lie algebroids concentrated in non-positive degrees over an almost derived critical locus
S=\mathbf{Spec}(R)
with:

R:=\left(\left(\Sym_{A}\mathbb{T}_{A}[1]\oplus\mathscr{L}_{S}[2]\right),\delta_{S}\right)

We will restrict to non-positively graded perfect Lie algebroids, consider the
underived
tangent complex,
\mathscr{T}_{B}
defined as the underived module of derivations of
B
. Since
A
is cofibrant, we have that
\mathscr{T}_{A}\simeq\mathbb{T}_{A}
. We will keep writing
\mathbb{T}_{A}
bearing in mind that we use the model given by
\mathscr{T}_{A}
.

Since we take a perfect
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroid
\mathscr{L}
, its Chevalley–Eilenberg algebra is the completion of a semi-free algebra. Up to picking a connection, we have that:

\mathscr{T}_{\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})}\simeq{\mathrm{CE}}(\mathscr{L})\otimes_{A}\left(\mathbb{T}_{A}\oplus\mathscr{L}[1]\right)

together with a differential making it a module over
\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})
. We also have:

h^{*}\mathscr{T}_{\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})}\simeq\mathbb{T}_{A}\oplus^{\rho}\mathscr{L}[1]

with
h:\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})\to A
. Note that this is exactly the same as
h^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{L}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{L}}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{L}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{L}}$}}}\right]}
.

We will consider an underived analogue to the de Rham algebra defined as:

\mathrm{DR}(B):=\left(\cSym_{B}\Omega_{B}^{1}[-1],D=d_{\mathrm{dR}}+\delta_{B}\right)

where
\Omega_{B}^{1}
is the module of Kähler differentials whose dual is
\mathscr{T}_{B}
.

Just like the derived version, this algebra is filtered complete and
d_{\mathrm{dR}}
increases the weight by
1
while
\delta_{B}
preserves the weight. Then (closed)
p
-forms of degree
n
on
\mathbf{CE}(\mathscr{L})
are
defined
similary to Proposition
1.4.17
by:

\mathscr{A}^{p}(B,n)\simeq\left|\mathrm{DR}(p)(B)[n+p]\right|_{\Delta}

\mathscr{A}^{p,\mathrm{cl}}(B,n)\simeq\left|F^{p}\mathrm{DR}^{\mathrm{cpl}}(B)[n+p]\right|_{\Delta}\simeq\left|\prod_{i\geq p}\mathrm{DR}(p+i)(B)[n+p]\right|_{\Delta}

We refer to
[
PS20
, Section 3.4]
for the more explicit description of these forms.

5.2.1.
Strictification

In this section we will consider an infinitesimal BV construction as the following data, fixing an almost derived critical locus
S
of almost finite presentation and assuming that it admits an infinitesimal BV construction:

–

Y:=\mathbf{Spec}(\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L}))
where
\mathscr{L}
is a perfect Lie algebroid on
S
concentrated in non-positive degree.

–

\omega_{Y}
a
(-1)
-shifted symplectic structure on
Y
.

–

\gamma
the data of the Lagrangian correspondence defining the generalized symplectic reduction.

Such a tuple will denoted
(L,S,\omega_{Y},\gamma)
. Moreover, we are going to consider
S
of the form
S=\mathbf{Spec}(R)
with:

R:=\left(\Sym_{A}\left(\mathbb{T}_{A}[1]\oplus\mathscr{L}_{S}[2]\right),\delta_{S}\right)

We will be interested in understanding these infinitesimal BV constructions only up to the following notion of equivalence:

Definition 5.2.1
.

An equivalence
(\mathscr{L},S,\omega_{Y},\gamma)\to(\mathscr{L}^{\prime},S,\omega_{Y}^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime})
is the following data:

–

An equivalence between the Chevalley–Eilenberg algebras:

f:\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L}^{\prime})\overset{\sim}{\to}\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})

Note that this induces an equivalence between the “infinitesimal quotient stacks”,
Y\overset{\sim}{\to}Y^{\prime}
.

–

A homotopy between closed
2
-forms:

\omega_{Y}\sim f^{*}\omega_{Y^{\prime}}

–

A homotopy between the Lagrangian correspondences:

\gamma\sim f^{*}\gamma^{\prime}

For now let us chose
S
that admits a generalized symplectic reduction and
(\mathscr{L},S,\omega_{Y},\gamma)
be an infinitesimal BV construction.

Lemma 5.2.2
.

The non-degeneracy condition of the Lagrangian correspondence implies that there is a quasi-isomorphism:

\phi:R\otimes_{A}\mathscr{L}_{S}^{\vee}[-2]\overset{\sim}{\to}\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-2]

Proof.

Consider the following commutative diagram, obtained by using a connection on
\mathbf{Crit}(f)
and on

(for simplicity we will omit the notation

Using the results of Section

.

.

Proof.

Using the equivalence

between perfect

-algebroids, this implies that the associated Chevalley–Eilenberg algebras are equivalent since the Chevalley–Eilenberg functor preserves weak equivalences between

Definition 5.2.6
.

We define a (necessarily strict) symplectic
2
-form
\omega^{\mathrm{st}}
of degree
-1
on

by the following map of graded space:

\begin{split}\mathscr{T}_{\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})}^{\sharp}=&\left(\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})\otimes_{R}i^{*}\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}\oplus\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})\otimes_{A}\left(\mathscr{L}_{S}^{\vee}[-2]\oplus\mathscr{L}_{S}[1]\right)\right)^{\sharp}\\
\to&\left(\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})\otimes_{R}i^{*}\mathbb{L}_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}[-1]\oplus\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})\otimes_{A}\left(\mathscr{L}_{S}^{\vee}[-2]\oplus\mathscr{L}_{S}[1]\right)\right)^{\sharp}=\left(\Omega^{1}_{\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})}\right)^{\sharp}[-1]\end{split}

given by the identity plus

. This is a
(-1)
-shifted symplectic form when we forget the differential on

(denoted by the

Remark 5.2.7
.

We define
\omega^{\mathrm{st}}
as the identity plus the canonical symplectic structure from
\mathbf{Crit}(f)
, and therefore its pullback,
h^{\star}\omega^{\mathrm{st}}
, is exactly given by
i^{*}\omega_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}+\omega_{\phi}
. This is compatible with the result of Lemma
5.2.5
. However, nothing ensures us that
\omega^{\mathrm{st}}
is compatible with the differential so it might not even be a
2
-form on
\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})
itself.

Theorem 5.2.8
.

The
(-1)
-shifted symplectic form
\omega
on
Y
can be described by
124
124

124

Note that neither summand is actually a
2
-form as they might not be compatible with the differential.
:

\omega=\omega^{\mathrm{st}}+\tilde{\omega}

with
h^{\star}\omega^{\mathrm{st}}=i^{*}\omega_{\mathbf{Crit}(f)}+\omega_{\phi}
and
h^{\star}\tilde{\omega}=0
.

Proof.

From the following Lemma
5.2.5
, we know that
h^{\star}\omega_{0}=h^{\star}\omega^{\mathrm{st}}
. Now, it follows that
\omega-\omega^{\mathrm{st}}=\tilde{\omega}
is such that
h^{\star}\tilde{\omega}=0
.
∎

In the end, we find that although our construction has similarities to the classical construction of BV, working up to homotopy and with almost derived critical loci adds so much more flexibility that we cannot completely recover a notion of “uniqueness up to equivalence” of the BV construction as can be found in
[
FK14
]
for example.

Moreover, our construction does not provide a
BV charge
and we do not have a good way to phrase this condition in a meaningful homotopy invariant way. However, even if we do not have a BV charge, the infinitesimal quotient we obtain is
(-1)
-shifted symplectic with a symplectic structure compatible with the differential on the algebra of functions. We do not think that a BV charge should exist in such degree of generality.

Nevertheless, it turns out that a rather large class of example of BV construction admits a BV charge. As we will see, a BV construction is Hamiltonian as soon as the symplectic structure is given by
\omega^{\mathrm{st}}
(without the extra terms).

5.2.2.
Hamiltonian vector field and BV charge

The goal of this section is to prove that if we have a BV construction
(\pi_{S}^{*}\mathscr{L}_{S},\omega_{Y},\gamma)
such that
\omega_{Y}=\omega^{\mathrm{st}}
, then there is a BV charge and we can give a formula for the BV charge provided by the homological perturbation lemma.

The BV charge is nothing but a Hamiltonian vector field for the natural differential on the Chevalley–Eilenberg algebra,
\mathrm{CE}(\pi_{S}^{*}\mathscr{L}_{S})
, associated to the Lie algebroid of symmetries on
S
. To simplify the notations, in this section, we will denote
\mathscr{L}:=\pi_{S}^{*}\mathscr{L}_{S}
the
\mathscr{L}_{\infty}
-algebroid over
R
. The key insight that will make this section work is the following proposition:

Proposition 5.2.9
.

There is an
isomorphism
(we are considering the
strict
construction of these graded mixed algebras) of graded mixed algebras:

\mathrm{Pol}(\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L}),-1)\overset{\simeq}{\to}\mathrm{DR}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L}))

such that:

–

\mathrm{Pol}(\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L}),-1)
denotes the graded mixed complex of
(-1)
-shifted polyvector fields on
\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})
with mixed differential given by
\left[\Pi^{\mathrm{st}},\right]_{\mathrm{SN}}
, where the bracket is the
Schouten–Nijenhuis
bracket, and
\Pi^{\mathrm{st}}
is the bivector field defining the (strict) Poisson structure dual to
\omega^{\mathrm{st}}
.

–

\mathrm{DR}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
is the graded mixed version of
\mathrm{DR}
described at the beginning of Section
5.2
.

–

The map induces the identity of
\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})
in weight
0
and sends a derivation
X\in\mathscr{T}_{\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})}
to
\iota_{X}\omega^{\mathrm{st}}\in\Omega^{1}_{\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})}[-1]
.

Definition 5.2.10
.

A vector field
X\in\mathscr{T}_{\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})}
of degree
1
is called
Hamiltonian
if:

X=\left[\Pi^{\mathrm{st}},Q\right]

for some
Q\in\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})
(the part of weight 0). In particular this is equivalent, using Proposition
5.2.9
, to saying that
\iota_{X}\omega^{\mathrm{st}}=d_{\mathrm{dR}}Q
.

If we consider
\delta_{\mathrm{CE}}\in\mathscr{T}_{\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})}
of degree
1
. Then finding a BV charge amounts to show that
\iota_{\delta_{\mathrm{CE}}}\omega^{\mathrm{st}}
is
d_{\mathrm{dR}}
-exact.
First we will see with Theorem
5.2.25
that we have a strong deformation retract:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{DR}(R)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{DR}(\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L}))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i_{\infty}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{\infty}}

Then
\iota_{\delta_{\mathrm{CE}}}\omega^{\mathrm{st}}
is exact
for the total differential
if and only if
p(\iota_{\delta_{\mathrm{CE}}}\omega^{\mathrm{st}})
is exact for the total differential.
We will see in Corollary
5.2.14
that
p(\iota_{\delta_{\mathrm{CE}}}\omega^{\mathrm{st}})=d_{\mathrm{dR}}f
and restricted to the weight
0
part, given by
A
, the total differential is
D=\delta_{A}+d_{\mathrm{dR}}=d_{\mathrm{dR}}
. Therefore we have that:

\iota_{\delta_{\mathrm{CE}}}\omega^{\mathrm{st}}=D(i_{\infty}(f)+h_{\infty}(\iota_{\delta_{\mathrm{CE}}}\omega^{\mathrm{st}}))

Moreover, in Lemma
5.2.29
we show that
i_{\infty}
preserves the de Rham weight and
h_{\infty}
decreases it by
1
. Since
\iota_{\delta_{\mathrm{CE}}}\omega^{\mathrm{st}}
has de Rham weight at most
1
(since it is valued in
\Omega^{1}_{\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})}
), we have that:

Q:=i_{\infty}(f)+h_{\infty}(\iota_{\delta_{\mathrm{CE}}}\omega^{\mathrm{st}})\in\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})

Moreover,
Q
is of degree
0
and therefore
Q\in\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L})
. This implies that:

DQ=d_{\mathrm{dR}}Q+\delta_{\mathbf{CE}}Q

Since the de Rham weight of
\iota_{\delta_{\mathrm{CE}}}\omega^{\mathrm{st}}
is exactly
1
and
\delta_{\mathbf{CE}}Q
has de Rham weight
0
, this implies that
\delta_{\mathbf{CE}}Q=0
and we get:

\iota_{\delta_{\mathrm{CE}}}\omega^{\mathrm{st}}=d_{\mathrm{dR}}Q

We have proven the following:

Theorem 5.2.11
.

A BV construction as above with strict symplectic structure has a BV charge given by the formula:

Q:=i_{\infty}(f)+h_{\infty}(\iota_{\delta_{\mathrm{CE}}}\omega^{\mathrm{st}})\in\mathrm{CE}{(\mathscr{L})}

We now need to state and prove the claims we used to prove this theorem. First recall that the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential respects the Chevalley–Eilenberg filtration and can therefore be decomposed in weight components:

\delta_{\mathrm{CE}}:=\delta_{0}+\delta_{1}+\cdots

In what follows we will consider two different filtrations:

–

The filtration coming from the de Rham algebra we will call the
de Rham weight
. It is denoted as before by
F^{p}\mathrm{DR}(\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L}))

–

The filtration induced by the Chevalley–Eilenberg filtration that we will call the
Chevalley–Eilenberg weight
. It is denoted by
F_{\mathscr{L}}^{p}\mathrm{DR}(\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L}))
.

We refer to Definition
5.2.21
for more details on those filtrations.

Lemma 5.2.12
.

We have the following:

(1)

\delta_{0}
restricted to
R
is exactly the differential on
R
,
\delta_{R}
.

(2)

The restriction of
\delta_{0}
to
\mathscr{L}_{S}[2]
is such that
(\iota_{\delta_{0}})_{|\mathscr{L}_{S}[2]}\omega\in F_{\mathscr{L}}^{1}\mathrm{DR}(A)

(3)

For
g\in A
,
\iota_{dg}
is a derivation on
\Sym_{A}\mathbb{T}_{A}[1]
and
\iota_{\iota_{dg}}\omega=d_{\mathrm{dR}}g
.

Proof.

The first claim is clear by definition of the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential.

For the second claim,
(\delta_{0})_{|\mathscr{L}_{S}[2]}
is zero on element generated by
A
and
\mathbb{T}_{A}[1]
and non-zero on
\mathscr{L}_{S}[2]
. Such a derivation is a linear combination of elements of the form
a\frac{\partial}{\partial\pi}
for
\pi\in\mathscr{L}
and
a\in R
. But
\iota_{a\frac{\partial}{\partial\pi}}\omega^{\mathrm{st}}=a\omega^{\mathrm{st}}(\frac{\partial}{\partial\pi},-)
. Since
\omega^{\mathrm{st}}
pairs
\mathscr{L}[2]
and
\mathscr{L}^{\vee}[-1]\in F^{1}\mathbf{DR}(A)
, it shows that
a\omega(\frac{\partial}{\partial\pi},-)\in F^{1}\mathbf{DR}(A)\cap F_{\mathscr{L}}^{1}\mathbf{DR}(A)
.

For the last claim, everything happens as if we are working on
\mathbf{Crit}(f)
with its canonical symplectic structure. By definition we have:

\iota_{\iota_{dg}}\omega_{0}=\omega_{0}^{\flat}(\iota_{dg})

We want to translate the problem in the Poisson setting. To do so we recall that
\omega_{0}^{\flat}
and
\Pi^{\flat}
are inverses of each other. Applying
\Pi^{\flat}
to the equality
\iota_{\iota_{dg}}\omega_{0}=dg
, we obtain:

\Pi^{\flat}\iota_{\iota_{dg}}\omega_{0}=\Pi^{\flat}(dg)

But
\Pi^{\flat}\iota_{\iota_{dg}}\omega_{0}=\Pi^{\flat}\omega_{0}^{\flat}(\iota_{dg})=\iota_{dg}
. Therefore we are left to prove that:

\iota_{dg}=\Pi^{\flat}(dg)=\{g,-\}

But on
\mathbf{Crit}(f)
, the Poisson structure is on
\Sym_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}\mathbb{T}_{X}[1]
and is induced by the pairing
\langle f,X\rangle=X(f)
because it is the Poisson structure associated to the canonical symplectic structure. Therefore
\{g,-\}
sends an element of
\mathscr{O}_{X}
to
0
and sends
X\in\mathbb{T}_{X}[1]
to
X(g)=dg.X=\iota_{dg}X
, which shows that
\iota_{dg}X=\{g,X\}
.
∎

The lemma above describes
\iota_{\delta_{0}}\omega^{\mathrm{st}}
. We now turn to the description of the terms of higher filtration
\delta_{\geq 1}
.

Lemma 5.2.13
.

\iota_{\delta_{\geq 1}}\omega^{\mathrm{st}}\in F_{\mathscr{L}}^{1}\mathrm{DR}(\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L}))

Proof.

Since
\delta_{\geq 1}
is valued in
F_{\mathscr{L}}^{1}\mathrm{DR}(\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L}))
then so is
\iota_{\delta_{\geq 1}}\omega^{\mathrm{st}}
.
∎

Corollary 5.2.14
.

p(\iota_{\delta_{\mathrm{CE}}}\omega^{\mathrm{st}})=d_{\mathrm{dR}}f

Proof.

We use Lemma
5.2.12
and Lemma
5.2.13
in combination with Lemma
5.2.18
saying that:

F_{\mathscr{L}}^{1}\mathrm{DR}(\mathrm{CE}(\mathscr{L}))\subset\ker(p)

This shows that:

p(\iota_{\delta_{\mathrm{CE}}}\omega^{\mathrm{st}})=p(d_{\mathrm{dR}}f)=d_{\mathrm{dR}}f

∎

5.2.3.
Deformation retract of de Rham algebras

The goal of this section is to compute the de Rham complexes of linear and Chevalley–Eilenberg stacks. This is a purely technical section that is required for the proof of Theorem
5.2.11
.

For linear derived stacks

Let
X=\mathbf{Spec}(A)
with
A
cofibrant of almost finite presentation and
\mathscr{F}\in\mathbf{Perf}(X)
concentrated in non-negative degrees. The linear stack associated to
\mathscr{F}
can be represented by
B=\Sym_{A}\mathscr{F}^{\vee}\in\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{\leq 0}}
endowed with the differential
\delta_{B}=\delta_{A}+\delta_{\mathscr{F}^{\vee}}
.

Notation 5.2.15
.

In this section we will use the following notations:

\beta_{1\cdots k}:=\beta_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_{k}

\hbox{\hskip 455.45732pt\hskip-9.90627pt\hbox{$\beta_{1\cdots k}^{i}$}\hskip-9.90627pt\hskip-455.45732pt\raisebox{19.26097pt}{\hbox{$\scalebox{-1}{\hbox{\raisebox{-3.34055pt}{\resizebox{53617400}{141084}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\mathchoice{\raisebox{-853.45891pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-853.45891pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-157.14236pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.98pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.7pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-157.14285pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\h 455.45732pt}=\beta_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_{i-1}\wedge\beta_{i+1}\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_{k}

We will write:

\mathrm{DR}^{\mathrm{gr}}(B)\simeq\Sym^{\mathrm{gr}}_{A}\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]

And the mixed structure of
\mathrm{DR}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
is the de Rham differential. Moreover, using a connection on
\mathscr{F}
, we have:

\Omega^{1}_{B}\simeq\pi^{*}(\mathscr{F}\oplus^{\nabla}\mathbb{L}_{A})

Then we get:

\begin{split}\mathrm{DR}(B)\simeq&\cSym_{A}\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]\otimes_{A}\cSym_{A}\mathscr{F}^{\vee}[-1]\otimes_{A}\Sym_{A}\mathscr{F}^{\vee}\\
\simeq&\Sym_{A}\left(\widehat{\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]}\oplus\widehat{\mathscr{F}^{\vee}[-1]}\oplus\mathscr{F}^{\vee}\right)\end{split}

Where the differential on the right hand side is describe by the following:

Lemma 5.2.16
.

The total differential is given by:

D_{B}=d_{\mathrm{dR}}+\delta_{\mathscr{F}^{\vee}}+\delta_{A}^{v}+\delta_{\mathscr{F}^{\vee}}^{v}+\delta_{\nabla}

with:

–

d_{\mathrm{dR}}
the de Rham differential.

–

\delta_{A}^{v}
the vertical differential on
\mathrm{DR}(A)
extended by zero on
\mathscr{F}^{\vee}[-1]
and
\mathscr{F}^{\vee}
.

\delta_{A}^{v}=\delta_{A}+\delta_{\mathbb{L}_{A}}

–

\delta_{\mathscr{F}^{\vee}}^{v}
the differential on
\mathscr{F}^{\vee}[-1]
coming from the differential
\delta_{\mathscr{F}^{\vee}}
on
\mathscr{F}^{\vee}
extended
B
-linearly and by
0
on
\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]
and
\mathscr{F}^{\vee}
.

–

\delta_{\mathscr{F}^{\vee}}=\delta_{B}-\delta_{A}
is the differential on
\mathscr{F}^{\vee}
.

–

\delta_{\nabla}
the part of the differential induced by the connection, valued in:

\cSym_{A}\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]\otimes_{A}\Sym_{A}^{\geq 1}\mathscr{F}^{\vee}

Proof.

By definition we have
D_{B}=d_{\mathrm{dR}}+\delta_{B}^{v}
the decomposition in de Rham and vertical differential. Moreover
\delta_{B}^{v}
restricted to
B
is
\delta_{B}
itself and
\delta_{B}^{v}
on
\mathbb{L}_{B}[-1]
is the natural differential on
\mathbb{L}_{B}[-1]
. Using Proposition
1.2.39
, we have:

\mathbb{L}_{B}[-1]\simeq B\otimes_{A}\left(\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]\oplus^{\nabla}\mathscr{F}^{\vee}[-1]\right)

where the right hand side is the
A
-module with differential given by

\delta_{B}+\delta_{\mathscr{F}^{\vee}}^{v}+\delta_{\mathbb{L}_{A}}+\delta_{\nabla}

Moreover
\delta_{B}+\delta_{\mathbb{L}_{A}}=\delta_{\mathscr{F}^{\vee}}+\delta_{A}^{v}
and
\delta_{\nabla}
is the part of the differential sending
\mathscr{F}^{\vee}[-1]
to an element in
\left(\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]\otimes_{A}\mathscr{F}^{\vee}\right)[-1]
via the covariant derivative.
∎

We are now ready to define the maps we need for the deformation retract. Before that we want to define two filtrations:

–

The
de Rham filtration
, denoted
F^{p}\mathrm{DR}(B)
, given by the complete filtration associated with the graded mixed structure on
\mathrm{DR}(B)
. This is the filtration associated with the ideal generated by
\mathbb{L}_{A}[1]
and
\mathscr{F}^{\vee}[-1]
(see Example
B.2.4
).

–

The
\mathscr{F}
-filtration
denoted
F_{\mathscr{F}}^{p}\mathrm{DR}(B)
induced by the natural filtration on
\Sym_{B}\mathscr{F}^{\vee}
of the symmetric algebra, generated by the terms
\mathscr{F}^{\vee}
and
\mathscr{F}^{\vee}[-1]
in
\mathrm{DR}(B)
.

Definition 5.2.17
.

There are maps:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{DR}(A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{DR}(B)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}

with:

–

i
is the map induced by the projection
\mathbb{A}_{X}(\mathscr{F})\rightarrow X
and therefore respects the total differentials. This map preserves both the de Rham filtration and the
\mathscr{F}
-filtration.

–

p
is the map induced by the
0
section
X\rightarrow\mathbb{A}_{X}(\mathscr{F})
and therefore respects the total differentials. It also preserves both filtrations.

–

h
is a degree
-1
derivation defined on homogeneous elements,
f\in B
,
\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1],i=1\cdots p
,
d\xi_{i}\in\mathscr{F}^{\vee}[-1],i=1\cdots m
and
\eta_{i}\in\mathscr{F}^{\vee},i=1\cdots m^{\prime}
by:

h(f\alpha_{1\cdots p}\wedge(d\xi)_{1\cdots m}\wedge\eta_{1\cdots m^{\prime}})=\frac{1}{m+m^{\prime}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\epsilon_{h}f\alpha_{1\cdots p}\wedge\hbox{\hskip 455.45732pt\hskip-17.09496pt\hbox{$(d\xi)_{1\cdots m}^{i}$}\hskip-17.09496pt\hskip-455.45732pt\raisebox{19.26097pt}{\hbox{$\scalebox{-1}{\hbox{\raisebox{-3.34055pt}{\resizebox{53617400}{141084}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\mathchoice{\raisebox{-853.45891pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-853.45891pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{10.00012pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-157.14236pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\displaystyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.4pt}{$\textstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.98pt}{$\scriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.7pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\kern-0.6pt\bigwedge\kern-0.6pt$}}}}}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-157.14285pt}{\resizebox{468892385}{36044800}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\resizebox{0}{0}{\ With
\epsilon_{h}
obeying the sign rule for
h
a degree -1 derivation:

\epsilon_{h}=(-1)^{n_{h}},\qquad n_{h}=\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}(|\xi_{j}|+1)+\sum_{j=i+1}^{m}(|\xi_{j}|+1)|\xi_{i}|

In short,
h
turns a

to a
\xi
. Therefore
h
preserves the
\mathscr{F}
-filtration and reduces the de Rham weight by
1
.

Lemma 5.2.18
.

\ker(p)=\prod_{p+q\geq 1}\cSym_{B}\mathbb{L}_{B}[-1]\otimes_{B}\cSym_{B}^{\geq p}\mathscr{F}^{\vee}[-1]\otimes_{B}\Sym_{B}^{\geq q}\mathscr{F}^{\vee}:=F_{\mathscr{F}}^{1}\mathrm{DR}(B)

Proof.

In other words, we need to show that the kernel of
p
is the ideal of
\mathrm{DR}(B)
generated by
\mathscr{F}^{\vee}
and
\mathscr{F}^{\vee}[-1]
. Since
p
is the map induced by the
0
section of the linear stack, it corresponds to the projection
\Sym_{B}\mathscr{F}^{\vee}\to B
and induces the projection:

\mathrm{DR}(B)\simeq\Sym_{A}\left(\widehat{\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]\oplus\mathscr{F}^{\vee}[-1]}\oplus\mathscr{F}^{\vee}\right)\to\cSym_{A}\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1]\simeq\mathrm{DR}(A)

Therefore the kernel of this map is indeed the ideal generated by
\mathscr{F}^{\vee}
and
\mathscr{F}^{\vee}[-1]
.
∎

Theorem 5.2.19
.

i
,
p
and
h
define a deformation retract:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{DR}(A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{DR}(B)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}

Proof.

It is straightfoward that
p\circ i=\mathrm{id}
. We need to show that
h
is an homotopy between
\mathrm{id}
and
i\circ p
that is
\mathrm{id}-i\circ p=[d,h]
. On generator of
\mathrm{DR}(B)
, denoted by
f\in B
,
\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{L}_{A}[-1],i=1\cdots p
,
d\xi_{i}\in\mathscr{F}^{\vee}[-1],i=1\cdots m
and
\eta_{i}\in\mathscr{F}^{\vee},i=1\cdots m^{\prime}
, we get:

(\mathrm{id}-i\circ p)(f\alpha_{1\cdots p}\otimes 1\otimes 1)=0

(\mathrm{id}-i\circ p)(d\xi_{1\cdots m}\wedge\eta_{1\cdots m^{\prime}})=d\xi_{1\cdots m}\wedge\eta_{1\cdots m^{\prime}}\ \ \text{if }\ m+m^{\prime}\neq 0

It is straightforward to check that
[d,h](f\alpha_{1\cdots p})=0
since
h
sends
\cSym_{B}\Omega^{1}_{B}[-1]
to zero. We only have to check this equation on terms of the form
d\xi_{1\cdots m}\wedge\eta_{1\cdots m^{\prime}}
.

We have:

\epsilon_{2}=(-1)^{n_{2}},\qquad n_{2}=n_{d}+\sum_{j=1}^{m}(|\xi_{j}|+1)+\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}|\eta_{j}||\eta_{k}|

\begin{split}n_{2}=&\sum_{j=1}^{m}(|\xi_{j}|+1)+\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}|\eta_{j}|+\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}|\eta_{j}|(|\eta_{k}|+1)+\sum_{j=1}^{m}(|\xi_{j}|+1)+\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}|\eta_{j}||\eta_{k}|\\
=&2\times\sum_{j=1}^{m}(|\xi_{j}|+1)+2\times\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}|\eta_{j}|(|\eta_{k}|+1)\end{split}

since
n_{2}
is even,
\epsilon_{2}=1
and:

\sum_{k=1}^{m^{\prime}}\epsilon_{2}d\xi_{1\cdots m}\wedge\eta_{1\cdots m^{\prime}}=m^{\prime}\times d\xi_{1\cdots m}\wedge\eta_{1\cdots m^{\prime}}

Finally we have:

\epsilon_{hd}=(-1)^{n_{hd}},\qquad n_{hd}=n_{d}+\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}(|\xi_{j}|+1)+\sum_{j=i+1}^{m}(|\xi_{j}|+1)|\xi_{i}|+|\xi_{i}|(|\eta_{k}|+1)

\begin{split}n_{hd}=&\sum_{j=1}^{m}(|\xi_{j}|+1)+\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}|\eta_{j}|+\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}|\eta_{j}|(|\eta_{k}|+1)+\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}(|\xi_{j}|+1)\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad+\sum_{j=i+1}^{m}(|\xi_{j}|+1)|\xi_{i}|+|\xi_{i}|(|\eta_{k}|+1)\\
=&\sum_{j=1}^{m}(|\xi_{j}|+1)+\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}|\eta_{j}|(|\eta_{k}|+2)+\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}(|\xi_{j}|+1)\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad+\sum_{j=i+1}^{m}(|\xi_{j}|+1)|\xi_{i}|+|\xi_{i}|(|\eta_{k}|+1)\end{split}

Now to show the result, we need to show that
n_{hd}=n_{dh}+1\mod 2
but a straightfoward calculation show that:

n_{hd}-n_{dh}=1

This shows that:

[d,h](d\xi_{1\cdots m}\wedge\eta_{1\cdots m^{\prime}})=\frac{1}{m+m^{\prime}}\left((m+m^{\prime})\times d\xi_{1\cdots m}\wedge\eta_{1\cdots m^{\prime}}\right)=d\xi_{1\cdots m}\wedge\eta_{1\cdots m^{\prime}}

∎

Theorem 5.2.20
.

(p,i,h)
forms a strong deformation retract. In other words we have:

ph=hi=h^{2}=0

Proof.

5.3.
Examples of BV Constructions

In this section we will show that our framework encompasses and generalizes many of the already existing constructions (within the restriction of our framework). In particular we recover the two classes of constructions given by:

–

The BV construction on the Koszul–Tate resolution of
f
.

–

The equivariant derived critical locus for a functional with off-shell symmetries (infinitesimal or not).

For the second type of construction, we will see that this recovers the BV formalism for group actions as discussed in
[
BSS21
]
, the infinitesimal BV formalism for off-shell actions of Lie algebroids and in the most general case, the BV formalism for off-shell actions of groupoids.

We will also see that for off-shell actions, the heuristics described in Constructions
5.0.2
and
5.0.1
coincide.

5.3.2.
Group actions and moment maps

This section motivates a notion of BV construction for group actions instead of the infinitesimal actions of their Lie algebras. The idea is that such a construction would remember the global action of the group and therefore global phenomena induced by the group action. This idea is discussed in more details in
[
BSS21
]
where they study the
G
-equivariant derived critical locus as a model for such a refined notion of BV construction. We argue that this is an instance of BV construction in our sens, and it is a particular example of the more general construction in Section
5.3.4
.

We are interested in the BV construction where the action on
S
is given by an action of a
group

G
. Again, given an arbitrary almost derived critical locus, nothing ensures the existence of such a BV construction. However, we will see that given a group action of off-shell symmetries (Definition
5.1.14
), we can always construct an almost derived critical locus
S
whose generalized symplectic reduction is given by a quotient of
S
by an action of
G
.

Let
G
be an affine algebraic group acting on
X
such that
f:X\to\mathbb{A}_{k}^{1}
is
G
-invariant. Then there is moment map
\mu:T^{*}X\to\mathfrak{g}^{*}
(Definition
4.3.2
) whose symplectic reduction is
T^{*}\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{G}$}}}\right]
(Example
4.3.7
).

From Example
4.3.11
, we know that by taking the Lagrangian intersection of
\mu
, we have a
(-1)
-shifted moment map
\mu_{-1}:\mathbf{Crit}(f)\to\mathfrak{g}^{*}[-1]
whose symplectic reduction is
\mathbf{Crit}(\left[f\right])
. We will show that
\mathbf{Crit}(\left[f\right])
is a BV construction for the inclusion
Z(\mu)\to\mathbf{Crit}(f)
. All we are lacking is to show that
Z(\mu_{-1})
is an almost derived critical locus:

Lemma 5.3.2
.

Z(\mu_{-1})
is an almost derived critical locus.

Proof.

Consider the following diagram where all squares are pullbacks:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z(\mu)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\star}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T^{*}X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{g}^{*}\times X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{g}^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mu\times\pi}

The left most square is a pullback of linear stacks over
X
therefore we have:

Z(\mu)\simeq\mathbb{A}_{X}(\mathbb{L}_{X}\times_{\mathfrak{g}^{*}\otimes\mathscr{O}_{X}}\mathscr{O}_{X})\simeq\mathbb{A}_{X}(\mathbb{L}_{X}\oplus^{\mu}\mathfrak{g}^{*}[-1]\otimes\mathscr{O}_{X})

In particular, since
X=\mathbf{Spec}(A)
, it is affine and its algebra of functions is
\Sym_{A}\left(A\otimes\mathfrak{g}[1]\oplus\mathbb{T}_{X}\right)
.

Now consider the commutative diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T^{*}X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{g}^{*}\times X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces df}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s_{0}}

This diagram is commutative because
f
is
G
-equivariant and taking the limit of this diagram either first horizontally and then vertically or vice versa, we get an equivalence:

Z(\mu_{-1}):=\mathbf{Crit}(f)\times_{\mathfrak{g}^{*}[-1]\times X}X\simeq X\times_{Z(\mu)}X

The right hand side is clearly affine with algebra of functions:

A\otimes_{\Sym_{A}\mathbb{T}_{A}\oplus^{\mu}A\otimes\mathfrak{g}[1]}A\simeq\Sym_{A}\left(\mathbb{T}_{A}[1]\oplus^{\mu}A\otimes\mathfrak{g}[2]\right)

and the differential restricted to
\mathbb{T}_{A}[1]
is the contraction
\iota_{df}
. This shows that
Z(\mu_{-1})
is an almost derived critical locus.
∎

This lemma together with Example
4.3.21
shows the following:

Theorem 5.3.3
.

Let
X
be an Artin stack and
G
an affine group of off-shell symmetries acting on
X
.
Then
\mathrm{Crit}(\left[f\right])
is a generalized symplectic reduction of
Z(\mu_{-1})\to\mathbf{Crit}(f)
and is therefore an off-shell BV construction on
f
(with
S=Z(\mu_{-1})
).

We have seen with Proposition
4.2.6
and Example
4.1.8
that
\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.75pt}{$\displaystyle{Z(\mu_{-1})}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X\times\mathfrak{g}}$}}{\raisebox{3.75pt}{$\textstyle{Z(\mu_{-1})}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X\times\mathfrak{g}}$}}{\raisebox{2.625pt}{$\scriptstyle{Z(\mu_{-1})}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X\times\mathfrak{g}}$}}{\raisebox{1.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{Z(\mu_{-1})}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X\times\mathfrak{g}}$}}}\right]
is the formal completion of the map
Z(\mu)\to\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.75pt}{$\displaystyle{Z(\mu_{-1})}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{3.75pt}{$\textstyle{Z(\mu_{-1})}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{2.625pt}{$\scriptstyle{Z(\mu_{-1})}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{Z(\mu_{-1})}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{G}$}}}\right]
.

Corollary 5.3.4
.

If
Y:=\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{S}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{S}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{S}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{S}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{G}$}}}\right]
is a BV construction obtained by an action of off-shell symmetries (that is a BV construction as in Theorem
5.3.3
) such that
G
acts on
X
. Then the formal completion

\widehat{Y}\simeq\widehat{Y_{S}}\simeq\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{S}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X\times\mathfrak{g}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{S}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X\times\mathfrak{g}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{S}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X\times\mathfrak{g}}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{S}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X\times\mathfrak{g}}$}}}\right]

is an infinitesimal BV construction in the sens of Definition
5.1.8
.

Proof.

This is a direct consequence of Theorem
5.1.13
.
∎

Remark 5.3.5
.

One of the intersecting feature of the BV construction for a
G
-action on
X
of off-shell symmetries is that it can be understood both from the point of view of Construction
5.0.1
and of Construction
5.0.2
. For the first point of view, it is given, by definition, by a quotient of an almost derived critical locus (fitting in a Lagrangian correspondence). For the second point of view, we have shown that this is also the derived critical locus of the quotient map
\left[f\right]:\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{G}$}}}\right]\to\mathbb{A}^{1}
(i.e. the equivariant derived critical locus):

\mathbf{Crit}(\left[f\right])\simeq\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{G}$}}}\right]\times_{T^{*}\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{G}$}}}\right]}\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{G}$}}}\right]\simeq\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.75pt}{$\displaystyle{Z(\mu_{-1})}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{3.75pt}{$\textstyle{Z(\mu_{-1})}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{2.625pt}{$\scriptstyle{Z(\mu_{-1})}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{G}$}}{\raisebox{1.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{Z(\mu_{-1})}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{G}$}}}\right]

5.3.3.
Lie algebroid action and moment maps

In the previous section we had the BV construction from a group action of off-shell symmetries. In this section we will show that a similar construction can be made from an infinitesimal action of a Lie algebroid of off-shell symmetries.

We know from Example
4.3.21
, that if
\mathscr{L}
is a Lie algebroid of off-shell infinitesimal symmetries on
X
(Definition
5.1.15
), then
\mathbf{Crit}(f)\to L^{*}[-1]
is a
(-1)
-shifted moment map with infinitesimal symplectic reduction given by the
\mathscr{L}
-equivariant derived critical locus
\mathbf{Crit}(\left[f\right])
.

Just like in Lemma
5.3.2
, we can show that
Z(\mu_{-1})
is an almost derived critical locus if
\mathscr{L}
is of almost finite presentation and concentrated in non-positive degrees (see Proposition
4.2.34
knowing that
X
is a smooth algebraic variety).

This proves the following:

Theorem 5.3.6
.

Given a Lie algebroid of off-shell symmetries
\mathscr{L}
, then
\mathbf{Crit}(\left[f\right])
is an infinitesimal BV construction (for
S=Z(\rho_{-1}^{*})
).

Again, this infinitesimal BV construction from a Lie algebroid of off-shell symmetries on
X
can be understood both from the point of view of Construction
5.0.1
and of Construction
5.0.2
. For the first point of view, it is by definition a weak infinitesimal quotient of an almost derived critical locus
Z(\rho_{-1}^{*})
. For the second point of view, this is the derived critical locus of the quotient map
\left[f\right]:\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{L}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{L}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{L}}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{L}}$}}}\right]\to\mathbb{A}^{1}
.

5.3.4.
BV construction for groupoid action

This section provides the most general BV construction for off-shell symmetries. It is very similar to both Sections
5.3.2
and

\simeq&\left(\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]\times_{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]_{\mathrm{DR}}}X_{\mathrm{DR}}\right)\times_{\left(T^{*}\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]\times_{\left(T^{*}\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.6994pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.6994pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\rai \simeq&\widehat{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]_{X}}\times_{\widehat{\left(T^{*}\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]\right)_{Z(\mu)}}}\widehat{\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]_{X}}\\
\simeq&\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]\times_{T^{*}\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{L}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{L}}$}}{\raisebox{1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.67416pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{L}}$}}{\raisebox{1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.19583pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{L}}$}}}\right]}\left[{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{X}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.6994pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathscr{G}}$}}}\right]\\
\simeq&\mathbf{Crit}(\left[f\right]_{\mathscr{L}})\end{split}

where the fifth equivalence follows from Proposition
4.3.32
and Corollary
4.2.7
.
∎

This proposition implies that if
\mathscr{L}
integrates to a smooth Segal groupoid, then the infinitesimal BV construction obtained via Proposition
5.1.18
out of the BV construction given by
\mathbf{Crit}(\left[f\right]_{\mathscr{G}})
is equivalent to the infinitesimal BV construction given by
\mathbf{Crit}(\left[f\right]_{\mathscr{L}})
from Theorem
5.3.6
.

Appendix A
Model Categorical Setup

A.1.
Good Model Structures

In this section, are are going to define the notion of “good” model structure. First, recall that
\Mod_{k}
is equipped with its projective model structure where weak equivalences are quasi-isomorphims and fibrations are degree-wise surjective morphisms. Moreover,
\Mod_{k}
satisfies the monoid axiom
130
130

130

The monoid axiom in a symmetric monoidal model category
\mathscr{M}
(
[
SS00
, Definition 2.1]
) is an axiom on the model structure given in
[
SS00
, Definition 2.2]
which gives some results (
[
SS00
, Theorem 3.1]
) on the model structure on modules and algebras over a commutative monoid in
\mathscr{M}
.
as well as some other properties ensuring that we have a model structure on commutative monoids in
\Mod_{k}
(namely commutative differential graded
k
-algebras) and on modules over those. We formalize these properties to define the notion of good model structure.

Definition A.1.1

(
[
CPT+17
, Section 1.1]
)
.

Consider
\mathscr{M}
a closed symmetric monoidal
\Mod_{k}
-enriched (with tensor and cotensor) combinatorial model category. In other word,
\mathscr{M}
is a symmetric monoidal

\Mod_{k}
-model algebra as in
[
Hov99
, Definition 4.2.20]
. Moreover,
[
CPT+17
, Proposition A.1.1]
shows that
\mathscr{M}
is
stable
. Then
\mathscr{M}
will be called a
good model category
if it satisfies:

–

The unit
1
is a cofibrant object in
\mathscr{M}
.

–

For any cofibration
j:X\to Y
in
\mathscr{M}
, any object
A\in\mathscr{M}
, and for any morphism
u:A\otimes X\to C
in
\mathscr{M}
the strict push-out square in
\mathscr{M}
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\otimes X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\otimes Y}

is a homotopy pushout square.

–

For any cofibrant object
X\in\mathscr{M}
, the functor
X\otimes-:\mathscr{M}\to\mathscr{M}
preserves weak equivalences (i.e.
X
is
\otimes
-flat).

–

\mathscr{M}
is a tractable model category, that is, there are generating sets of cofibrations
I
, and trivial cofibrations
J
in
\mathscr{M}
with cofibrant domains.

–

Equivalences are stable under filtered colimits and finite products in
\mathscr{M}
.

Notation A.1.2
.

Given a symmetric monoidal category
\mathscr{M}
, we denote by
\mathrm{cdga}_{\mathscr{M}}
the category of unital commutative monoids in
\mathscr{M}
and we will call them
algebras
in
\mathscr{M}
.
For the categories of graded algebras, filtered algebras, complete filtered algebras, graded mixed algebras and weak graded mixed algebras (see Appendix
B
and
C
), we will write
\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{gr}}
,
\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{filt}}
,
\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{cpl}}
,
\mathrm{cdga}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
and
\mathrm{cdga}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
respectively.

Definition A.1.3
.

A
(left)-module
N\in\mathscr{M}
over an algebra
A\in\mathrm{cdga}_{\mathscr{M}}
is a (left) action
\mu:A\otimes M\to M
satisfying the usual axioms of a module.

The category of
A
-module is denoted
\Mod_{A}^{\mathscr{M}}
.
For the categories of graded modules, filtered modules, complete filtered modules, graded mixed modules, weak graded mixed modules, we will use the simpler notations
\Mod_{A}^{\mathrm{gr}}
,
\Mod_{A}^{\mathrm{filt}}
,
\Mod_{A}^{\mathrm{cpl}}
,
\Mod_{A}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
and
\Mod_{A}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
respectively.

Proposition A.1.4
.

Take
\mathscr{M}
a good model category then:

–

\mathscr{M}
satisfies the monoid axiom and therefore the category
\mathrm{cdga}_{\mathscr{M}}
has a canonical model structure (defined via the free-forget adjunction).

–

For any
A\in\mathrm{cdga}_{\mathscr{M}}
, the category of
A
-modules is endowed with the structure of a symmetric monoidal combinatorial
model category, for which the equivalences and fibrations are defined in
\mathscr{M}
. In particular, fibrations and weak-equivalences are detected in
\mathscr{M}
. Moreover,
\Mod_{A}^{\mathscr{M}}
carries a model structure making it a good model category (see the introduction of
[
CPT+17
, Section 1.3.1]
).

–

For any equivalence
A\to A^{\prime}
in
\mathrm{cdga}_{\mathscr{M}}
, the extension-restriction Quillen adjunction:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Mod_{A}^{\mathscr{M}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Mod_{A^{\prime}}^{\mathscr{M}}}

is a Quillen equivalence.

Remark A.1.5
.

Since
\Mod_{A}^{\mathscr{M}}
is a good model category we can take again commutative monoids and module in
\Mod_{A}^{\mathscr{M}}
which essentially gives us
A
-algebras in
\mathscr{M}
and their modules.

Remark A.1.6
.

In
[
Lur07
, Theorem 1.5.14]
, it is shown that there is an equivalence:

\Mod_{A}^{\mathscr{M}}\simeq\Stab\left(\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}^{\mathscr{M}}\right)

Moreover,
[
Lur07
, Remark 1.5.17]
tells us that if the tensor product is exact in each variable, then taking
N\in\Mod_{A}^{\mathscr{M}}
then its image under the composition:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Mod_{A}^{\mathscr{M}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Stab\left(\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}^{\mathscr{M}}\right)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}^{\mathscr{M}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega^{\infty}}

is given by the square zero extension
A\boxplus N\to A
defined in
A.2.1
.

Given
F:\mathscr{M}\to\mathscr{M}^{\prime}
a symmetric monoidal functor between two good model categories. Then it naturally induces functors:

F:\mathrm{cdga}_{\mathscr{M}}\to\mathrm{cdga}_{\mathscr{M}^{\prime}}\qquad F:\Mod_{A}^{\mathscr{M}}\to\Mod_{F(A)}^{\mathscr{M}^{\prime}}

Example A.1.7
.

We have the following good model categories:

–

\Mod_{k}
is a good model category and we will denote:

\mathrm{cdga}:=\mathrm{cdga}_{\Mod_{k}}\qquad\Mod_{A}:=\Mod_{A}^{\Mod_{k}}

for all
A\in\mathrm{cdga}
. Thanks to Proposition
A.1.4
, for all
A\in\mathrm{cdga}
we have that

is a good model category.

–

Given
\mathscr{M}
a good model category, the category of graded mixed objects in
\mathscr{M}
, denoted
\mathscr{M}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
is again a good model category for its injective model structure (see Appendix
C
).

In particular for
\mathscr{M}=\Mod_{k}
we get graded mixed complexes, algebras and modules denoted by
\Mod_{k}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
,
\mathrm{cdga}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
and
\Mod_{A}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
for
A\in\mathrm{cdga}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
.

Assumption A.1.8
.

In what follows, we will use two extra conditions on our good model structure:

(1)

The tensor product is exact in each variables.

(2)

The tensor product commutes with coproducts.

All the examples of good model categories we consider satisfy these two additional conditions.

A.2.
Cotangent Complex in
\mathscr{M}

Let
\mathscr{M}
be a good model category satisfying Assumptions
A.1.8
. We are going to recall the construction of the tangent and cotangent complexes in such a good model category
\mathscr{M}
. We will also discuss some functoriality properties with respect to the choice of
\mathscr{M}
.

Definition A.2.1
.

Given any
B
-module
N
, we can construct the
trivial square zero extension
(see
[
TV08
, Section 1.2.1]
),
{B\boxplus N}
, given by the direct sum as a
B
-module, and with the product defined by the following map:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(FA\oplus FM)\otimes(FA\oplus FM)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(FA\otimes FA)\oplus\left((FA\otimes FM)\oplus(FM\otimes FA)\right)\oplus FM\otimes FM}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FA\oplus FM}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sim}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mu_{A}\oplus(\mu_{M}+\mu_{M})\oplus 0}

This defines a functor
B\boxplus-
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Mod_{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{cdga}_{A//B}^{\mathscr{M}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\boxplus M}

Example A.2.2
.

If
\mathscr{M}=\Mod_{k}
then
A\boxplus M
is the commutative algebra with product:

(a,m)\dot{(}a^{\prime},m^{\prime})=(aa^{\prime},am^{\prime}+a^{\prime}m)

The main point of this definition is to get the following description of derivations:

Lemma A.2.3
.

There is an isomorphism of
B
-modules
131
131

131

This can in fact be enriched either in
\Mod_{B}^{\mathscr{M}}
or in
\Mod_{B}
.
:

\Hom_{\mathrm{cdga}_{A//B}^{\mathscr{M}}}\left(B,B\boxplus M\right)\cong\Der_{A}^{\mathscr{M}}(B,M)

Definition A.2.4
.

Given
f:A\to B
, the
cotangent complex of
B
relative to
A
is defined as the
B
-module
\mathbb{L}_{B/A}^{\mathscr{M}}
representing derived
A
-linear derivations:

\Hom_{B}\left(\mathbb{L}_{B/A}^{\mathscr{M}},M\right)\cong\mathbb{R}\Der_{A}(B,M)

Construction A.2.5
.

Thanks to
[
CPT+17
, Lemma 1.3.4 and Remark 1.3.6]
, the functor:

B\boxplus-:\Mod_{B}\to\mathrm{cdga}_{A//B}^{\mathscr{M}}

has a derived left adjoint
\mathbb{L}^{\mathscr{M}}
and by definition we have:

\mathbb{L}_{B/A}^{\mathscr{M}}:=\mathbb{L}^{\mathscr{M}}(A\to B\overset{\mathrm{id}}{\to}B)

Definition A.2.6
.

In general, the relative tangent complex of
f:A\to B
is the
B
-module of derived
A
-linear derivations of
B
:

\mathbb{T}_{B/A}^{\mathscr{M}}:=\mathbb{R}\Der_{A}^{\mathscr{M}}(B,B)

Using the defining property of the cotangent complex we get:

\mathbb{T}_{B/A}^{\mathscr{M}}\simeq\Hom_{B}^{\mathscr{M}}\left(\mathbb{L}_{B/A}^{\mathscr{M}},B\right)

Proposition A.2.7
.

As explained in Proposition
A.1.4
, given a morphism
f:B\to B^{\prime}
of
A
-algebras, we get an adjunction:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}:\Mod_{B}^{\mathscr{M}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Mod_{B^{\prime}}^{\mathscr{M}}:f_{*}}

Then we get a map of
B^{\prime}
-modules:

f^{*}\mathbb{L}_{B/A}^{\mathscr{M}}\to\mathbb{L}_{B^{\prime}/A}^{\mathscr{M}}

Moreover the cofiber of this map is
\mathbb{L}_{B^{\prime}/B}^{\mathscr{M}}
.

Proof.

Any derivation
\phi:B^{\prime}\to M
restricts to a derivation
\phi:B\to f_{*}M
inducing a map
132
132

132

This is induced by the restriction map:

\underset{\mathrm{cdga}_{/B^{\prime}}^{\mathscr{M}}}{\Hom}(B^{\prime},B^{\prime}\boxplus M)\to\underset{\mathrm{cdga}_{/B^{\prime}}^{\mathscr{M}}}{\Hom}(B,B^{\prime}\boxplus M)\simeq\underset{\mathrm{cdga}_{/B}^{\mathscr{M}}}{\Hom}(B,B\boxplus f_{*}M)

\Der_{B^{\prime}}(B^{\prime},M)\to\Der_{B}(B,f_{*}M)
. This induces a morphism:

\Hom_{B^{\prime}}(\mathbb{L}_{B^{\prime}/A},M)\to\Hom_{B}(\mathbb{L}_{B/A},f_{*}M)\simeq\Hom_{B^{\prime}}(f^{*}\mathbb{L}_{B/A},M)

and therefore induces a morphism
f^{*}\mathbb{L}_{B/A}\to\mathbb{L}_{B^{\prime}/A}
.

To compute the cofiber, we compute the fiber after applying
\Hom_{B^{\prime}}(-,M)
:

\mathrm{fiber}\left(\underset{\mathrm{cdga}_{A//B^{\prime}}^{\mathscr{M}}}{\Hom}\left(B^{\prime},B^{\prime}\boxplus M\right)\to\underset{\mathrm{cdga}_{A//B}^{\mathscr{M}}}{\Hom}\left(B,B\boxplus f_{*}M\right)\right)

In other words, this is the fiber of the map that sends a derivation
\phi:B^{\prime}\to M
to its restriction
\phi:B\to f_{*}M
. But this is exactly the same as the fiber:

\mathrm{fiber}\left(\underset{\mathrm{cdga}_{A//B^{\prime}}^{\mathscr{M}}}{\Hom}\left(B^{\prime},B^{\prime}\boxplus M\right)\to\underset{\mathrm{cdga}_{A//B^{\prime}}^{\mathscr{M}}}{\Hom}\left(B,B^{\prime}\boxplus M\right)\right)

which is given by derivations
\phi:B^{\prime}\to M
such that
\phi_{|B}\simeq 0
, and therefore
\phi
is valued a
B
-linear derivation. This proves that this fiber is equivalent to:

\underset{\mathrm{cdga}_{B//B^{\prime}}^{\mathscr{M}}}{\Hom}\left(B^{\prime},B^{\prime}\boxplus M\right)\simeq\Hom_{B}^{\prime}\left(\mathbb{L}_{B^{\prime}/B},M\right)

∎

Corollary A.2.8
.

Given
f:A\rightarrow B
and
g:B\rightarrow C
, we have a homotopy fiber sequence:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}^{\mathscr{M}}_{B/A}\otimes_{B}C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}^{\mathscr{M}}_{C/A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}^{\mathscr{M}}_{C/B}}

In particular for
A=k
we write
\mathbb{L}^{\mathscr{M}}_{B/k}=\mathbb{L}^{\mathscr{M}}_{B}
and we get:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}^{\mathscr{M}}_{B}\otimes_{B}C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}^{\mathscr{M}}_{C}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}^{\mathscr{M}}_{C/B}}

Proposition A.2.9
.

Consider the following pushout diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}

then we have a pushout diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{*}f^{*}\mathbb{L}^{\mathscr{M}}_{A}\simeq j^{*}g^{*}\mathbb{L}^{\mathscr{M}}_{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{*}\mathbb{L}^{\mathscr{M}}_{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j^{*}\mathbb{L}^{\mathscr{M}}_{C}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{L}^{\mathscr{M}}_{D}}

Lemma B.1.6
.

The colimit functor is symmetric monoidal:

\colim(FA\otimes FB)\simeq\colim(FA)\otimes\colim(FB)

Proof.

The goal is to compute:

\underset{n}{\colim}\bigoplus_{p+q=n}F^{p}A\otimes F^{q}B

The direct sums are finite direct sums and therefore they are coproducts. We need to compute the following colimit over the diagram
\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}
with a unique morphism
(i,j)\to(i^{\prime},j^{\prime})
if and only if
|i^{\prime}-i|+|j^{\prime}-j|\leq 1
.

\underset{p,q\in\mathbb{Z}}{\colim}F^{p}A\otimes F^{q}B

Since tensor product of modules commute with direct sums, we get:

\underset{p,q\in\mathbb{Z}}{\colim}F^{p}A\otimes F^{q}B\simeq\underset{p\in\mathbb{Z}}{\colim}F^{p}A\otimes\underset{q\in\mathbb{Z}}{\colim}F^{q}B\simeq A\otimes B

∎

Definition B.1.11

Lemma B.1.12
.

The underlying complex of a direct sum of filtered complexes is the finite sum of the filtered complexes:

\colim(FV\oplus FW)\simeq\colim(FV)\oplus\colim(FW)\simeq V\oplus W

Proof.

Since the direct sum of cochain complexes is their coproduct, it commutes with colimits and we have:

\underset{p\in\mathbb{Z}}{\colim}F^{p}(FV\oplus FW)=\underset{p\in\mathbb{Z}}{\colim}F^{p}V\oplus F^{p}W\simeq\underset{p\in\mathbb{Z}}{\colim}F^{p}V\oplus\underset{p\in\mathbb{Z}}{\colim}F^{p}W\simeq V\oplus W

∎

Lemma B.1.13
.

The completion of a finite direct sum of filtered complexes is the finite direct sum of their completions:

\widehat{FV\oplus FW}\simeq\widehat{FV}\oplus\widehat{FW}

Proof.

Using Lemma
B.1.12
, we must compute the following limit:

\lim_{p}{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{V\oplus W}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.5714pt}{$\displaystyle{F^{p}V\oplus F^{p}W}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{V\oplus W}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{F^{p}V\oplus F^{p}W}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{V\oplus W}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.58528pt}{$\scriptstyle{F^{p}V\oplus F^{p}W}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{V\oplus W}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.83159pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{F^{p}V\oplus F^{p}W}$}}}\simeq\lim_{p}{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{V}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.5714pt}{$\displaystyle{F^{p}W}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{V}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{F^{p}W}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{V}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.58528pt}{$\scriptstyle{F^{p}W}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{V}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.83159pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{F^{p}W}$}}}\oplus{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{V}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.5714pt}{$\displaystyle{F^{p}W}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{V}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{F^{p}W}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{V}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.58528pt}{$\scriptstyle{F^{p}W}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{V}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.83159pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{F^{p}W}$}}}

Finite direct sums of complexes coincide with the finites products of the same complexes and therefore commute with limits:

\widehat{FV\oplus FW}\simeq\lim_{p}{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{V}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.5714pt}{$\displaystyle{F^{p}V}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{V}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{F^{p}V}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{V}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.58528pt}{$\scriptstyle{F^{p}V}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{V}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.83159pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{F^{p}V}$}}}\oplus{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{W}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.5714pt}{$\displaystyle{F^{p}W}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{W}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{F^{p}W}$}}{\raisebox{2.39166pt}{$\scriptstyle{W}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-2.58528pt}{$\scriptstyle{F^{p}W}$}}{\raisebox{1.70833pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{W}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.83159pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{F^{p}W}$}}}\simeq\widehat{FV}\oplus\widehat{FW}

It is not hard to see using the same manipulations that the complete filtration on

coincide with the natural complete filtration on

.
∎
