, we look at graded objects on
\mathscr{M}
, introducing a “weight grading” and then add a “mixed differential” that will increase that weight.

Definition C.1.1
.

We consider the category of
graded object in
\mathscr{M}
denoted by
\mathscr{M}^{\mathrm{gr}}
. Its objects are families
(V(p))_{p\in\mathbb{Z}}
of elements in
\mathscr{M}
and its morphism are the weight preserving morphisms.

Remark C.1.2
.

Graded objects in
\mathscr{M}
can be viewed as the functor category
\mathrm{Fun}(\mathbb{Z},\mathscr{M})
where the only morphisms in
\mathbb{Z}
are the identities. As such it comes with the projective model structure where fibration, cofibration and weak-equivalences are defined object-wise.

Remark C.1.3
.

\mathscr{M}^{\mathrm{gr}}
is clearly enriched in
\Mod_{k}^{\mathrm{gr}}
(since
\mathscr{M}
is enriched in
\Mod_{k}
) by taking the weight-wise enrichment
\mathscr{M}
.

Notation C.1.4
.

Take
E\in\mathscr{M}^{\mathrm{gr}}
.

–

The
weight
p
part of
E
is denoted
E(p)

–

We denote by
E((q))
the graded object whose weight grading is shifted by
q
such that:

E((q))(p):=E(p-q)

In particular, if
V
is concentrated in weight
0
, then
V((-p))
is concentrated in weight
p
.

–

A morphism
f:E\to E^{\prime}
is the data of a collection of morphisms in each weight denoted:

f_{p}:E(p)\to E^{\prime}(p)

Definition C.1.5
.

A
graded mixed complex

E
in
\mathscr{M}
is given by:

–

A graded object
E\in\mathscr{M}^{\mathrm{gr}}
.

–

A morphism called the
mixed differential
:

\epsilon:E\to E((-1))[-1]

such that
\epsilon^{2}=0
. This decomposes into maps:

\epsilon_{p}:E(p)\to E(p+1)[-1]

increasing the weight by
1
.

We denote by
\mathscr{M}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
the category of graded mixed complexes whose morphisms are weight-preserving morphisms that respect the mixed differentials.

From the assumptions on
\mathscr{M}
,
\mathscr{M}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
is enriched in
\Mod_{k}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
(denoted by
\underset{\mathscr{M}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}}{\iHom}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(-,-)
) but also in
\Mod_{k}
by defining:

\underset{\mathscr{M}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}}{\iHom}(E,F):=\ker\left(\epsilon:\underset{\mathscr{M}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}}{\iHom}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(E,F)(0)\to\underset{\mathscr{M}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}}{\iHom}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}(E,F)(1)[1]\right)

Lemma C.1.6
.

Denote
\mathbf{1}[\epsilon]:=\mathbf{1}\boxplus\mathbf{1}((1))[1]
the square zero extension of
\mathbf{1}
by
\mathbf{1}((1))[1]
viewed as a module over
\mathbf{1}
of weight
-1
and degree
-1
. Then a graded mixed complexes is exactly a graded
\mathbf{1}[\epsilon]
-module:

\mathscr{M}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}\simeq\Mod_{\mathbf{1}[\epsilon]}^{\mathrm{gr}}

Moreover the projection
\mathbf{1}[\epsilon]\to\mathbf{1}
induces an adjunction:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{M}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}\simeq\Mod_{\mathbf{1}[\epsilon]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Mod^{\mathrm{gr}}_{\mathbf{1}}\simeq\mathscr{M}^{\mathrm{gr}}}

Proof.

The projection
\mathbf{1}[\epsilon]\to\mathbf{1}
induces a forgetful functor
141
141

141

This functor forgets the mixed differential.
:

\Mod_{\mathbf{1}[\epsilon]}^{\mathrm{gr}}\to\Mod_{\mathbf{1}}^{\mathrm{gr}}\simeq\mathscr{M}^{\mathrm{gr}}

We get this way the collection of objects
(E(p))_{p\in\mathbb{Z}}
. The structure of
\mathbf{1}[\epsilon]\simeq\mathbf{1}\boxplus\mathbf{1}((1))[1]
-module on
E
is given by a product
\mathbf{1}((1))[1]\otimes E\to E
which is given by a map
\epsilon:E\to E((-1))[-1]
. The square-zero product is equivalent to saying that
\epsilon^{2}=0
.
∎

Proposition C.1.7
.

There is a model structure on
\mathscr{M}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
whose weak equivalences and cofibrations are defined through the forgetful functor:

\mathscr{U}_{\epsilon}:\mathscr{M}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}\to\mathscr{M}^{\mathrm{gr}}

Definition C.1.8
.

The hom-tensor adjunction (applied to the unit
\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{M}}
and using the
\Mod_{k}
enrichment) induces the following adjunctions:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Mod_{k}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{M}:\left|-\right|}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Mod_{k}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{M}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}:\left|-\right|}

where
\left|-\right|
are called
realization functors
. In particular, for
\mathscr{M}=\Mod_{k}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
the first adjunction defines a realization functor:

\left|-\right|:\Mod_{k}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}\to\Mod_{k}

Proposition C.1.9

(
[
CPT+17
, Proposition 1.5.1]
)
.

When
\mathscr{M}=\Mod_{k}
, then we have:

\left|-\right|:=\iHom(k,-)

This is the derived internal Hom which is computed by taking a cofibrant resolution
\tilde{k}\to k
in the projective model structure
142
142

142

The projective model structure is the model structure on graded mixed complexes induced by the projective model structure on
\Mod_{k}
.
. In particular we get:

\left|E\right|:=\iHom(\tilde{k},E)\simeq\prod_{p\geq 0}E(p)

where the right hand side is endowed with the total differential
D_{E}:=d_{E}+\epsilon
.

Remark C.1.10
.

It will turn out that graded mixed complexes can be seen as complete filtered objects (see Section
C.2
). Under this fully-faithful inclusion, denoted by
\tot
, we have that:

\left|E\right|:=\underset{\Mod^{\mathrm{cpl}}}{\iHom}(\tot(k),\tot(E))

where
\tot(k)
is in fact a fibrant cofibrant complete filtered object such that
F^{p}k=k
if
p\geq 0
and
0
otherwise. Then we can also use Definition
C.1.12
, Corollary
C.1.13
and Remark
B.1.4
to prove the proposition.

This avoids the difficulty of taking a cofibrant replacement for
k
.

Remark C.1.11
.

Similarly, if
\tilde{k}((-q))\to k((-q))
is a cofibrant resolution we we can define:

F^{p}\left|E\right|:=\iHom(k((-q)),E)\simeq\prod_{p\geq q}E(p)

where the right hand side is again endowed with the total differential
D_{E}=d_{E}+\epsilon
. As the notation suggests this define a filtration on
\left|E\right|
which coincide with the natural filtration by taking the Hom functor from Remark
C.1.10
but enriched in complete filtered objects.

Definition C.1.12
.

First observe that the derived hom gives us for all
q\in\mathbb{Z}
:

\Hom(k((-q)),k((-q-1)))\simeq k

Picking
1\in k
corresponds to taking a collection of maps
k((-q))\to k((-q-1))
.
They induce, for all
p\in\mathbb{Z}
, the following maps:

F^{p+1}\left|E\right|\to F^{p}\left|E\right|

defining a filtered object whose colimit is
\left|E\right|
itself. This filtration is complete and we denote by
\tot(E)
this filtered object, which defines a functor:

\tot:\Mod_{k}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}\to\Mod_{k}^{\mathrm{cpl}}

This generalizes the functor of Construction
B.1.8
.

Corollary C.1.13
.

If
E\in\Mod_{k}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
is non-negatively weighted, then we have:

\colim\tot(E)\simeq\left|E\right|

Remark C.1.14
.

In general
\colim\circ\tot
is called the
Tate realization
of
E
(see
[
CPT+17
, Definition 1.5.2]
).

We have seen in Example
A.1.7
that if
\mathscr{M}
is a good model category then
\mathscr{M}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
is also a good model category and therefore its category of commutative monoids has a natural model structure, and modules over those also form good model categories (see Section
A.1
).

Notation C.1.15
.

We denote by
\mathrm{cdga}_{\mathscr{M}}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
the category of commutative monoid in
\mathscr{M}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
.

Given
A\in\mathrm{cdga}_{\mathscr{M}}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
, we denote by
\Mod_{A}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
the category of commutative monoid in
\mathscr{M}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
.

C.2.
Weak Graded Mixed and Complete Filtered Objects

We observed thanks to Definition
C.1.12
that graded mixed complexes give complete filtered object. But the functor
\tot
is not an equivalence and its essential image is given by the filtered objects whose differential has a weight decomposition concentrated in weight
0
and
1
.

If the following we will define a notion of
weak
graded mixed complex whose mixed differential increases the weight by an arbitrary degree, so that the complete filtered realization of those will recover all complete filtered objects.

Definition C.2.1

(
[
CCN21
, Definition 2.23]
)
.

A
weak graded mixed complex in
\mathscr{M}
is a weight graded complex
E\in\mathscr{M}^{\mathrm{gr}}
equipped with maps in
\mathscr{M}
of weight
k
and degree
1
for all
k\geq 1
:

\delta_{k}:E\to E((-k))[-1]

such that:

\left(d+\sum_{k\geq 1}\delta_{k}\right)^{2}=0

with
d
the differential on
E
.

This condition can be rephrased as:

d\circ\delta_{k}+\delta_{k}\circ d+\sum\limits_{i+j=k}\delta_{i}\circ\delta_{j}=0

We denote by
\mathscr{M}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
the category of graded mixed complexes whose morphisms are morphisms of graded objects that commute with
\delta_{k}
.

We have seen in Lemma
C.1.6
that graded mixed complexes are modules over
\mathbf{1}[\epsilon]
. It turns out that weak graded mixed complexes are module over a
cofibrant resolution
of
\mathbf{1}[\epsilon]
.

Lemma C.2.2
.

Consider
\mathbf{1}[\epsilon_{i}\ |\ i\geq 1]
the semi-free commutative monoid in
\mathscr{M}
generated by
\epsilon_{i}
in degree
1
and weight
i
with differential given, for all
k\geq 1
, by:

\delta(\epsilon_{k})=-\sum_{i+j=k}\epsilon_{i}\epsilon_{j}

Then this is a quasi-free resolution of
\mathbf{1}[\epsilon]
.

Lemma C.2.3
.

The category of weak graded mixed complexes is equivalent to the category of graded modules over
\mathbf{1}[\epsilon_{i}\ |\ i\geq 1]
.

Proof.

The proof is essentially an adaptation of the proof of Lemma
C.1.6
.
∎

Remark C.2.4
.

This description of weak graded mixed complexes makes it a good model category as it is a category of modules over the good model category
\mathscr{M}^{\mathrm{gr}}
.

Corollary C.2.5
.

The inclusion of strict graded mixed complexes in weak graded mixed complexes is an equivalence:

\mathscr{M}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}\simeq\Mod_{\mathbf{1}[\epsilon]}^{\mathrm{gr}}\to\Mod_{\mathbf{1}[\epsilon_{i}\ |\ i\geq 1]}^{\mathrm{gr}}\simeq\mathscr{M}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}

This equivalence is part of the extension-restriction of scalars adjunction associated to the weak equivalence
\mathbf{1}[\epsilon_{i}\ |\ i\geq 1]\to\mathbf{1}[\epsilon]
. Therefore this is a Quillen equivalence thanks to Proposition
A.1.4
.

In a similar way to homotopy algebraic structures (such as
L_{\infty}
-algebras or algebroids for example), weak graded mixed complexes come equipped with a notion of
\infty
-morphism between weak graded mixed objects.

Definition C.2.6
.

An
\infty
-morphism between weak graded mixed complexes
E
and
E^{\prime}
is the data of a collection of maps
\phi_{k}:E\to E^{\prime}
of degree
0
and weight
k
such that for all
k\geq 0
we have:

\sum_{i+j=k}(\epsilon_{i}\phi_{j}+\phi_{i}\epsilon_{j})=0

where
\epsilon_{0}=d
by convention. We denote by
\mathscr{M}_{\infty}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
the category of weak graded mixed complexes with the
\infty
-morphisms.

Remark C.2.7
.

From
[
CCN21
, Remark 2.26]
,
\mathscr{M}_{\infty}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
has almost a model structure and the inclusion
\mathscr{M}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}\to\mathscr{M}_{\infty}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}
induces an equivalence between the
\infty
-categories obtained after localizing at the weak-equivalences.

The totalization functor of Construction
B.1.8
and Definition
C.1.12
can be extended to an equivalence from weak graded mixed complexes.

Proposition C.2.8

(
[
CCN21
, Proposition 2.27]
)
.

The functor:

\tot:\Mod_{k}^{h\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}\to\Mod_{k}^{\mathrm{cpl}}

sending
E
to the complete filtered cdga whose underlying filtered graded module is given by Construction
B.1.8
to which we add the total differential
D=d+\sum_{k\geq 1}\epsilon_{k}
, induces an equivalence of
\infty
-categories.

Remark C.2.9
.

The realization functor of Definition
C.1.8
extends to weak graded mixed complexes. Moreover, if
\mathscr{M}=\Mod_{k}
, we get an analogue of Proposition
C.1.9
expressing the realization as:

\left|E\right|\simeq\prod_{p\geq 0}E(p)

together with the total differential
D_{E}=d_{E}+\epsilon_{1}+\epsilon_{2}+\cdots
.

Lemma C.2.10
.

If
E
is a non-negatively weighted weak graded mixed object, then:

\colim\tot(E)\simeq\left|E\right|

Proof.

This is a direct consequence of Remark
C.2.9
.
∎

Lemma C.2.11
.

We have a commutative diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Mod_{k}^{\epsilon-\mathrm{gr}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Mod_{k}^{\mathrm{cpl}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Mod_{k}^{\mathrm{gr}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tot}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Forget}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Gr}}

where
\mathrm{Forget}
is the functor that forgets the mixed differentials
\epsilon_{i}
for
i\geq 1
induced by the scalar extension along
\mathbf{1}[\epsilon_{i}\ |\ i\geq 1]\to\mathbf{1}
. It is similar to the adjunction in Lemma
C.1.6
.

Appendix D
Formal Moduli Problem and Koszul Duality Context

This section aims to describe the notion of formal moduli problems. In Section
3.1
, we talk about the formal moduli problems under a base corresponding to a Lie algebroid. It is similar to the well known correspondence between Lie algebras and (commutative) formal moduli problems. We are going to present the general theory behind such correspondences and the essential definitions and tools involved to understand them.

D.1.
Formal Moduli Problems

This section is about axiomatizing the notion of deformation functors. The idea is that deformations can be understood as functors sending a class of “small parameter objects” called “Artinian”, to a space of deformations along such objects. For example such a deformation functor assigns for each choice of Artinian local algebra
A
an
\infty
-groupoid of deformations of
X
along
\mathbf{Spec}(A)
. As the category of local Artinian algebras and the notion of “infinitesimal” object will play an important role, we will start, following
[
Lur11
]
,
[
CG18
]
and
[
CCN20
]
, by defining a general framework in which we can speak of deformations along such objects.

D.1.1.
Artinian and small algebras in a deformation context

The general idea behind Artinian algebras is to have a class of algebras considered “small” so that deforming along those algebras amounts to consider
infinitesimal
deformations, that is, looking at the formal neighborhood of what we want to deform. We will always assume that our ambient category
\mathscr{A}
, in which we will define the notion of Artinian object, has a terminal object. This leads to the general framework of deformation context:

Definition D.1.1

(
[
Lur11
, Definition 1.1.3]
)
.

A
deformation context
is a pair
\left(\mathscr{A},\{E_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}\right)
where
\mathscr{A}
is a presentable
143
143

143

\mathscr{A}
is presentable if it is generated by a small set of “small objects” under homotopy colimits.

\infty
-category and
\{E_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}
is a set of objects in
\mathbf{Stab}(\mathscr{A})
144
144

144

Recall that objects in
\mathbf{Stab}(\mathscr{A})
correspond to spectrum objects on
\mathscr{A}_{*}
, i.e., a sequence
E=(\cdots,a_{2},a_{1},a_{0},a_{-1},\cdots)
of pointed objects of
\mathscr{A}
, such that
a_{i}
is equivalent to the loop space
\Omega a_{i+1}
. For
n\geq 0
, we denote
\Omega^{\infty-n}E=a_{n}
.
, the stabilization of
\mathscr{A}
.

Intuitively,
\{E_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}
correspond to the first-order objects we want to deform along. To compare with the classical picture, we take
\mathscr{A}
to be the category of algebras. Then first order deformation are deformations along
k[\epsilon]
, and we take it as the underlying object of the spectrum
E=(\cdots,k[\epsilon_{2}],k[\epsilon_{1}],k[\epsilon_{0}],\cdots)
, where
k[\epsilon_{i}]
is the
2
-dimensional
k
-augmented algebra with
\left|\epsilon_{i}\right|=-i
and
\epsilon_{i}^{2}=0
.

In our situation, the family
\{E_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}
will always contains only a single spectrum object. Here are some other examples of deformation contexts.

Example D.1.2
.

–

For
\mathscr{A}=\Mod_{A}
(with
A\in\mathrm{cdga}
), we can defined the deformation context
\left(\Mod_{A},\{E\}\right)
with only one spectrum object (
[
CG18
, Example 2.2]
):

E=\left(A\boxplus A[n]\right)_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}

–

Given
A\in\mathrm{cdga}
, we consider
\mathscr{A}=\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}
and and we can define the following deformation context
145
145

145

Note that
\mathbf{Stab}(\mathrm{cdga}_{/A})\simeq\mathbf{Stab}(\mathrm{cdga}_{A//A})\simeq\Mod_{A}
.
:

\left(\mathrm{cdga}_{/A},\{E=\left(A\boxplus A[n]\right)_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\}\right)

where
A\boxplus A[n]
is the square zero extension of
A
by
A[n]
(
[
CG18
, Remark 2.5]
). We will call this deformation context
\mathscr{A}_{/A}
.

From a deformation context, we can define the notion of “small” objects and morphisms using
\Omega^{\infty-n}E_{\alpha}
as building blocks.

Definition D.1.3

(
[
Lur11
, Definition 1.1.14]
)
.

Given a deformation context
\left(\mathscr{A},\{E_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in T}\right)
we say that:

–

A morphism
f:B\rightarrow B^{\prime}
is called
elementary
if it is given by a pullback of the form:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\star}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega^{\infty-n}(E_{\alpha})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

for some
\alpha\in T
and
n\geq 1
.

–

A morphism
f:B\rightarrow B^{\prime}
is called
small
if it is a finite composition of elementary morphisms.

–

An object
B\in\mathscr{A}
is called
Artinian
, if the morphism
\mathscr{A}\rightarrow\star
is small
146
146

146

Artinian objects can be though as “small” objects. In fact they are called “small” in
[
Lur11
]
.
. We denote by
\mathbf{Art}_{\mathscr{A}}
the full sub-category of
\mathscr{A}
given by small objects.

Example D.1.4
.

Going back to the example of
A
-augmented algebras, we have
\Omega^{\infty-n}E=A\boxplus A[n]
so that in order to compute the homotopy pullback of
\star\to\Omega^{\infty-n}E
, one can replace the point
\star=A
by the algebra
A\boxplus(A[n]\oplus A[n-1])
(notice that
n\geq 1
), with differential induced by the identity
A[n]\to A[n-1]
.

The strict pullback exhibits therefore
B
as a square zero extension of
B^{\prime}
along
A[n-1]
.

We will now specialize these definitions to the deformation contexts we are interested in, namely
\mathscr{A}_{/A}
.

Proposition D.1.5
.

The category
\mathbf{Art}_{/A}
is the smallest full sub-category of
\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}
such that:

–

A\boxplus A[n]\in\mathbf{Art}_{/A}
for all
n\geq 0

–

For any
B\in\mathbf{Art}_{/A}
and any map
B\rightarrow A\boxplus A[n]
with
n\geq 1
, the homotopy pullback
B\times_{A\boxplus A[n]}A
is also Artinian:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B\times_{A\boxplus A[n]}A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxplus A[n]}

Proof.

By definition, we have that
A\boxplus A[n]
is Artinian since the map
A\boxplus A[n]\rightarrow A
is elementary, given by the pullback:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxplus A[n]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\boxplus A[n+1]}

Moreover, the map
B\times_{A\boxplus A[n]}A\rightarrow B
is elementary, therefore if
B
is Artinian, then the composition
B\times_{A\boxplus A[n]}A\rightarrow B\rightarrow 0
is small as well. Therefore
\mathscr{A}_{/A}
satisfies the properties given in the proposition. It is the smallest such category because any Artinian object can be obtained by definition from some
A\boxplus A[n]
in finitely many pullbacks along
A\rightarrow A\boxplus A[n]
for
n\geq 1
.
∎

D.1.2.
Formal moduli problems

The main idea is that a “formal moduli problem” is a functor sending
B
to an
\infty
-groupoid of deformations. For example, given an object
X
, we will be interested in studying the functor that sends an Artinian object
A
to the “space of all deformations” of
X
along
A
.

Definition D.1.6

(
[

, Definition 1.1.14]
)
.

\left(\mathscr{A},\{E_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in T}\right)

–

Deformations along the point (terminal object) are trivial:

Definition D.1.7
.

For any
B\in\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}
the following functor is a formal moduli problem:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B):\mathbf{Art}_{/A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Gpd}_{\infty}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\qquad\qquad C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underset{\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}}{\Map}\left(B,C\right)}

Moreover we get a functor
\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}\rightarrow\FMP_{A}
sending
B
to
\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)
.

\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)
is called the
formal spectrum
of
B
over
A
.

Proposition D.1.8
.

Following
[
Lur11
, Lemma 1.1.20]
, a morphism
f:B\rightarrow C
between Artinian algebras,
B,C\in\mathbf{Art}_{/A}
is small if and only if it induces a surjection of commutative rings
H^{0}(B)\rightarrow H^{0}(C)
. Therefore the second condition of Definition
D.1.6
can be rephrased as follows:

Any pullback in
\mathbf{Art}_{/A}
such that
H^{0}(B)\rightarrow H^{0}(C)
or
H^{0}(B^{\prime})\rightarrow H^{0}(C)
is surjective is sent to a pullback in
\mathbf{Gpd}_{\infty}

It recovers the classical Schlessinger condition (see
[

]
).

It is an old heuristic that (commutative) deformation problems (over
k
) are classified by Lie algebras and it is due to a kind of duality (Koszul duality context) that is in fact related to the Koszul duality of the Lie and commutative operads (see
[
CCN20
]
). This heuristic is formalized by the following theorem:

Theorem D.1.9

(See
[
Lur11
]
and
[
Pri10
]
)
.

There is an equivalence of
\infty
-categories:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{MC}\colon\mathbf{Alg}_{\mathbf{Lie}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\FMP\colon\mathbb{T}[-1]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sim}

Warning D.1.10
.

For
\mathfrak{g}
a Lie algebra, the one thinks of
\mathbf{MC}
as the functor assigning to an Artinian algebra
A
the space space of Maurer--Cartan elements
148
148

148

The space of Maurer–Cartan elements of a Lie algebra
\mathfrak{g}
is the space of elements
x\in\mathfrak{g}
satisfying the Maurer–Cartan equation:

dx+\frac{1}{2}[x,x]=0

. Unfortunately, this space does not generally define a formal moduli problem, but is not far from doing so. Indeed, on finite dimensional
\mathfrak{g}
, the Maurer–Cartan functor gives the correct functor. The functor
\mathbf{MC}
generalizes the Maurer–Cartan functor in order to circumvent this problem.

D.2.
Formal Moduli Problems and Koszul Duality

The goal of this section is to make sensee of the generalization of Theorem
D.1.9
to an arbitrary Koszul duality context while discussing the specific example of formal moduli problem under
\mathbf{Spec}(A)
and Lie algebroids.

D.2.1.
Tangent complex of a formal moduli problem

The goal of this section is to explain that the algebra controlling a given formal moduli problem is in some sens the “tangent” of this formal moduli problem. This explains why first-order deformations and obstructions to lifting deformations are controlled by the tangent complex.

To motivate the following definition, we will start by explaining the example of the formal spectrum (Definition
D.1.7
) of an
A
-augmented commutative algebra
B
. We have that

\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)(C)=\underset{\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}}{\Map}\left(B,C\right)

In the case of first order deformations,
C=A[\epsilon]
, this mapping space corresponds to the tangent complex of
\mathrm{Spec}(B)
at the point
f:\mathbf{Spec}(A)\rightarrow\mathbf{Spec}(B)
.
It is shown in
[
TV08
, Proposition 1.4.1.6]
that the geometric realization of connective truncation of
\mathbb{T}_{B,f}\simeq f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{B}
is given by:

(17)

\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)(A\boxplus A[n])\simeq\underset{\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}}{\Map}(B,A\boxplus A[n])\simeq\underset{A}{\Map}(A,f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{B}[n])\simeq\left|f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{B}[n]\right|

Indeed the map
f:B\to A
induces a map:

\underset{\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}}{\Map}\left(A,A\boxplus M\right)\to\underset{\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}}{\Map}\left(B,A\boxplus M\right)\simeq\underset{\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}}{\Map}\left(B,B\boxplus f_{*}M\right)

The right hand side is represented by
f^{*}\mathbb{L}_{B}
and with
M=A
we recover the claim.

This motivates the definition of the ‘‘tangent’’ as the evaluation of the formal moduli problem functor at all ‘‘first-order elements’’
149
149

149

Recall that such “first-order” objects correspond to the elements in
\{\Omega^{\infty-n}(E_{\alpha})\}_{\alpha\in T,n\in\mathbb{N}}
, for example the square zero extensions
A\boxplus A[n]
in the case of
A
-augmented algebras.
of a given deformation context.

Definition D.2.1

(Tangent Functor,
[
Lur11
, Section 1.2]
)
.

Given a deformation context
\left(\mathscr{A},\{E_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}\right)
, we define
the tangent complex
of a formal moduli problem
F
at
\alpha
to be the spectrum object:

F(E_{\alpha})\in\mathbf{Sp}\coloneqq\mathbf{Stab}(\mathbf{sSet})

which we denote
150
150

150

This notation is by analogy to the tangent complex but is a priori only a (collection of) spectrum objects. However, we will see that
\mathbb{T}_{F}
can be “represented” by an actual tangent complex.

\mathbb{T}_{F}
in case there is only a single
\alpha\in T
.

This spectrum object verifies
\Omega^{\infty-n}F(E_{\alpha})\simeq F(\Omega^{\infty-n}E_{\alpha})
for all
n\geq 0
(see
[
Lur11
, Remark 1.2.7]
). Notice that the tangent complex
\mathbb{T}_{F}
is not actually a cochain complex but rather only a spectrum object a priori. These two categories are related by the composition:

(18)

\Mod_{A}\mathrel{{\mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits}}\Mod_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathrel{{\mathop{\simeq}\limits}}\mathbf{Stab}(\mathbf{sAb})\mathrel{{\mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits}}\mathbf{Stab}(\mathbf{sSet})=\mathbf{Sp}

Proposition D.2.2

(
[
CCN20
, Lemma 2.15]
)
.

A formal moduli problem
F\in\FMP_{A}
has a unique pre-image in
\Mod_{A}
under the functor (
18
), which we also denote by
\mathbb{T}_{F}
.

Moreover for any
n\geq 0
, we have an equivalence:

\underset{\Mod_{A}}{\Map}\left(A[-n],\mathbb{T}_{F}\right)\simeq F(A\boxplus A[n])

It turns out that the associated spectrum object to
f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{B}
(given by the composition (
18
)) coincides with the spectrum object given by the collection of
\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)(A\boxplus A[n])
so that the cotangent complex
f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{B}
is the representative of tangent functor
\mathbb{T}_{\mathbf{Spf}_{A}(B)}
, thanks to the equivalence (
17
).

D.2.2.
Koszul Duality Context

Going back again to the setting of a general deformation context
\mathscr{A}
, we are looking to identify an
\infty
-category of algebraic objects
\mathscr{B}
to
\FMP_{\mathscr{A}}
.

The formal spectrum
\mathbf{Spf}
from in Definition
D.1.7
is a functorial way to construct formal moduli problems out of objects of
\mathscr{A}
.
Assuming the existence of the desired equivalence, we could construct a functor:

\mathfrak{D}\colon\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{op}}\mathrel{{\mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits}}\FMP_{\mathscr{A}}\mathrel{{\mathop{\to}\limits}}\mathscr{B}.

This functor should be interpreted as a “weak duality” functor, which is not an equivalence, but at least its restriction to Artinian objects should behave as an equivalence into a subcategory of
\mathscr{B}
given by “good” objects.

In this section, we introduce the notion of Koszul duality context as the appropriate axiomatic framework that enables us to obtain the desired equivalence, which we give with Theorem
D.2.11
.

Definition D.2.3

(Dual Deformation Context,
[
CG18
, Definition 2.11]
)
.

A pair
\left(\mathscr{B},\{F_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in T}\right)
is called a
dual deformation context
if
\mathscr{B}
is a presentable
\infty
-category and
\mathscr{F}_{\alpha}\in\mathbf{Stab}(\mathscr{B}^{\mathrm{op}})
.

We say that an object (resp. morphism) of
\mathscr{B}
is
good
if it is Artinian when considered in
\left(\mathscr{B}^{\mathrm{op}},\{F_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in T}\right)
151
151

151

Here
\left(\mathscr{B}^{\mathrm{op}},\{F_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in T}\right)
is generally not a deformation context since
\mathscr{B}^{\mathrm{op}}
will in general not be presentable. However the definition of Artinian object still makes sensee in
\mathscr{B}^{\mathrm{op}}
.
. We denote by
\mathscr{B}^{\mathrm{gd}}
the full sub-category of good objects of
\mathscr{B}
.

Example D.2.4
.

–

If
A\in\mathrm{cdga}
. Then
\left(\Mod_{A},\left(A[n]\right)_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\right)
is a deformation context and since taking the opposite category exchanges the suspension and desuspension functor, we get the dual deformation context
\left(\Mod_{A},\left(A[-n]\right)_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\right)
.

When
A
is bounded and concentrated in non-positive degrees,
[
CG18
, Lemma 2.16]
tells us that an element
M\in\Mod_{A}
in this dual deformation context is good if it is perfect and cohomologically concentrated in positive degrees (see also
[
CG18
, Remark 2.17]
)

–

There is a dual deformation context:

\left(\mathrm{LieAlgd}_{A},\{\mathrm{Free}(0:A[-n]\to\mathbb{T}_{A})\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\right)

Note that every good Lie algebroid have underlying cofibrant
A
-module and is finitely generated (when forgetting the differential) over
\mathbb{T}_{A}
(see
[
Nui19b
, Lemma 6.10]
).

Definition D.2.5

(Koszul Duality Context,
[
CG18
, Definition 2.18]
)
.

A
weak Koszul duality context
is the data of:

–

A deformation context
\left(\mathscr{A},\{E_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in T}\right)

–

A dual deformation context
\left(\mathscr{B},\{F_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in T}\right)

–

An adjunction:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{D}:\mathscr{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{B}^{\mathrm{op}}:\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}}

such that for all
n\geq 0
, there is an equivalence
\Omega^{\infty-n}E_{\alpha}\simeq\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}\left(\Omega^{\infty-n}F_{\alpha}\right)
.

It is called a
Koszul Duality
context if the following hold:

(1)

for every object
B\in\mathscr{B}^{\mathrm{gd}}
, the counit morphism
\mathfrak{D}\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}A\rightarrow A
is an equivalence.

(2)

For each
\alpha
, the functor

\varTheta_{\alpha}:\mathscr{B}\rightarrow\mathbf{Sp}

sending
B\in\mathscr{B}
to the spectrum object given by:

\left(\Map_{\mathscr{B}}(\Omega^{\infty-n}E_{\alpha},B)\right)_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\in\mathbf{Sp}

is conservative and preserves sifted colimits.

Remark D.2.6
.

A weak Koszul duality context together with condition (1) gives us a weak deformation theory according to the terminology of Lurie,
[
Lur11
, Definition 1.3.1]
. A Koszul duality context is an example of a
deformation theory
according to
[
Lur11
, Definition 1.3.9]
.

Example D.2.7
.

Let
A\in\mathrm{cdga}^{\mathrm{\leq 0}}
bounded. We have a Koszul duality context given by the dualization (
[
CG18
, Example 2.20]
):

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(-)^{\vee}:\left(\Mod_{A},\left(A[n]\right)_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\right)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\left(\Mod_{A}^{\mathrm{op}},\left(A[-n]\right)_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\right):(-)^{\vee}}

Example D.2.8

(
[
CG18
, Theorem 3.9]
and
[
Nui19b
]
)
.

With the (dual) deformation context of Examples
D.1.2
and
D.2.4
, if
A
is cofibrant non-positively graded, almost finitely presented and eventually coconnective (in other words satisfies Assumption
3.2.2
), then we have a Koszul duality context:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{CE}:\mathrm{LieAlgd}_{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\left(\mathrm{cdga}_{/A}\right)^{\mathrm{op}}:\mathfrak{D}}

Proposition D.2.9

(
[
CG18
, Proposition 2.22]
)
.

Given a Koszul duality context (with the same notations as in Definition
D.2.5
), we have the following:

–

\mathfrak{D}\left(\Omega^{\infty-n}E\right)\simeq\Omega^{\infty-n}F
for all
n\geq 0
.

–

For every Artinian object
A\in\mathbf{Art}_{\mathscr{A}}
, the unit map
A\rightarrow\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}\mathfrak{D}A
is an equivalence.

–

The adjunction
\mathfrak{D}\dashv\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}
induces an equivalence:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{D}:\mathbf{Art}_{\mathscr{A}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\left(\mathscr{B}^{\mathrm{gd}}\right)^{\mathrm{op}}:\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}}

–

If
M\in\mathbf{Art}_{\mathscr{A}}
and
f\colon A\rightarrow B
is a small morphism in
\mathscr{A}
then
\mathfrak{D}
sends the pullback diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

to a pullback diagram.

Corollary D.2.10
.

Given a Koszul duality context, we can construct the following functor:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi:\mathscr{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Fun}\left(\mathscr{B}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathbf{Gpd}_{\infty}\right)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Fun}\left(\mathscr{A},\mathbf{Gpd}_{\infty}\right)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\circ\mathfrak{D}}

Then
\psi
factor through
\FMP(\mathscr{A},\{E_{\alpha}\})
and we get a map:

\Psi:\mathscr{B}\rightarrow\FMP(\mathscr{A},\{E_{\alpha}\})

It turns out that the definition of Koszul duality context ensures that the map
\Psi:\mathscr{B}\rightarrow\FMP(\mathscr{A},\{E_{\alpha}\})
is in fact an equivalence.

Theorem D.2.11

(
[
CG18
, Theorem 2.33]
or
[
Lur11
, Theorem 1.3.12]
)
.

Given a Koszul duality context as above, the functor
\Psi
is an equivalence:

\Psi:\mathscr{B}\rightarrow\FMP(\mathscr{A},\{E_{\alpha}\})

Proposition D.2.12

(
[
CG18
, Proposition 2.36]
)
.

We have the following commutative diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\FMP\left(\mathscr{A},\{E_{\alpha}\}\right)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{Sp}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varTheta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T}

Remark D.2.13
.

This diagram shows that
TF
is equivalent to
\varTheta(\mathbb{T}_{F})
with
\mathbb{T}_{F}\in\mathscr{B}
so that this tangent functor has more structure that being just a spectrum object. Moreover when
\mathscr{A}=\mathscr{A}_{/A}
and
F=\mathbf{Spf}(B)
then
\mathbb{T}_{F}=f^{*}\mathbb{T}_{B}
with
f:B\to A
(see Lemma
1.3.27
).
